articles.title: NLEx completes dredging of Tulaoc River section
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Dredging of the NLEx section of the Tulaoc River is complete, and as of Sept. 8, NLEx Corp. reports there is no more pooling of rainwater on the expressway shoulder. The company…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Dredging of the NLEx section of the Tulaoc River is complete, and as of Sept. 8, NLEx Corp. reports there is no more pooling of rainwater on the expressway shoulder.

The company added that the work is continuing upstream from the Manila Bay outfall toward Tulaoc and the expressway, carried out with government and private sector partners. Deployment upstream was not possible during the flooding itself, when standing water blocked truck access.
Sheet piles installed along the alignment to keep water out of the NLEx system are being monitored through the rainfall now forecast.

Dredging is one part of the flood mitigation measures on the corridor. A mobile pumping unit is deployed at the kilometer 56 marker, with L-type flood barriers and modular mesh-and-liner units along the alignment and crews pre-positioned at Meycauayan, Paso de Blas, San Fernando and Balintawak.

Toll relief for journeys the expressway did not deliver—P113 for Class 1, P281 for Class 2 and P338 for Class 3—was credited to motorists’ RFID accounts the following day, with no claim form required.

“Our section of the river is dredged, and there is no water on the shoulder,” NLEx Corp. said. “The work is moving upstream from the bay, and we are watching the sheet piles perform through the next rainfall.” /cb

articles.title: DSWD gets lower budget for 4Ps, AICS in 2027 NEP
articles.summary: Two of the flagship programs of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) will get budget cuts under the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 11:28pm
Two of the flagship programs of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) will get budget cuts under the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

According to a "24 Oras" report by Tina Panganiban-Perez, the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) was allocated P99.1 billion in 2027 to cover 3.5 million households. For 2026, DSWD received P112.9 billion for 4.4 million households.
For 2025, the poverty threshold—the minimum income required for a family to meet its basic food and non-food needs—was set at a national average of P14,634 per month, up from P13,873 in 2023.
This means a family whose monthly income falls below the threshold is considered poor.
On a daily basis, the poverty threshold is equivalent to a family income of about P487.
For a typical family of five, this translates to about P97 per person per day.
Poor and near-poor families, or those earning 10 percent higher than the poverty threshold, are among the beneficiaries of the 4Ps program.
But DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian said near-poor families should include those earning 25 percent above the poverty threshold.

"We met with PSA (Philippine Statistics Authority) yesterday. It is high time to revisit the statistical definition of the near poor so that it is not only limited to 10% above the poverty threshold but up to 25% above the threshold because these are households with the same characteristic of poor but just above the poverty line," Gatchalian explained.
Meanwhile, the budget for the social pension of indigent senior citizens also suffered a slight cut, from P51.8 billion this year to P51.8 billion in the 2027 NEP.
Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS), which has P63.9 billion in 2026, got a drastic cut under the 2027 NEP at P33 billion.
Several lawmakers raised concern about the possibility of the AICS fund being used for politics.

"Iyong AICS naman, may proseso siyang pinagdaraanan. Anybody can refer, pero dadaan pa rin yan sa masusing pagsusuri at pag-aaral ng ating mga social worker. The vetting process is there. That's our safety net," he said.
The DSWD also sought additional budget for its Quick Response Fund (QRF) for calamities. From P3 billion in 2026, the QRF was allocated only P1 billion in 2027. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
articles.summary: Médecins Sans Frontières is urging world leaders to increase funding to help the millions who need aid.

blocks.text: Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned.
Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said.
MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action.

The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance.
MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance.
According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year.
"War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan.

"MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours."
This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment.

"After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years.
Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year.
In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said.
According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing.

It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June.
As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city.
In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10.
According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children.
"If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said.
At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said.
In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide.
According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger".
The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war.

Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.

articles.title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
articles.summary: Palestinians strongly back a ban on settlement goods, but Israel's government says it is a "big mistake".

blocks.text: Dates are among the agricultural products commonly exported from Israeli settlements in the West Bank
ByYolande Knell
Middle East correspondent
Juicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank.
This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law.

The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements.
Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's president says it is a "grave miscalculation".
Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting".
Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods.

"As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Settler farmer Avigdor Arbel does not believe Israel will ever give up the Jordan Valley

blocks.text: Settler farmer Avigdor Arbel does not believe Israel will ever give up the Jordan Valley

West Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution.
At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high".

With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities.

In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years.
Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant".

Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported.
In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful".
As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories".
"I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Jordan Valley is a fertile strip of land that comprises nearly 30% of the West Bank

blocks.text: The Jordan Valley is a fertile strip of land that comprises nearly 30% of the West Bank
Medjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley.

"These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho.

Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive.
Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank.
Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs.
Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs.
The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure.

This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK.
Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth.
"Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says.
"They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim says half his date farms have no fruit because of a water shortage

blocks.text: Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim says half his date farms have no fruit because of a water shortage

Israeli-state support for settlements, as well as their relatively easy access to global markets, means that Palestinian farmers struggle to compete. Palestinian businesses face greater restrictions and costs to export across Israeli-controlled borders.

Palestinians want the wide swathe of fertile land in the Jordan Valley - along the West Bank's border with Jordan - as part of their own hoped-for future state, along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
However, Avigdor Arbel, the settler date farmer, does not believe that his country will ever give up the Jordan Valley. He has lived there since the 1970s.

Within years of Israel's capture of the West Bank from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East War, the Israeli government began encouraging its citizens to move to this area to counter what it saw as the security risk along the border.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, not including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, alongside three million Palestinians.
There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements, formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to the Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now.
Current UK and EU laws require labels for settlement goods. Agricultural produce commonly exported includes mangoes, avocados, herbs and grapes.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israeli settlers diverted a Palestinian village's water to fill a pool in the Jordan Valley this summer

blocks.text: Israeli settlers diverted a Palestinian village's water to fill a pool in the Jordan Valley this summer
There have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced.

A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders.

However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned.
"A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says.

"I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot believes sanctions could help curb settlement growth

blocks.text: Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot believes sanctions could help curb settlement growth
Speaking just before the UK move was announced, Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it would amount to "gross interference" in Israel's upcoming elections, due in late October.
"I believe it will prove to be a grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history," he warned.
Israel's government is threatening retaliation for any UK ban on settlement goods.

"If Britain acts against the State of Israel, the State of Israel will act against Britain," the Israeli Foreign Secretary, Gideon Saar, told an Israeli podcast last week. When I approached him at a diplomatic event on Monday to ask for more details about which steps could be taken, he declined to answer.
Israel recently expelled two Dutch diplomats from a US-led centre in charge of co-ordinating the shaky Gaza ceasefire, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements.
Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium.
Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel.

articles.title: Flushing the toilet can release a ‘plume’ of breathable pathogens – and closing the lid won’t stop their escape
articles.summary:
New research shows turbulent flushes create toilet-generated aerosols that can transmit legionella, influenza and norovirus

  • Get our

blocks.text: Flushing toilets release particles into the “breathing zone” of adults and can remain suspended in the air for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found.
And closing the lid might not be enough to avoid a “plume” of potential pathogens.
Meanwhile, previous research has shown public toilets are an inescapable hotbed of microbes.
Flinders University researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, publishing the results in the Science of the Total Environment journal.
They found microbes from the water used for flushing or from contamination of the bowl ended up as aerosols, with more “turbulent” flushing releasing more particles.

That included bioaerosols – aerosols that contain biological material and can transmit pathogens including legionella, influenza and norovirus. There are differing reports about whether Covid spreads through toilet aerosols.

The researchers found higher levels of aerosols in the water and higher levels of turbulence during the flush increased the volume of particles suspended in the air, but the effects of bathroom ventilation and whether the lid was up or down were unclear.
Despite that, lead author and PhD student Lira Adiyani said she would still recommend putting the lid down after using the toilet.
“Toilet flushing creates turbulence that can release aerosols into the surrounding air,” she said.
“Some studies detected these aerosols at adult breathing height, indicating a potential pathway for inhalation exposure.
“The more microbes present in the toilet, the more bioaerosols may be released. Therefore, larger flush volumes generally produce more aerosols.”
Adiyani said “based on the available evidence” she would still recommend closing the lid as a precautionary measure, “while recognising that it does not completely prevent aerosols from escaping”.

In the report, the researchers wrote that the effects of indoor aerosols had been “understudied” despite the risk of infection. This had “important implications for risk assessment, building design, and infection control in an era of water security pressures and emerging infectious diseases”, they wrote.
“Indoor aerosols influence air quality and human health as their small size allows them to penetrate deep into the respiratory tract when inhaled, providing a direct exposure pathway.”
Co-author, environmental health professor Harriet Whiley, said people didn’t have to be worried in their own homes, unless someone in the house was immunocompromised.
She said the team was working on “protecting the most vulnerable through good design” in places such as hospitals and aged care environments.
after newsletter promotion

They are increasingly concerned about “opportunistic pathogens” that can be present in water, particularly recycled or rainwater. “They don’t affect healthy people,” she said. “But if you’re immunocompromised you can get very sick, and it can be fatal.”
So it’s about getting “an effective flush with less volume and less turbulence”, she said.
Dr Lotti Tajouri, an associate professor in molecular genetics at Bond and Murdoch universities wasn’t involved in the research but warned bathroom dangers go well beyond the toilet.
His own research is particularly focused on public toilets and mobile phone use in toilets.
“As soon as you enter a toilet, consider everything contaminated,” he said.
The door will have microbes on it, as will the floor – so you should never put anything on it, he said. Then you might touch the lid, after which you flush with the lid up or down.
If it’s up, you get the “plume” effect, an “explosion or aerosols … you are literally sprayed [with]”.

Flushing with the lid down might limit your exposure to the plume, but depending on the cleanliness of the toilet, previous users have left microorganisms on every surface anyway. “The roof, the walls, the floor,” he said.

Then, you touch the toilet door again, before (hopefully) washing your hands. But you will probably touch the taps again, blow microorganisms around with the hairdryer, touch the exit door and then touch your phone.

“Studies show between 50% and 80% of people use mobile phones in the toilet. For younger generations it’s almost 100%,” he said. “They will contaminate their phones and fingers with fecal microorganisms – salmonella, campylobacter, all sorts of bacteria and viruses.
“The less contact you have, the better it is.”

articles.title: Organised crime driving illicit cigarette factory boom ‘in almost every EU state’
articles.summary: Bloc losing €13bn in revenue with one in 10 cigarettes illegal, watchdog reports

blocks.text: The illegal trade in tobacco is booming in the EU, according to a report by the bloc’s financial watchdog, with almost one in 10 cigarettes produced illicitly or smuggled, causing an estimated €13bn loss in tax revenue each year.

The European Court of Auditors (ECA) said in a report on Tuesday that the trade had “changed significantly” in recent years as smuggling, while still “a problem”, was overtaken by illicit manufacturing, which has increased dramatically in the bloc.

Organised crime gangs are moving production inside the EU “to shorten supply chains and get closer to consumers”, said the ECA’s Petri Sarvamaa. “Illegal production sites have now been detected in almost every EU member state.”

The ECA cited the example of a large-scale illicit cigarette factory in Belgium dismantled by police last year. It operated around the clock, with 50 workers running four production lines, each able to produce 1m cigarettes every hour.

During a raid on the largest illegal facility so far uncovered, in Spain, police seized 3m packs of cigarettes valued at €15m, five tonnes of raw tobacco worth €5m, and made 20 arrests. The factory’s products had been distributed across six EU countries.

“The scale is quite remarkable,” Sarvamaa said. “Last month French authorities dismantled a cross-border operation that had been supplying the city of Lille only since last December but had already made 120 deliveries of 7,500 packs each.”

The ECA report said such illicit cigarette factories, which usually operate for two- to four months, were using sophisticated equipment and employing experienced technicians to set up and maintain their machinery.

The organised crime groups that run them split production across multiple facilities and often locate them in border regions, tailoring their operations by producing specific brands for individual markets and even developing new tobacco products.

The damage goes beyond lost tax revenue. The trade “undermines public health policies by making tobacco products cheaper and more accessible, especially to young people”, Sarvamaa said. It also feeds organised crime and finances other illegal activities.

While, overall, tobacco consumption has continued to fall across the EU, the quantity of illicit tobacco products has risen steadily, reaching about 8.8 % of total cigarette consumption in 2023 (the latest figures available), the report said – although information about the size, structure or economic impact of the trade remains “incomplete and unreliable”.

The report said the EU and many member states had taken steps to combat the trade, but were hampered because European law in the area was not harmonised and member states’ efforts were uneven, leaving enforcement gaps.

National control systems and enforcement have different definitions of offences and of penalties, encouraging criminals to move to the more lax jurisdictions, and information exchanges in the bloc were inconsistent.

“Criminals involved in the illicit tobacco trade are succeeding not because Europe lacks legislation but because gaps remain in coordination, information and enforcement,” Sarvamaa said. “Organised crime has a strategy. We need one too.”

articles.title: Trump’s call to rename New Mexico ‘New America’ is a distraction tactic, Democrats say
articles.summary:
Amid unpopular Iran war and persistent inflation, governor says state has had its name since before US existed

Democrats have hit back against

blocks.text: Democrats have hit back against Donald Trump’s suggestion that the state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America”, accusing the US president of trying to distract from his war on Iran and rising prices.

The administration moved to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” hours after Trump’s return to office in January 2025. In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, it moved to do the same with Lake Ontario, moving to rename it as “Lake America”.
The president spent Labor Day posting memes on social media platform in support ⁠of changing the ⁠name ​of the state of New Mexico to “New America” as tense trade negotiations ⁠with Mexico ramp up.

On Sunday Trump claimed that ‌he had received suggestions to change the name ‌of the state and that he liked the idea. “So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform. “Wow, I Love It!!!”

The US federal government has no authority to change a state’s name. Any renaming would require New Mexico voters to approve an amendment to the state constitution through a ballot measure. The state ⁠is currently governed by Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat. ​She ​has been in ​the job since 1 January 2019, ​and was re-elected ‌in 2022.
The ​governor said ​in a post on X: “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate – it’s been ours since before the United States existed.”

“While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring,” she wrote. “Americans are also spending more at the grocery store, losing access to health care and wondering if they’ll ever be able to afford a home.”

New Mexico’s senior senator, Martin Heinrich, blasted the president’s recent efforts to rename bodies of water via executive order. “Three things I will always call by their actual names,” Heinrich wrote. “The Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, New Mexico.”
His colleague in the Senate, Ben Ray Luján, echoed the sentiment.
“It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be,” he said, adding that Trump will “always be a sinvergüenza” – a spanish word for scoundrel – and “corrupt”.

Melanie Stansbury, one New Mexico’s Democratic US House representatives, was also resolute. “WE ARE NOT CHANGING OUR NAME!” she said in a video, standing on the banks of the Rio Grande, which runs through the state. “New Mexico is New Mexico. We are fiercely proud of our name, our people, and our places, including this river.”

Even Greg Hull, the Republican nominee running to replace Grisham, who is term-limited, denounced the president’s suggestion. “New Mexico does not need a new name. This state carries the history of Native nations and Spanish explorers who named this land nearly five hundred years ago, and generations of families who built New Mexico into what it is today. That identity is not up for negotiation,” Hull said in a statement to Santa Fe Public Radio.

articles.title: Senate Committee of the Whole to tackle Pax Silica issue
articles.summary: The Senate is set to take up the issue of the Pax Silica initiative through the Committee of the Whole, which will assemble the entire Upper Chamber into a panel for one specific issue.

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 10:56pm
The Senate is set to take up the issue of the Pax Silica initiative through the Committee of the Whole, which will assemble the entire Upper Chamber into a panel for one specific issue.
Senator Juan Miguel Zubiri made the motion to refer the Pax Silica to the Committee of the Whole during a Senate session on Tuesday.

“So that all members can be represented. All Committee Chairs can be represented but you’re the presiding officer, Mister President,” Zubiri said, addressing Senate President Sherwin “Win” Gatchalian.

“And I think it would be best to show that we are serious either in support or we're concerned about Pax Silica because it's really a very, very important measure that needs to be given undue attention and the discussions will not be limited only to the environment and economic affairs,” he added.

The Vice Chairs of the Committee of the Whole would be the current chairs of the Committee on Environment, Committee on Cultural Communities and Muslim Affairs, Committee on Economic Affairs, Committee on Trade, Commerce and Entrepreneurship.
Explainer: Pax Silica– why are people worried?
Respectively, these would be senators Raffy Tulfo, Robin Padilla, Risa Hontiveros, and Bam Aquino. Zubiri himself would also be a Vice Chair as the Chair of the Committee on Foreign Relations.
Gatchalian said that the matter was urgent since the project was already ongoing.
“I will heed to your suggestion. With that motion, is there any objection? Hearing none, the motion of the Majority Leader to create the Paxilica Committee of the Whole is approved,” Gatchalian said.
Previous occasions when the Senate assembled the Committee of the Whole include the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, as well as agricultural smuggling in 2022.

The Pax Silica initiative in the New Clark City in Tarlac has generated concerns on its possible impact on the environment and energy security. Locals in the area also fear displacement and homelessness should the project push through. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: British family speaks out over nine-year ordeal after husband is abducted by Saudi Arabia
articles.summary:
Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017

A British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and…

blocks.text: A British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and coercion of her husband at the hands of Saudi authorities, after nine years of “failed” quiet diplomacy.
The businessman Rami Naimi was first abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from a trip to Australia with his father. After being tortured, he was released the following year.

The father of three, who is the son of Ali Al-Naimi, a former Saudi oil minister and head of the state oil company Aramco, was detained again in 2022 and held for two years. Last year he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial.

He was initially detained alongside 400 of the kingdom’s most powerful people in an infamous round-up at the the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Riyadh, which became the biggest and most contentious purge in the modern kingdom’s history.

Speaking out for the first time after years of what they described as a failed diplomatic process, his family has alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities.
Naimi now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical of Saudi Arabia and for attempting to leave the country without permission – both of which he denies.
“The first thing I wanted to do was speak out, but I was told no,” said his wife Mira Lozi, speaking alongside her son at a campaign launch to bring Naimi home in London on Tuesday.
Lozi, currently fighting cancer, fought back tears as she said she had been encouraged to keep silent since 2017 to help secure his release.

“For nine years my children and I have lived through a nightmare,” she said. “Saying the truth today is like a liberation, enough is enough and we’re just hoping that we can end this nightmare and all the governments will be able to help us.”

blocks.caption: Mira Lozi with her husband, Rami Naimi. Photograph: Bring Rami Home Campaign/PA

blocks.text: Naimi left Saudi Arabia aged 13 and travelled for years between the UK, US and Middle East as a businessman. His family claim he was abducted in Dubai in 2017 returning home from a book tour trip from Australia with his father.

They say he was blindfolded and forcibly taken by car to Abu Dhabi and then by private jet to Saudi Arabia. He was surprised to find himself with the others who had been rounded up, his family said, as he is not a journalist, activist or politician.

His abduction in 2017 came as the kingdom’s elite were detained at a five-star hotel in Riyadh during a purge in which princes, tycoons and ministers were stripped of their fortunes. Accounts later surfaced detailing torture and coercion, and the event preceded the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, whose assassination at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018 sparked revulsion around the world.

Naimi was held at the hotel and tortured, electrocuted, waterboarded and psychologically abused for three months, his family said. He was told, falsely, that his father was being tortured next door. He was released in January 2018 after signing a “settlement agreement”.

He was subsequently forced to sign a document pledging to surrender 5bn Saudi riyals, later “discounted” to 1bn riyals (£200m) – which the family says neither he or they possess. Naimi was placed under electronic surveillance and banned from leaving the kingdom.

His family said he was disappeared again for nearly two years in 2022, and subjected to further torture, and emotional and psychological abuse. They said they had no idea if he was alive or dead, and learned only through the help of his legal team and diplomats that he was being held in Saudi’s notorious Al Ha’ir prison.

It was after his release in March 2025, with an electronic tag and subject to a travel ban, that he learned of charges against him claiming he had “exploited” his father’s official influence. Naimi faced allegations he acted as an agent for a US company in Saudi Arabia and helped Aramco to secure a contract to provide technology to prevent diesel smuggling.

After seven years without charges, Naimi, an EU citizen, was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment following a secret trial. Now he is unable to leave Saudi Arabia and his communications with his family remain monitored. He has no idea, the family said, of their decision to go public with his case.
“Until today we have no idea why Rami was targeted,” said Lozi, who is too frightened to return to Saudi Arabia or travel to the United Arab Emirates.
“It really is something out of a movie. It’s shocking and we just want to end this nightmare,” said his 21-year-old son, Ali, who was 12 when his father was abducted.

In recent years the UK’s relationship with Saudi Arabia has come under scrutiny over the flow of arms between the two countries, Riyadh’s use of public executions and targeting of exiled activists and dissidents.
“Any family making a decision like this needs to be supported by the government,” said human rights lawyer Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC, who is leading the case.

As the family hopes to meet the new prime minister and foreign secretary, Gallagher said the recent appointment of a special envoy for Britons detained overseas does not go as far as campaigners, experts and parliamentarians had called for.
Gallagher described it as: “Tea and sympathy for a very limited group of people.”

Last month the Guardian reported that X had become the latest US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.
The UK Foreign Office declined to comment. The Saudi embassy in London has been approached for comment.

articles.title: 50 years after his death, Mao still shapes China
articles.summary: Mao Zedong was perhaps the most influential, and certainly one of the most controversial, figures in 20th-century China. Even five decades after his death, the legacy of his era continues to…

image.caption: Mao's teachings remain part of China's official ideology, and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen SquareImage: Noel Celis/AFP

blocks.text: On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died. The revolutionary leader who led the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to power and founded the People's Republic of China left behind a profoundly contradictory historical legacy.
He shaped the narratives of revolution, nation-building and national independence, but also left behind immense social trauma as a result of successive political campaigns and persecutions.
50 years of transformation: How far has China moved away from Mao era?
Over the past five decades, China has undergone radical changes.

When Mao died, China was still a poor and relatively isolated communist state. Today, it is the world's second-largest economy, deeply embedded in the supply and value chains of global capitalism, with a vast private sector, a large urban middle class and a highly digitalized society.

Zhang Lun, a professor at Cergy-Paris University, said Mao left behind four major political legacies: the authoritarian and highly centralized political system; a model of governance that relies on revolution and political campaigns to solve social problems; populist tendencies marked by anti-elitism and anti-rationalism; and utopian visions of egalitarianism and moralism.

From the perspective of political legacies, Zhang argues, the most fundamental change in China over the past five decades has been "de-Maoization" — while its greatest challenge has been that this process was never fully completed.

blocks.caption: Mao's insistence on the CCP's supremacy is still a fundamental principle in China todayImage: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The legacy that never left: The party's supremacy
Mao's name remains written into the CCP's constitution, while his thought remains part of China's official ideology and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

Mao helped forge the Chinese Communist Party, and his insistence on the party's supremacy over the state and society has remained a fundamental principle throughout the decades, said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt, professor at the University of Zurich.

Veteran journalist and political commentator Chang Ping agrees, adding that what has truly endured is the institutional core of the principle that "the party leads everything," serving a state vision of being able to "concentrate resources to accomplish major tasks."
The CCP, he said, can pursue such objectives "at all costs" — meaning the interests of ordinary people can be sacrificed to the maximum extent necessary to preserve the regime.
A return to the 'Mao era?'

Under current leader Xi Jinping, a number of political concepts and methods of governance associated with the Mao era — such as ideological unity and the spirit of "struggle" — have again attracted attention.

Xi's actions such as abolishing the presidential term limits, strengthening his personal authority and the incorporation of his political thought into the party and state constitutions have invited comparisons between him and Mao.
Chang argues that the very term "return" is misleading, since elements of the Mao era have never fully disappeared.
Zhang holds a similar view.

Authoritarian rule, political rigidity, weak rule of law and the lack of effective guarantees for citizens' rights, he argues, are not only important elements of Mao's political legacy but also among the most significant continuities between the Mao era and China's current political system, he underscored.
And Xi, who personally suffered during the Cultural Revolution, seems even move closer to Mao-era policies.
"What Xi learned from the Cultural Revolution was not the lesson of a victim, but the lesson of power," Chang said.
The lesson was not that "such a system must never exist again," but rather that "whoever loses power is at the mercy of others," he added.
Felix Wemheuer, professor of modern China studies at the University of Cologne, echoed this view.

"The conclusion Xi appears to have drawn from his own experience of the Cultural Revolution was clearly not that Mao should be completely abandoned," he said, "but rather that, for political reasons, Mao's historical status as the founder of the state, the military and the party must be upheld."
Wemheuer views the current CCP leadership's approach to Mao as "fundamentally Machiavellian and pragmatic."

In economic policy, for instance, there is no sign of a return to the Mao era, he said. Today's China operates a highly dynamic model of state capitalism, with a mix of ownership forms coexisting and maintaining a strong private sector. Nor is there any indication that China intends to return to the Mao-era model of a communist welfare state.
The same applies to the idea of "self-reliance." Today's China could hardly afford to withdraw from the global economy and international supply chains.
Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world?
Xi remains a product of the system Mao created

Experts say similarities between Mao and Xi can be seen in areas such as the emphasis on the CCP's supremacy, the elevation of a core leader, and populist elements that stress a close connection between the people and the leadership.
Wemheuer argues that Xi possesses neither Mao's historical authority nor his personal charisma.

The two also exercise power in fundamentally different ways. Mao could bypass party institutions, go for years without convening a party congress and mobilize the masses against the party and state apparatus.
Mao himself was a populist with certain anarchic tendencies, Wemheuer said, and even tolerated the temporary collapse of the party-state system at the grassroots level in 1966-67.

Xi, by contrast, would never allow such a situation to occur, the expert stressed. Xi places greater emphasis than Mao on control and top-down governance, consolidating power by strengthening institutions and the party apparatus.
Mittelstaedt likewise cautions against equating Xi with Mao.

First, Mao was a revolutionary who destroyed existing institutions during the Cultural Revolution and was fundamentally anti-bureaucratic in his political orientation. Xi, Mittelstaedt argues, does the opposite.
Second, Mao stood above the party. His power came from "being Mao himself" rather than from the party's institutional structures.
Xi, by contrast, is "a party man through and through." His authority derives from party institutions, and he governs through those institutions, Mittelstaedt pointed out.
"At the end of the day," he noted, "Xi Jinping remains a product of the system Mao created."
Mao nostalgia among younger generations?

China has also seen recurring waves of Mao nostalgia, with some Chinese citizens invoking Mao online and expressing longing for what they describe as an era without social inequality, when everyone supposedly had enough to eat.
Chang argues that what they are longing for is neither Mao himself nor the real Mao era.

The actual Mao era, Mittelstaedt said, was marked by rigid hierarchies, pointing to the urban-rural household registration divide, different levels of privileges and supplies for officials, and a system in which one's family background could determine one's fate. It was, in many respects, more unequal than China today — and voicing grievances could be fatal.

The imagined vision of a more equal world, he underlined, is therefore actually an indictment of the present situation, with widening inequality, soaring housing prices, and persistently limited social mobility.
Still, many express the dissatisfaction with contemporary reality through Mao's image and language.

In Chang's view, this is connected to the continuing contraction of space for public criticism in China. When forms of political expression such as independent trade unions, street protests, free media and opposition parties are tightly restricted, Mao remains a historical symbol that official ideology cannot entirely exclude.

The result is a striking irony, he said, pointing to some people invoking Mao's language of anti-bureaucracy, resistance to oppression and even "rebellion" to criticize what they see as corruption, inequality and abuses of power in Xi's China today.

Mittelstaedt said this makes Mao a double-edged sword. He remains an important symbol of the CCP's political legitimacy — but parts of the revolutionary language he left behind can also be turned into standards by which contemporary reality is measured and criticized.
What is China's NPC and why does it matter?

articles.title: Paris mayor launching investigation after Hindu group visit limits female staff at Eiffel Tower
articles.summary: The Eiffel Tower reopened Tuesday, a day after one of the world's most-visited landmarks was closed by a strike to protest what a union official called "unacceptable" management instructions limiting…

image.caption: Pedestrians walk past the Eiffel Tower in Paris on Tuesday, a day after staff walked out over the limiting of the presence of female staff during a visit by a Hindu religious group. (Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The Eiffel Tower reopened Tuesday, a day after one of the world's most-visited landmarks was closed by a strike to protest what a union official called "unacceptable" management instructions limiting the presence of women during a visit by a Hindu delegation on Saturday.
Group known as BAPS offered 'sincere apologies' to anyone hurt or inconvenienced by incident

The Eiffel Tower reopened on Tuesday, a day after one of the world's most-visited landmarks was closed by a strike to protest what a union official called "unacceptable" management instructions limiting the presence of women during a visit by a Hindu delegation on Saturday.

Diane Davoine of the CGT union told The Associated Press that anger grew among staff of the iconic, 330-metre tower over the weekend after management told employees that female workers should ″not be in contact″ with a visiting delegation from Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha.

The group, known as BAPS, is a worldwide religious and civic organization within the Swaminarayan sect, a branch of Hinduism. It has been holding celebrations to mark the inauguration of a traditional Hindu stone temple in the French capital.

In a written statement emailed to the AP on Tuesday, the group said it co-ordinated with the Eiffel Tower's management to minimize disruption to staff and visitors ahead of a visit by a delegation of some 100 people.

The co-ordination was "never, at any point, intended as a request rooted in gender, and any suggestion to the contrary does not reflect the spirit or values of our fellowship or the delegation," the statement said.

BAPS said it "remains firmly committed to the principles of equality, mutual respect, and service to all, regardless of gender, background, or belief — values that lie at the very heart of our tradition's teachings and community work worldwide."
In an earlier statement, the group offered "sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation."
The company that operates the Eiffel Tower did not immediately comment. The 137-year-old tower is visited by some seven million people each year.

Davoine said the tower often hosts special delegations, including U.S. President Donald Trump, visiting royals and celebrities like Britney Spears, and staff are happy to accommodate. But she said the instructions on Saturday were exceptional and ″unacceptable.″
In a message on X, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said he would launch an investigation.

"Gender equality will never stop at the foot of our historic monuments, or anywhere else in this city," he said. "It must apply everywhere and to everyone. I will ensure that it does — everywhere, without exception."

It was not the first time the tower has been closed by industrial action. It was shut for six days in February 2024 because of striking employees demanding better maintenance of the historic landmark and higher wages.

articles.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations worsen
articles.summary: For years, Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the EU, but the new government has dropped the pro-Kremlin stance.

blocks.text: Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities.
"This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details.
Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor Orbán for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance.

The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful".

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow from the moment his Tisza party was elected in April. He and the foreign minister have both called on Russia to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.

In May Anita Orbán summoned the Russian ambassador to protest against a big drone attack on the Transcarpathia region of Ukraine that is home to a large Hungarian minority. Commentators have pointed out that her predecessor had not summoned the ambassador since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion in 2022.

Then last month Magyar formally broke with the previous Fidesz government's policies, with new guidelines spelling out that Russia's conduct in Ukraine "poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger".
Russia's Ambassador to Budapest, Evgeny Stanislavov, reacted bitterly to Anita Orbán's intention to continue "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules".
Budapest's promise of pragmatic co-operation was worth absolutely nothing, he complained, adding that Hungary's "extremely unfriendly step constitutes an unprecedented and ungrounded escalation".

Before Magyar was voted into office, Hungary had for years insisted on maintaining close relations with Moscow, partly citing cheap Russian oil imports. Viktor Orbán objected to the EU's supply of aid to Ukraine and repeatedly delayed packages of sanctions on Russia.

Ahead of the April elections, independent Russian investigative website Agentsvo reported that 15 of the 47 Russian embassy staff in Budapest were linked to Russian intelligence agencies and six more might be linked.

Former Hungarian counter-intelligence chief András Telkes told the BBC that even though "Russian spying activity" had been investigated before the election, the Fidesz government had prevented any action being taken.
The Russian embassy in Budapest had also rejected as false a report alleging that three Russian military intelligence officers had travelled to Budapest to influence the Hungarian vote.
Russia has routinely denied its embassies are used for espionage. However, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled across Europe since 2022, and Russia has responded in kind.

Telkes told the BBC that the big question now was how Moscow would respond: "If 10 Hungarian diplomats were to be expelled from Moscow, in a tit-for-tat move, that would effectively close the Hungarian embassy there."

articles.title: Family of slain teen calls for death penalty in murder trial of singer D4vd
articles.summary:
David Burke’s defense argues there is no evidence he had any intent of killing 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez

The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has called for the singer…

blocks.text: The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has called for the singer D4vd, who is on trial suspected of killing the girl, to face the death penalty.

D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, in July was ordered to stand trial over the killing of Rivas, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of his Tesla car on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
In a statement on Monday, which would have been her 16th birthday, Celeste’s family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.

“If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter,” read a family statement, released via their attorney.
A separate statement from Celeste’s family said that they were “reliving unforgettable moments even though she is no longer here” – and that they were “experiencing so many emotions”.

Prosecutors allege that Burke, a 21-year-old who began his music career by uploading montages of the video game Fortnite, stabbed and killed Celeste and subsequently severed her limbs as he sought to prevent her from revealing their sexual relationship which began when he was 18 and she was 13 – or too young to legally consent – in November 2023.
Celeste’s body was found in the front trunk of Burke’s Tesla in a Los Angeles tow yard. The car had been towed away after being left on a street near Burke’s home, according to prosecutors.
Celeste was last seen on 23 April 2025, according to court documents, with the prosecution alleging that Burke stabbed her several times and mortally wounded her after she went to his home.

The singer was arrested in April of this year and charged with multiple crimes, including first-degree murder, lewd and lascivious acts with an individual under 14, and mutilating a body. He has pleaded not guilty to all of these charges, the most serious of which carries a potential death penalty.

During a preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors said that Burke met Celeste when she was 11, and began sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18. A year before her death, the pair also exchanged messages about how she had become pregnant – she assured him the baby was his – and that she had an abortion.

The hearing also included the submission of photos of the two of them kissing and lying in bed. The pictures showed that she had “David” tattooed in red ink on a finger – one of two that had been cut off when her body was found.

Burke’s defense argued there is no evidence that he had any intent of killing Celeste and that no witnesses or cameras captured her entering his house in the timeframe he is alleged to have killed her.

Burke has had a troubled defense to the charges, however, with his high-profile lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter withdrawing from the case in late August. No reasons were given for the withdrawal.
The lawyers were replaced by a lawyer from the Los Angeles county public defender’s office. Burke has been ordered held without bail, with a trial date yet to be set.

articles.title: Air traffic control issue causes flight delays and disruption across UK
articles.summary:
Departures from London airports worst hit with most flights since 2pm affected as National Air Traffic Services investigates technical problem

Flights around the UK are facing delays and…

blocks.text: Flights around the UK are facing delays and disruption due to an air traffic control issue which has affected a string of airports including Heathrow and Gatwick and is expected to take “some time” to resolve.
Departures from London airports are most severely affected, with few take-offs since a fault was reported early on Tuesday afternoon.
Most flights due to depart Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted and London City airports since 2pm appeared to have been delayed or are yet to take off. Manchester airport has also been affected.
The air traffic control service Nats said at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”.

Nats later added that it had identified the problem, which was in its flight processing system. It said: “Our engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible. We recognise the ongoing disruption to travel, for which we sincerely apologise.
It continued: “Flights are still departing and airspace is open, but recovery will take some time. We will provide further updates as soon as possible.”

The UK’s biggest airport, Heathrow, said planes were continuing to arrive, although Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely to continue until the evening.
In a statement, Heathrow added: “We are supporting our local Nats team in their efforts to resolve the issue as quickly as possible. We will provide updated information when we have it.
“We apologise to those disrupted and advise passengers to check with their airline for latest flight information.”
Heathrow’s website showed several flights due to depart this afternoon have been cancelled. British Airways said it was experiencing some disruption and was in touch with its customers.
Belfast City airport warned of “some disruption” to flights after the technical issue affecting Nats.
“Due to the technical issue referenced below, there may be some disruption to flights due to arrive in and depart from Belfast City airport,” they said in a statement.”

A Birmingham airport spokesperson apologised to customers and advised them to “arrive at Birmingham airport (BHX) in line with their airline’s check-in requirements and to contact their airline directly for the latest flight information and updates.”
Edinburgh airport said it was aware of the issue which “may impact operations”.

articles.title: Aquaculture players seek say in Pangasinan projects amid flooding
articles.summary: CALASIAO, Pangasinan — Aquaculture industry players in Pangasinan are urging authorities to include them in consultations for development projects, saying they are often left to bear the consequences…

blocks.text: CALASIAO, Pangasinan — Aquaculture industry players in Pangasinan are urging authorities to include them in consultations for development projects, saying they are often left to bear the consequences of decisions in which they have little or no say.

“We are a big part of the country’s food security, but we are often overlooked by the government when projects, such as solar farms in the mountains, are being planned and implemented,” said Christopher Sibayan, president of the Samahan ng Magbabangus sa Pangasinan (SAMAPA) in a recent interview.
Sibayan said massive flooding this year inundated fishponds for weeks, causing them to overflow and allowing fish stocks to escape into rivers and other waterways.

Binmaley, Labrador, Lingayen and Bugallon, major aquaculture areas, were severely affected by nearly monthlong flooding brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat, and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng.
Industry players believe developments in upland areas, including solar farms in Bugallon and Labrador, may have worsened the flooding.
William Go, a SAMAPA coordinator, said some solar farm projects involved cutting trees that could have helped lessen the impact of heavy rains.
Sibayan said solar companies should have installed water-impounding facilities so rainwater collected by solar panels would not rapidly flow downhill into rivers and fishponds.
“Without the panels, rainwater could flow more slowly. But the water is collected by the panels and ran rapidly flow downstream all at once,” Go said.
Vita Mamaril, a fisheries industry leader in Bugallon, said the flooding this year was unusually severe.
“Bugallon has always experienced flooding, but it was only this year that the flooding became so massive and took weeks to subside,” she said.
She also disputed claims that all mountains where solar farms were established had already been denuded.
“It is not true that all the mountains were denuded. Cayanga was still forested before a solar farm was put up there,” she said.
Sibayan said the flooding showed how developments upstream could affect the fisheries sector downstream.
“What is happening in the mountains directly or indirectly affects us in the lowlands, including those of us in the fisheries sector,” he said.
Fishpond operators also lost millions of pesos in fish stocks and inputs after floodwaters overtopped pond embankments.
One Binmaley operator, who requested anonymity, estimated his losses at about P5 million in fingerlings and feeds. The fish weighed about 200 grams each when they escaped.
“That does not even include the income we would have earned if the stocks had grown to harvestable size and were sold after another two to three months,” he said.
Another bangus producer in Labrador said he lost about 500,000 fingerlings being raised in a nine-hectare fishpond.
Manuel Estrada of Labrador said high-value fish, including malaga, lapu-lapu and talakitok, were also affected after the salinity of river water dropped to zero because of the flooding.
Workers also lost their livelihood.
Melchor Valdez, a fishpond “harvester” in Bugallon, said many ponds now had few or no fish stocks left to harvest.
“Bugallon fishponds have no stocks to harvest, so I have no work,” Valdez said.
He said flooded palay farms were also leaving agricultural workers without income.
“Even the palay farms in my barangay in Estanza, Lingayen, are flooded, so there is nothing to harvest there either,” said Valdez, who also works as a palay harvester. /das

articles.title: Ratko Mladic’s funeral casts shadow over Bosnia and Herzegovina vote
articles.summary: Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade, attended by Serbian and Bosnian Serb leaders, has deepened regional tensions and could affect the upcoming election in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

image.caption: Mladic, who was dubbed the 'Butcher of Bosnia' for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, was buried with military honors in Serbia on MondayImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: Belgrade has made a point of insisting that it did not organize a state funeral for former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide in Srebrenica and crimes against humanity in 2017.

But when the body of a war criminal is flown home accompanied by the country's justice minister, when ceremonies unfold with military honors in state-controlled venues in the presence of senior political leaders and when clear condemnation of glorification of the deceased is absent, the message is unambiguous.
The impact of this message is being felt beyond Serbia's borders.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina — the state created by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, which comprises two entities linked by a weak central government — reactions were as deeply divided as the country itself.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: Two entities, two narratives
Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity covering about 49% of the country's territory, sent its officials to the funeral.

blocks.caption: Ratko Mladic was mourned by many in Republika Srpska, the majority Serb entity in Bosnia and HerzegovinaImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Public discourse there was dominated by narratives of "defending the people" and "the injustice of international courts."
"Without Ratko Mladic, there would be no Republika Srpska," was the refrain among thousands of mourners at the funeral in Belgrade.
Sarajevo, the seat of the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sees this approach as a continued policy of relativizing war crimes and a threat to stability.
Bosnia and Herzegovina cools diplomatic ties with Serbia
In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entity where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, the response was very different and the tone sharp.
Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic described Serbia's official response as a conscious choice by Belgrade, not something imposed on it.

He announced measures to cool diplomatic ties with Serbia, withdrawing almost all staff from the country's embassy in Belgrade, leaving only the ambassador, explaining that he lacks the authority to close the embassy but can reduce its presence to a minimum. The move effectively froze day-to-day diplomatic communication on the ground.

blocks.caption: Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic announced that he would be withdrawing almost all staff from the country's embassy in BelgradeImage: Denis Zuberi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: "We will pull out everyone we can; consular services will be relocated to Zagreb and Podgorica," he said.
Denis Becirovic, chair of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, called the funeral with military honors an "anti-civilizational act" and warned of far-reaching consequences for the entire region.
For representatives of Mladic's victims, any public glorification of the former general is a direct insult to the families of those killed.
Political point-scoring
Mladic's death and funeral are not just about the past.
At a time when both Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are facing general elections — Bosnia on October 4 and Serbia likely just a few weeks later — emotions become a resource.
In both countries, parts of the electorate still see Mladic as a symbol of resistance, which means that every gesture in support of him scores political points with these voters.

As the general election in Bosnia and Herzegovina approaches, sharp condemnations from Sarajevo are seen as evidence that the central government is "defending the state" and "the dignity of victims." This, too, is being turned into political capital.

blocks.caption: Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Denis Becirovic called Mladic's funeral with military honors an 'anti-civilizational act'Image: NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Republika Srpska, the presence of officials at the funeral and the narrative of "injustice" strengthen the position of those building their identity in opposition to international rulings.
Yet there are no "winners." The more political points anyone scores on this issue, the worse relations become and the further accession to the EU recedes into the distance — for both countries.

Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka, is clear about who is responsible for these political narratives: "The main culprits are the political elites, because in 30 years we have not moved forward. There has been no critical confrontation with the dark side of history," she says. "This is a darkening of civilizational consciousness."
Topic went on to say that Mladic's funeral "is a welcome gift to the protagonists of ethno-nationalist policies" and noted that these people still hold power in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"Such an institutional stance towards crimes provokes a reaction on the other side, and then everyone exploits the situation, trapping us in a vicious circle where each tries to extract political profit," Topic says.
A divided society and frozen relations

After Mladic's funeral, the Office of the High Representative (OHR) in Bosnia, which was created after the war to oversee the implementation of the US-brokered Dayton Peace Agreement, stressed that Bosnia's future cannot be built on glorifying those responsible for the worst crimes of the past.

blocks.caption: Mladic was convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1990s Bosnian War. Pictured here: headstones of victims of the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre Image: Elvis Barukcic/AFP

blocks.text: "Glorifying convicted war criminals, as well as denying genocide and other war crimes, creates divisions, inflicts additional pain on victims and their families, and undermines the reconciliation process," said the OHR.
Bosnia remains a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 31 years since the war ended.

The fact that the ideology that helped spark that war still lives on, means that Mladic's funeral did not close a chapter in the region's history, it tore open a new one, measuring the Balkans' willingness to step out of the shadow of the 1990s.
While politicians seek to score political points, citizens pay the price of frozen relations.

articles.title: Police: No incident at 2 Quezon City schools amid alleged threat
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Quezon City Police District (QCPD) on Tuesday said no violent incident had been reported at the Batasan Hills National High School and E-Claro Academy amid an alleged…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Quezon City Police District (QCPD) on Tuesday said no violent incident had been reported at the Batasan Hills National High School and E-Claro Academy amid an alleged threat.
In a statement, the QCPD said the Batasan Police Station had coordinated with the respective schools’ managements and conducted a verification of the purported security concern.
“As of Sept. 8, 2026, no violent incident related to the alleged threat has been reported or recorded at either school,” the police noted.
It explained that the threat stemmed from a social media post, but it did not expound on the nature of the security concern.

“The QCPD likewise coordinated with the Quezon City District Anti-Cybercrime Team to verify the authenticity and determine the source of the alleged Facebook Messenger threat, as well as to identify the individual who may be responsible for the post,” it added.
In response, the city police district detailed that it had heightened police visibility and intensified security measures in coordination with the schools’ stakeholders.
The police also urged the public to remain calm, refrain from sharing unverified information and report suspicious activity.
“The QCPD assures the public that all reported threats are taken seriously and are subject to immediate verification and appropriate police action,” it stressed. /das

articles.title: San Roque Dam stops spillway discharge in Pangasinan
articles.summary: CALASIAO, Pangasinan — The two spillway gates of the San Roque Multipurpose Dam in San Manuel, Pangasinan, were closed at 7:30 p.m. on Tuesday (Sept. 8), ending the dam’s discharge, according to the…

blocks.text: CALASIAO, Pangasinan — The two spillway gates of the San Roque Multipurpose Dam in San Manuel, Pangasinan, were closed at 7:30 p.m. on Tuesday (Sept. 8), ending the dam’s discharge, according to the National Power Corp. (Napocor).
The gates, 2A and 2B, were closed at one meter and 1.5 meters, respectively. The dam’s water elevation was 277.14 meters above sea level (masl) at the time.
The San Roque Power Corp. (SRPC), which operates the dam, initially opened the two spillway gates by one meter each on Sept. 2, when the water level was 283.68 masl.

Continued rain and inflow from the Binga Dam pushed the water level to 285.13 masl on Sept. 5. The SRPC opened an additional 0.5 meter on Sept. 6 and increased the total gate opening to three meters at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, an hour before the gates were closed.
The dam’s mandatory spilling level is 280 masl. /mcm
