articles.title: Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more states
articles.summary: Alarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory

blocks.text: Thousands of Germans have staged protests against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) after the party’s watershed victory in a state election, warning it posed a danger in two more polls this month.

Demonstrators at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate held a peaceful pro-democracy rally denouncing the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD, which has called for mass deportations of asylum seekers and a rollback of state support for renewable energy and public broadcasting.

The party captured its best-ever state result in the former communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, with clear momentum heading into regional elections in the capital and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic coast, on 20 September.

Police reported 5,000 protesters, while organisers said they drew more than 14,000 people in a campaign to mobilise voters against the AfD. Posters in the crowd read: “Fascism is no alternative”, “Stop the Nazi AfD: end racism and cuts to social services” and “History has its eyes on us”.
With less than two weeks to election day, demonstrators at the Berlin rally cautioned against resignation and cynicism after Sunday’s shock result.

The AfD’s nearly 44% vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the best for a nativist party since the Nazi period, is a “disgrace that makes you furious and stunned”, Jens-Christian Wagner, the director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, said from the stage.

blocks.caption: Protesters throng the roads around the Brandenburg Gate, Berlin, on Monday after the AfD victory. Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/Alamy

blocks.text: Wagner sounded the alarm that the AfD, although it fell just short of an absolute majority, was on the brink of taking power in Saxony-Anhalt, a first for the far right since the second world war. That “should not be accepted in silence”, he said.

Max Schneller, 17, a member of the far-left Linke, from Saxony-Anhalt, said activists in the state would fight any attempts by an AfD government to target minorities. “We will not start categorising our neighbours according to their origin, religion or skin colour – we are too humane to hate,” he said to loud applause.

The AfD is three votes short of the support necessary to form a government under its candidate, the media-savvy firebrand Ulrich Siegmund, who hopes to peel off dissenters from the remaining parties willing to play kingmaker.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has since 2023 listed the state chapter of the party as rightwing extremist, saying it poses a threat to democratic norms.

Hundreds of anti-AfD protesters also gathered in Potsdam, near Berlin, with rallies also organised in Münster, Göttingen, Dresden, Aachen, Bamberg, Darmstadt, and Halberstadt, in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD captured nearly half the votes, local media reported.

blocks.caption: A protester in Berlin on Monday. Photograph: Maryam Majd/Reuters

blocks.text: In Halle, the region’s second largest city, leftist groups and civil society organisations have been staging a protest camp since election day.

The AfD is leading in voter intent polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%. However, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) of the state premier, Manuela Schwesig, mounted a remarkable comeback over the summer and is now scoring above 30%.

In Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the picture is more mixed, with several parties jockeying for first place. It is governed by a coalition of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the SPD.
The CDU, the party of chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose record unpopularity is reported to have weighed heavily with voters in Saxony-Anhalt, holds a wafer-thin lead in the capital, with about 20%.
Hot on its heels is the Linke, which has focused on soaring housing costs in its campaign, and the AfD, followed by the SPD and the ecologist Greens, both polling in the mid-teens.

Merz has vowed to stay in office and fight for a signature package of painful reforms, arguing the only way to defeat the AfD is to get Europe’s top economy moving again and repair its creaking social welfare system.
However, the SPD, his junior coalition partner, has indicated its willingness to backtrack on some of the most unpopular measures to shore up support for the embattled government.
Analysts say the dispute could further destabilise the shaky coalition.

articles.title: EU court rules against Belgian far-right party in IKEA case
articles.summary: A European court has backed Ikea's challenge against a Belgian far-right party, saying the use of Ikea-style visuals could harm the company's reputation.

image.caption: Vlaams Belang used graphics resembling the retailer's iconic assembly instructions in a political campaign.Image: Walter Cicchetti/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: A top European Union court ruled in favor of Ikea in a challenge brought by the company against Belgian far-right and Flemish separatist party Vlaams Belang.

The popular Swedish brand may prevent the Belgian party from using its signature illustrations. Vlaams Belang launched the "Ikea Plan" in 2022, a proposal to reform the country's migration and asylum laws.
The plan included images similar to Ikea's furniture assembly instructions. Ikea filed a legal complaint in 2023, accusing the far-right party of unlawfully using its branding.
What did the court rule?

"A proprietor of a trademark with a reputation may prevent that mark from being used by a political party where the latter has not demonstrated that its freedom of expression takes precedence over the rights and interests of that proprietor," the ECJ court said in a statement.

Vlaams Belang argued that the campaign was protected under freedom of expression. However, the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice found this argument insufficient, ruling that the use of Ikea's branding could harm the company's name and reputation.
The Luxembourg judges urged the Belgian court to issue a ruling on the matter in light of the decision by the European Court of Justice.
What did Vlaams Belang and IKEA say about the ruling?
In a statement, Vlaams Belang said it had taken note of the judgement, adding that it "will thoroughly study its scope in the context of the further legal proceedings."
Meanwhile, IKEA representatives welcomed the judgement.

"Inter IKEA strongly believes in and has great respect for freedom of expression. At the same time, the company cannot accept the use of IKEA’s trademarks in a way that harms their reputation or distinctiveness", Inter IKEA, a Netherlands-based holding company that handles the Swedish firm's intellectual property, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.
Besides its anti-immigration stances, Vlaams Belang also advocates for the independence of Flanders — the northern, Dutch-speaking part of Belgium.
While it made considerable gains in 2024 elections, other parties refuse to cooperate with it.

articles.title: UK announces trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the measures were in response to what he called "settler terrorism" in the occupied territories. The measures are part of the UK's efforts to support a two-state…

image.caption: Foreign Secrety Ed Miliband announced the measures in the House of Commons [File: July 29, 2026]Image: Leon Neal/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The United Kingdom on Tuesday announced trade restrictions on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The center-left Labour Party government has previously sanctioned some Israeli settlers and illegal outposts over violence against Palestinians and illegal development in the West Bank.
What did Miliband say?
"I can announce today that we will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced in the House of Commons.
"We will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion," Miliband said.
The foreign secretary said those financing or facilitating illegal settlement would "face the full force of UK sanctions."
Before announcing the sanctions, Miliband said that "settler terrorism was rampant" and referenced various instances of violence in the West Bank.
Miliband accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by settlers in the West Bank.
Why is the UK restricting trade
The measures appear to be setting the tone for relations between Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Israel.

According to a Downing Street readout of a phone call between the British leader and US President Donald Trump on the phone on Monday, Burnham laid out "the UK's commitment to working towards peace and security in the region," and stressed the importance of the two-state solution two-state solution in Israel and the Palestinian territories.
The United Kingdom recognized Palestinian statehood last year in an attempt to revive efforts to achieve a two-state solution.

It also comes Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government forges ahead with settlement construction in the West Bank, raising fears among some Western governments that it threatens any possible two-state solution.
The measures also come amd flaring tensions in the West Bank that have involved violent attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers.
The UK has previously condemned the violence while calling for civilians to be protected and for those responsible to be held accountable.
Israel warns it will 'act against Britain'
Ahead of the announcement, Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar already indicated that Israel would respond.
"If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," Saar warned.

Israel's hard-line public security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly recognize the Falkland Islands as "Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently steal from the Argentine people."
This is a developing story. Check back here for updates.

articles.title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing
articles.summary: In strongest condemnation ever by UK government, Ed Miliband announces sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements

blocks.text: Israeli “terrorists” are conducting ethnic cleansing in the West Bank with the tacit backing of the government, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has said as he announced sweeping sanctions, alongside France and Canada, on trade with Israeli settlements.

In the strongest condemnation ever issued by the UK government, Miliband said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, saying such acknowledgment was “the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”
Miliband said that the government would now enact:

items: An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.
A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements.
A ban on the advertising in the UK of illegal settlement properties.
Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.
A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

blocks.text: Miliband said the action would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.

The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.

Miliband said those who financed or facilitated illegal settlements would “face the full force of UK sanctions” and that he expected the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months.
He stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts.
Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians. I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”
He said the British government had previously described settlements as illegal but had not described the occupation itself as unlawful, and that would now change.

France and Canada were also announcing bans on settlement goods on Tuesday, joining the Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway, which have either banned goods or were in the process of doing so.
Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust.
“I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.

“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”

He said to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.

Miliband said he felt a “deep sense of shame about what has unfolded in Palestine under the eyes of the international community” and said there had been “the most unimaginable trauma and suffering in the last three years – death, destruction and dehumanisation on an appalling scale”.
The foreign secretary said the action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine; one that not only condemned but took action.
“Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”
Miliband said the actions of the Israeli government in the West Bank meant more settlements had been approved in the last four years than in the last 20 years combined.
He said he believed the majority of the British people would support the ban on trade with illegal settlements. “Settlements are illegal. They should not be promoted in our country,” he said.
The UK government knew there were also concerns about arm sales to Israel, he said. The UK had already suspended more than 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza, but would now go further.

“We will now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation, in effect a double lock against arms sales. This means the ban on such exports will now remain as long as the occupation persists.”
He said the UK would support “full, robust and fair judicial processes” to determine if Israel had committed genocide and said the government would not pre-judge that process.

“This has been the case for all of the genocides since the 1948 genocide convention: Rwanda, Srebrenica, Cambodia, and acts against the Yazidi people. This will remain our policy. It is right that this issue has been brought before the ICJ [international court of justice] and I want to make it clear that we support the court in coming to its determination.”

However, he said that the most recent reports by international bodies found there was “increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed and we support legal processes to determine this”.
The UK would use the UN general assembly next week to “shine the clearest and harshest spotlight on what is happening and what must change”.

The steps set out by Miliband fall short of the full demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but are a sign the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies, such as Qatar, on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.

Both the US and Israel have threatened retaliation against Britain for the sanctions. The US ambassador to Israel, Mick Huckabee, said the US was considering what action to take, warning it may prohibit the UK from trade with several US states that have anti-BDS (boycott, divestment, sanctions) laws.
Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was “a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation” before the country’s elections in October.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, said: “If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain,” and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, called for the expulsion of the British ambassador.

articles.title: Japan's empty temples seek new ways to survive
articles.summary: With a declining population, shrinking congregations and growing economic pressures, temples are struggling to stay relevant. As more temples are sold or closed, is religion in decline in modern…

image.caption: Centuries-old temples like Odawara are struggling to stay relevant in modern Japan [FILE: October 2026]Image: Alexander Pöschel/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated altar.

Set in manicured gardens on the Chita Peninsula in central Japan, the 350-square-meter (3,767-square-foot) property is on the market for 482 million yen (€2.66 million). The estate agent's pitch says the price includes dismantling by "expert heritage craftsmen" and delivery to anywhere in Japan, where it would be fully restored into a "stunning" two- or three-bedroom home.
The sale and removal of the temple marks the end of its role in the local community in the hills above the Nagasawacho district, but it is a better fate than many places of worship across Japan.

There are around 77,000 temples across the country, but as many as 17,000 no longer have a full-time resident priest as congregations have shrunk — particularly in rural districts experiencing rapid depopulation — and financial pressures have taken their toll.
That means many temples are being sold off or simply shuttered and left to deteriorate quietly.
A temple brought back to life
Tomomi Iwayama took on the abandoned Ganshu-ji temple in Odawara, a coastal town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Tokyo, a decade ago. Today, he is the abbot of a growing congregation.
"The temple had no abbot for 70 years before I arrived because it was just so difficult to operate, and it has taken me until now to get it financially back on track," he told DW.
"Even in a relatively large urban area such as Odawara, which has around 200,000 residents, it has been very hard," he said. "In the countryside, it is much more difficult."

Iwayama's biggest problem is the country's shrinking population: fewer worshippers and falling demand for funerals and other traditional rites make it harder to finance the temple's upkeep. He has worked hard to reach out to the local community and has had success in selling plots in the temple graveyard.

blocks.caption: Odawara Castle was built in the mid-15th century [FILE: March 2018]Image: Koji Sasahara/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One innovation that has attracted attention is the temple's "smart graveyard," where families scan a card, and a robotic system recovers a relative's ashes from the columbarium.
Temples in rural areas of Japan face far greater challenges, he said.

"Young people in villages usually leave to go to university, and then they find a job in one of the big cities, so they rarely go back," he said. "Maybe they will go back once a year to pay their respects to their ancestors at the village temple, but that is not enough for the temple to get by on."

Equally, when the head priest of a rural temple retires, his children are unlikely to want to take the role on because of these challenges. All too often, Iwayama said, the result is the temple closing.
But he denies the suggestion that religion in Japan is following the same path as in the West, where Christian congregation numbers have plummeted over the decades.
Faith in the Digital Age
Demand for Buddhism remains
"I sense there is still a lot of demand in Japan for Buddhism," he said, contrasting the fast-paced, technology-focused lives that people typically lead with the serenity that they are often seeking.

"Buddhism is a style of living, of an enlightened person," he said. "A lot of people are looking for that. And while the traditional rituals of funerals and anniversaries are declining and that revenue is shrinking, we are finding that more people want to take part in traditional temple cuisine cooking classes, meditation and other things that we can offer."
Temples that are not able to shift to offer experiences more in tune with modern Japan are at risk of closing, said Joey Stockerman, one of the founders of the Mokomoko online real estate service.
"We have had a temple on our site in the past, and we were approached by a foreign potential buyer, so there is certainly interest when these properties become available," he said.

Other foreigners who are long-term residents are doing their best to protect Japan's religious heritage for future generations. American journalist and author Jake Adelstein is currently a Zen priest at Zenshoin Temple in Tokyo's Toshima Ward and is training to become an abbot.

"I do not think that Japanese are becoming less religious; I believe they are becoming fewer because of population decline and they are becoming less wealthy because of the economic situation," he said.
Meet Japan’s AI Buddhist Robot

"Families want to keep the grave plot that they have had for generations, but for many of them it is just too expensive to maintain, and they often live a long way away, so they are unable to regularly visit to pay their respects," he said.
The annual fee for a grave can be up to 100,000 yen, while memorials and other rites can be an additional financial burden, Adesltein explained.
Young people shun religious careers

"Young people are not interested in a career as a priest because temples earn so little money, so there are positions that cannot be filled, and that is especially a problem in the countryside," he said.
Some temples have amalgamated their operations and share a priest, but that will become more difficult in the future, Adelstein said.
As elsewhere, Zenshoin Temple has started vegetarian cooking classes and Zen meditation sessions to appeal to the local community, and Adelstein hopes that will be enough to keep the temple open.
"The training to become an abbot is very tough, and the economics of a temple today often just do not add up, but I see it as a critical part of this society and this nation," he said.
Young people in Japan are leaving large cities

articles.title: San Fernando wants Tolentino’s confirmation as Dole secretary blocked
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Kamanggagawa party-list Rep. Elijah San Fernando on Tuesday said the Commission on Appointments (CA) should block the confirmation of Francis Tolentino as secretary of the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Kamanggagawa party-list Rep. Elijah San Fernando on Tuesday said the Commission on Appointments (CA) should block the confirmation of Francis Tolentino as secretary of the Department of Labor and Employment (Dole), criticizing his stance on the pending P85 wage increase for workers in Metro Manila.

San Fernando made the statement when asked if he would oppose Tolentino’s confirmation before the CA. Tolentino was appointed labor secretary in May following the resignation of former Secretary Bienvenido Laguesma due to health reasons.
“For us at Kamanggagawa party-list, we believe that his appointment should be blocked by the Commission on Appointments,” San Fernando told workers in an ambush interview.

During the House Committee on Appropriations’ briefing on the Dole’s proposed budget for next year, San Fernando and Tolentino clashed over the implementation of the P85 wage increase, which remains on hold pending court proceedings in Pasig City.

San Fernando maintained that the wage order is in effect because the injunction against it is unenforceable since the petitioners failed to post the P10 billion bond. Asked about Dole’s stance on the implementation of the wage order, Tolentino said the agency adheres to the position of its legal counsel, the Office of the Solicitor General, noting that “sans a posting of the bond, the writ is not in order.”

The lawmaker pressed Tolentino further, saying that despite his explanation, the wage order still could not be enforced. Tolentino disagreed, saying implementation was a matter for the court to decide, not the agency.
“If this is how the secretary of the Department of Labor and Employment conducts himself, then he should not be called the secretary of Labor and Employment,” San Fernando said.

“So the Dole’s mandate is clear: to protect, defend and advance the rights of workers. You saw earlier during the Dole budget deliberations and budget consideration that Secretary Tolentino did not stand up for them,” he added.

On June 30, Tolentino announced the “historic” P85 wage increase for minimum wage workers in Metro Manila. The first tranche of P65 was supposed to take effect July 25, while the second tranche of P20 was due Jan. 20 next year.

However, the Pasig City Regional Trial Court Branch 125 issued a temporary restraining order against the implementation of the P85 wage increase in the region until Aug. 13, following a petition filed by Readycon Trading and Construction Corp. and R-II Builders Inc. The implementation was further delayed after the court granted the two firms’ petition for a writ of preliminary injunction.
The Office of the Solicitor General has asked the Pasig court to resolve its pending motion for reconsideration seeking to lift the injunction that halted implementation of the P85 wage increase.
The INQUIRER has sought comment from Tolentino but has yet to receive a response. /das

articles.title: Heavy rains expected in parts of Luzon on Sept. 9
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Two weather systems are affecting the country and may bring gloomy skies with heavy rains until Wednesday, Sept. 9, the state weather bureau said. Philippine Atmospheric,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Two weather systems are affecting the country and may bring gloomy skies with heavy rains until Wednesday, Sept. 9, the state weather bureau said.

Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) weather specialist Daniel Villamil said in its 5 p.m. weather advisory that the trough, or extension, of Tropical Cyclone Krovanh will affect eastern Luzon within the next few hours.

“Two weather systems are affecting the country in the coming hours. The first is located east of the Philippines; the cloud formations we see are associated with the trough, or extension, of Tropical Cyclone Krovanh, formerly known as Typhoon Pilandok,” Villamil said.

According to Pagasa, the rains brought by Krovanh may bring gloomy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms over Cagayan Valley, Cordillera Administrative Region, and Aurora until Wednesday afternoon.

“Typhoon Pilandok is already far from our country and has moved out of our monitoring domain; however, cloud clusters associated with the trough, or tail, of the said typhoon remain, affecting the eastern part of Luzon,” he explained.
Meanwhile, the southwest monsoon will persist and bring cloudy skies with scattered rains over Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, Aklan and Antique on Wednesday, according to Pagasa.

Occasional rains may also prevail over Zambales, Bataan, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro, also due to the habagat. Likewise, the rest of Visayas may also experience isolated rain showers.
The weather bureau also said that Mindanao may be affected by partly cloudy to cloudy skies with localized thunderstorms. /mcm

articles.title: Brice Hernandez pleads not guilty in 2nd malversation case
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Public Works (DPWH) engineer Brice Hernandez on Tuesday pleaded not guilty in his second malversation case in the Sandiganbayan. Hernandez, along with…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Public Works (DPWH) engineer Brice Hernandez on Tuesday pleaded not guilty in his second malversation case in the Sandiganbayan.

Hernandez, along with former DPWH officials Arjay Domasig, Jaypee Mendoza, Juanito Mendoza, Christina Mae Pineda, Niño Morales, and Floralyn Simbulan, made the plea before the anti-graft court’s Fourth Division.
LIST: Big names, others arrested in flood control scandal

This division handles the malversation case over the alleged non-existent riverbank protection structure worth ₱77 million in Bulacan’s Balagtas town built by Sunwest, founded by former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co.
Co’s staff John Paul Estrada and Mark Tecsay remain at large.
For his part, Co could not participate in the proceedings as he was earlier declared by Sandiganbayan as a fugitive from justice.
A respondent declared as a fugitive from justice could not participate in the proceedings and could not seek any judicial relief unless they surrender voluntarily.

This is Co’s second malversation case, the first one being over a P289.4 million worth project in Oriental Mindoro’s Naujan town which prosecutors said was found to have serious structural deficiencies.
Aside from Hernandez and Co, this is also the second malversation case of Domasig, both Mendozas and Pineda.

Their first malversation case is handled by the Third Division over the alleged ghost flood control project of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in Bulacan’s Pandi town worth P92.8 million with former Sen. Bong Revilla as co-accused. Revilla is out on a P1 million bail. /mr

articles.title: Speaker Dy: Better farmers’ incomes key to food security
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — “Food security begins with farmer security,” according to Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III. Dy made that remark part of his message on Tuesday at the meeting convening farmers’…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — “Food security begins with farmer security,” according to Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III.
Dy made that remark part of his message on Tuesday at the meeting convening farmers’ and irrigators’ associations for the Sagip Saka Program at Rangie’s Villa in San Miguel, Bulacan.
The message was delivered on his behalf by Bulacan 2nd District Rep. Augustina Dominique “Ditse Tina” C. Pancho, a member of the House Committee on Agriculture.

“If we want a stable food supply, we must first make the livelihoods of our farmers stable,” Dy said, as he reiterated the House of Representatives’ support for stronger farmers’ and irrigators’ associations and the Sagip Saka Program.
Dy stressed that improving agricultural productivity must go hand in hand with ensuring that farmers have reliable markets for their produce.
“A farmer may have good land, sufficient water, and a good harvest, but if that farmer cannot find a fair and reliable market, his earnings will still be insufficient,” he said.

“And this is where Sagip Saka becomes especially important. The program helps bring government and institutional buyers closer to our farmers and their organizations. It gives farmers an opportunity to become not simply producers, but stronger participants in the agricultural value chain.”
‘We want to do more’
Citing figures from the Department of Agriculture, Dy said 13,656 registered enterprises were involved in the implementation of the Sagip Saka Act, with procurement awards reaching ₱2.92 billion.
“But we want to do more. Our objective is not just better productivity; our goal is better incomes for our farmers,” he said.
Agriculture is particularly close to the heart of the Dy, the former governor of Isabela, one of the country’s major agricultural provinces.
Among the first groups he invited and received in his office after assuming the House leadership was a group of farmers so that he could hear firsthand their experiences, needs, and proposals.
He said the House takes agricultural spending seriously because agriculture affects not only food production but also jobs, livelihoods, and food prices.

The proposed 2027 budget for the Department of Agriculture and its attached corporations, he noted, stands at about ₱198.4 billion, covering programs for production, farm mechanization, post-harvest facilities, market access, crop protection, and livestock development, among others.
“The House will make sure that every peso allocated for agriculture will be used properly and will result in concrete benefits for our farmers,” Dy said.
“We want agricultural spending to be felt not only in reports and statistics, but in higher yields, lower production costs, better market access and larger incomes for farming families.”

He also emphasized the importance of irrigators’ associations, noting that only 2.2 million hectares out of an estimated 3.13 million hectares of irrigable land were being served by irrigation systems as of the end of 2025.

According to him, strong farmers’ and irrigators’ organizations are crucial to making Sagip Saka work because “organized farmers have a stronger voice, greater bargaining power, better access to government support, and more opportunities to sell directly to buyers.”
“We want to reduce the distance between the farm and the market. And ultimately, we want farming to become a profitable and sustainable livelihood,” he said. /atm

articles.title: Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?
articles.summary: The panel discussion starting at 12:30 pm on September 10 brings together stakeholders to identify safety gaps and develop community-led solutions to protect children

blocks.text: The panel discussion starting at 12:30 pm on September 10 brings together stakeholders to identify safety gaps and develop community-led solutions to protect children
MANILA, Philippines – Concerned about your child’s safety and how you can ensure a more secure environment for them?

Watch the live panel discussion as Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH launches “Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?” This will be streamed on Rappler’s YouTube channel live from the Rappler Civic Hub in Pasig City on Thursday, September 10.

Organized in partnership with CyberGuardiansPH and Mental Health Youth Hub, this pilot initiative tackles rising school violence and digital risks by turning community discussions into concrete, multisectoral solutions.
Rappler head of community Pia Ranada moderates the conversation with key decision-makers and child protection advocates:

items: Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte shares local government strategies on community governance, child protection policies, and campus safety.
Police Capt. Wallen Arancillo, spokesperson for the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group, addresses online grooming, cyberbullying, and digital protection in off-campus hotspots.
Dr. Princess Gairanod, child protection specialist from the Philippine Pediatric Society, discusses student mental health, psychosocial care, and health safeguarding protocols.

blocks.text: After the panel discussion and Q and A, participants joining on-site can take part in a hands-on workshop to collectively develop concrete and actionable responses to threats facing children and schools across four Civic Circles:

items: Campus security and physical safety
Psychosocial care and mental health
Policy, governance, and accountability
Digital safety and off-campus hotspots

blocks.text: The solutions generated during the session may be featured on Rappler to encourage a broader discussion and possible adaptation by local governments, schools, families, and communities.
Bookmark this page to watch Rappler’s live broadcast.
To join the conversation, download the Rappler App on iOS or Android, tap the Chat tab, and enter the Education chat room while watching the stream. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Houthis strike Saudi Arabian cities in significant expansion of Middle East war
articles.summary:
Riyadh says it will retaliate after overnight attacks by Iran-backed Yemen group on oil facilities wound more than 70

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia,…

blocks.text: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war.
Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the overnight strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south.
The country would “take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty”, a foreign ministry statement said, demanding a halt to the Houthi strikes on Saudi territory and oil tankers in the Red Sea.

blocks.caption: A screen grab taken from footage released by the Saudi-backed National Resistance Forces in Yemen on Tuesday shows a fighter firing a grenade towards Houthi fighters. Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, said pro-government forces “will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve”.

The Houthis, who control most ⁠of Yemen’s populated areas including the capital, said ⁠they had launched a broad operation deep ​into Saudi territory using drones and missiles to strike an airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushait, and targets belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran on the Yemeni border, and the Aramco facility at Jizan.
Jizan, which is home to one of Saudi Arabia’s biggest refineries, is close to the border with Yemen and was damaged in an attack weeks ago.

Saudi authorities said women and children were among the 73 people hurt. The large numbers of people reportedly wounded suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the US and Israel began their war against Iran in February.

blocks.caption: A rocket being fired from a vehicle-based launcher by the Saudi-backed National Resistance Forces in Yemen. The US-Israel war against Iran has added a dangerous regional dimension to the long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.  Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Im…

blocks.text: While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been entangled in a long running conflict in Yemen, the US-Israel war against Iran has added a dangerous new regional dimension.

After a month of relative calm in August, Iran and the US have resumed exchanges of fire, sending ‌global oil prices back up to levels last seen in July. Brent crude prices were up more than 2% on Tuesday, above $99 a barrel.
Houthi attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the ‌war’s global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade. That war had calmed in recent years, but a ceasefire has broken down, with the Houthis threatening shipping at the mouth of the Red Sea.
The Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching airstrikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond.

blocks.caption: An image released by the Houthis that they say shows damage to the central prison in al-Hazm, Jawf province in Yemen. The Houthis accused Riyadh of escalating the war by launching airstrikes on Yemen.  Photograph: Ansarullah media centre/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, while cutting off Iran’s exports with a blockade ​just beyond it.

Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon reveal details of a “maritime exclusion zone” that will extend from the perimeter of the US blockade through the strait and into the Gulf itself.
Washington fired at Iranian tankers over the weekend in retaliation for Iranian fire at US warships. Iran said it had used new, more capable ballistic missiles to attack American ships.

Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council wrote on X: “In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles. Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to ⁠the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward US warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated.”
Andreas Krieg, a Gulf expert at King’s College London, said the Houthi attacks create an “extremely uncomfortable dilemma” for Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto Saudi ruler.
After four years of trying to withdraw from the Yemen conflict, “restraint now carries the risk of allowing the Houthis to dictate the spiral of escalation”, Krieg said.
AFP and Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Solon, DOLE chief clash over P85 wage hike implementation in Metro Manila
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Kamanggagawa party-list Rep. Elijah San Fernando and Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino clashed on Tuesday over the P85 daily minimum wage increase for Metro Manila workers. San…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Kamanggagawa party-list Rep. Elijah San Fernando and Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino clashed on Tuesday over the P85 daily minimum wage increase for Metro Manila workers.
San Fernando believes it should already be enforced as one criterion for the injunction has not been met.
His view was expressed at the House hearing on the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) proposed budget for 2027.

The lawmaker maintained that Wage Order No. 27 — which grants a P85 wage increase in two tranches — should be in effect because the petitioners have admitted that they could not post the P10 billion bond required by the Pasig Regional Trial Court (RTC).
The injunction bond serves as security for damages to the parties involved should the court decide to reverse its decision.

According to San Fernando, during the House committee on appropriations’ hearing on the judicary’s proposed 2027 budget, Court Administrator Ma. Theresa Gomez-Estoesta confirmed his belief that an injunction cannot be implemented if there is no bond posted.
“In the absence of a writ, nothing stops the DOLE from implementing the wage increase,” San Fernando said in Filipino.

“If that is the case, Secretary, why doesn’t the [DOLE] implement Wage Order No. 27? You yourself said that you stand by the government’s view that if there is no bond, there is no injunction,” the lawmaker asked the labor secretary.
“Therefore, the wage increase for minimum wage earner should have been implemented and given since July 25,” San Fernando told Tolentino.
“Yesterday, the judiciary said during their budget hearing, if there is no bond, there is no injunction. Therefore, Wage Order No. 27 should be in effect,” San Fernando recalled.
He then asked Tolentino for Dole’s stance on the implementation of the wage order.

blocks.caption: Sen. Francis Tolentino (File photo by NIÑO JESUS ORBETA / INQUIRER.net)

blocks.text: Tolentino answered in a manner that echoes the position of the Office of the Solicitor General, noting that “sans a posting of the bond, the writ is not in order.”
San Fernando once again asked why the agency could not enforce the wage order if the secretary himself said that he recognizes that there is no injunction if there is no bond.
Tolentino answered that DOLE believes the lifting the injunction “is not a matter of self help.”
He added: “This means that it is not (up to) Dole and litigants to decide if the process is wrong. The court will decide on this.”
San Fernando reiterated his point and stressed that the Pasig RTC does not have jurisdiction over the case in the first place.
He cited the Article 126 of the Labor Code where the provision prohibits any courts or entity from suspending any wage order issued.

“So what the Dole is saying is that no matter how long your explanation is, at the end of it all, you’re saying that you will not implement the wage hike,” Fernando was seeking clarification from Tolentino.
Tolentino said that he did not mean that DOLE does not want to implement the order. But he reiterated that “this depends on the decision of the judge.”
He added, “I will not argue even if this will be aired on social media.”
The lawmaker then told the secretary that under the Republic Act No. 6727 or the Wage Rationalization Act, regional wage boards have the authority to determine wages.
For his part, Tolentino said that he issued Administrative Order (AO) 264 which provides for unified guidelines for the implementation, monitoring and exemption from wage orders.

Dole earlier said the AO mandates the agency to ensure “that approved wage orders are effective and immediately executory 15 calendar days after its complete publication in a newspaper of general circulation.”

After hearing the secretary’s position, San Fernando moved to defer the committee’s consideration of DOLE’s proposed budget for next year, except for the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority.
The deferment recommendation was seconded by Akbayan party-list Rep. Percival Cendaña.
However, Cagayan de Oro Rep. Rufus Rodriguez objected to the motion.
This situation led to divide lawmakers in voting who were in favor or not in favor of San Fernando’s motion.
Seven lawmakers voted to defer the budget consideration for DOLE while 31 lawmakers were against it.
Last June 30, Tolentino announced the “historic” wage hike of P85 for minimum wage workers in Metro Manila.
The first tranche of P65 was supposed to be effective last July 25, while the second tranche of P20 was due on January 20 next year.
However, the Pasig City RTC Branch 125 issued a temporary restraining order on the implementation of the P85 wage increase until August 13.
This was followed by a petition filed by petitioners Readycon Trading and Construction Corp. and R-II Builders Inc.
The wage increase implementation was further delayed as the court granted the request for writ of preliminary injunction sought by the two firms.
The Office of Solicitor General has asked the Pasig court to resolve its pending motion for reconsideration to lift the freeze order that halted the implementation of the P85 wage hike. /apl

articles.title: IN CHARTS: Literacy of Filipino students in Grades 1 to 3
articles.summary: Around half of all students in Grades 1 to 3 still did not have proficient reading skills by the end of SY 2025-2026, the Department of Education's assessment shows

blocks.text: FIRST DAY. Students of Navarro Elementary School in General Trias City, Cavite, attend the first day of classes on June 8, 2026.
Dennis Abrina/Rappler
Around half of all students in Grades 1 to 3 still did not have proficient reading skills by the end of SY 2025-2026, the Department of Education's assessment shows

items: The Philippines is facing a significant learning crisis, particularly in literacy among children.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao has the highest percentage of struggling readers.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines faces a daunting challenge to fix the decades-long learning crisis in the country, starting with literacy in children’s early years of schooling.

Rappler checked the Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment (CRLA) results from the Department of Education (DepEd) for school year (SY) 2025-2026 to better understand the reading profiles of Key Stage 1 learners, or students in Grades 1 to 3. The data sets were accessed in early June.

Reflected in the data were literacy rates for mother tongue in Grade 1, Filipino in Grade 2, and English in Grade 3. Under the enhanced K to 10 curriculum, the DepEd offers English and Filipino starting Grade 2.

The DepEd’s curriculum standards also suggest that by the end of Grade 3, students are “becoming literate and increasingly fluent” in the use of English, while using their mother tongue to understand and express “familiar and developmentally appropriate texts” or discuss content in various learning areas.
Here are some data visualizations of the literacy of Grades 1 to 3 pupils in the Philippines:

Struggling readers are students assessed to be in low reading profiles. In terms of CRLA results, these are pupils in Grades 1 to 3 who were classified as emerging, broken down into lower or higher emergent.
By the end of SY 2025-2026, there were around 519,000 students from Grades 1 to 3 who struggled with reading. That’s 10% of all assessed students in Key Stage 1.
But the CRLA results also revealed that around half of all students in Grades 1 to 3 still cannot read “at grade level” or at the standard expected for their current grade.

By 2028, the Philippines is targeting 75% of Key Stage 1 learners to be reading at grade level, according to the National Education Plan 2026-2035, which was introduced by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) in January. (READ: [ANALYSIS] What does ‘at least nearly proficient’ mean in Philippine education?)
Among the regions, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) has the highest percentage of struggling readers.
Focusing at the end of Key Stage 1, over 22% of Grade 3 pupils in BARMM remain at low proficiency in literacy.
In its January report, EDCOM 2 stressed that children should be literate by the end of Grade 3 so they do not fall behind in later stages of schooling.
Senior technical officials of BARMM and various national government agencies are already preparing for the first meeting of the newly formed Bangsamoro Education Coordination Forum (BECF).

The BECF, a coordinating mechanism between the national and Bangsamoro governments, will attempt to address issues in early childhood care and development, curriculum and learning, learner support, governance and finance, teacher education, and higher and technical-vocational education in the autonomous region.

blocks.caption: This new coordinating body will try to improve Bangsamoro education

blocks.text: You can also check the percentage of struggling Grade 3 readers per schools division office in the table below.
There are improvements seen in the reading profiles of Grades 1 to 3 pupils, as data showed decreases in the share of struggling readers by the end of SY 2025-2026.
Still, half of the students remain below the proficient level.
That trend is seen throughout the Philippine basic education system.

In its analysis, EDCOM 2 found that while the results show “consistent improvement” within SY 2025-2026, around 18% or 3 million out of 16.5 million students remain in non-proficient reading levels. (READ: Most Grade 11 students struggle with reading. What now?)
The assessment was done after the first full year of implementation of the DepEd’s Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program.
The DepEd was given P8.9 billion for the initiative in 2026. However, for next year, the Department of Budget and Management did not include an allocation for the ARAL Program in the proposed budget.
The ball is with Congress as Education Secretary Sonny Angara appealed for an additional budget to fund the ARAL Program, as well as beef up various aspects of the sector.
Funding for basic education reached P1 trillion in 2026. Will the government push to at least keep the education budget at this level to address the country’s learning crisis? – Rappler.com

articles.title: Alberta man retraces his steps after traumatic brain injury, waking from coma
articles.summary: When Stan Dworkowski awoke from an eight-day coma with 24 broken ribs and a fractured skull, he could not recall his own age or the faces of his closest friends. He is now retracing his steps, hoping…

image.caption: Business owner Stan Dworkowski was found injured in a ditch not far from his truck-polishing shop in Nisku, Alta., on July 14, 2026. (Stan Dworkowski/Facebook)

blocks.text: Edmonton

When Stan Dworkowski awoke from an eight-day coma with 24 broken ribs and a fractured skull, he could not recall his own age or the faces of his closest friends. He is now retracing his steps, hoping to piece together the hours before he was injured.
Living with amnesia, Stan Dworkowski has turned detective on his own case
Stan Dworkowski is missing time.
When he awoke in an Edmonton hospital room from an eight-day coma with 24 broken ribs and a fractured skull, he could not recall his own age or the faces of his closest friends.
More than a month later, Dworkowski says he still has no memory of the day he was found on July 14 injured, lying in a ditch in an industrial park south of the city.

The 41-year-old man has been conducting his own investigation ever since, attempting to reconstruct the hours before he was found unresponsive along the side of the road near his business in Leduc County, on the western outskirts of Nisku, Alta.
Dworkowski said he was found near an electric dirt bike in the ditch and taken from the scene by paramedics. Weeks after his release from hospital, RCMP are now investigating how he was injured.
“What happened that day and what transpired, from the morning to the night, I don't know, as far as my memory of it.”
Social media search
Dworkowski said he suffered a brain bleed and a cranial fracture that left him with a traumatic brain injury and memory loss.
Along with head trauma and fractured ribs, he said his clavicle, orbital bone and pinky were broken and his shoulder was dislocated.
Dworkowski said he spent a week in the intensive care unit of the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton before transferring to the Glenrose Rehabilitation Hospital, returning home on Aug. 14.
In his search for information, he has published a series of social media posts — sharing photos and videos — in his search for witnesses and tips.

To track his movements on that day, Dworkowski analyzed GPS data from his phone, pored over surveillance footage sourced from surrounding businesses, acquired his medical records and tracked down the man who found him.
He said he wants to “solve the mystery” of what happened to him, hoping that by retracing his steps, something will jog his memory.
He said part of why he’s investigating is that he wonders how he could have been so seriously hurt. He’s gone back to the scene and still doesn’t understand how he ended up in the ditch.

Dworkowski said his colleagues have told him that he was working late inside his truck-polishing shop the night he was injured, and left his business on an electric dirt bike he borrowed from one of his employees.
He said surveillance footage shows him on the bike around 6:30 p.m., entering a property about two kilometres south of his shop, just across the road from where he was found.
He said, at this point, his GPS co-ordinates stop moving until his transfer to hospital.
If I was walking on the other side of the road, I probably would not have found him.- Brock Anderson
Brock Anderson found Dworkowski that evening and called paramedics to the scene.

In an interview with CBC News, the Fort McMurray man said he was staying in a hotel nearby before flying to B.C. for a family vacation. After his wife and kids went to bed around 8:30 p.m., he decided to go on a walk.
First he spotted a sandal. Then he came across Dworkowski, motionless in the tall grass, a few steps away from a dirt bike laying on its side.
“I could tell he was breathing, but he wasn't responsive,” Anderson said.
“It was quiet. The bike wasn't making any sounds. He wasn't making any sounds, so if I was walking on the other side of the road, I probably would not have found him.”
Anderson said he called an ambulance to the scene and left shortly after paramedics arrived.
He thought he would likely never get an update on the man he found but ended up connecting with Dworkowski after his colleague found one of his posts on social media.
Anderson said the pair spoke last week and he told Dworkowski where exactly he had been found and provided him with a video he had taken of the scene.
“He mentioned to me that he might have been laying in the ditch there for hours before I came,” Anderson said. “Obviously he didn't know what happened. There's a big gap.
“To be honest with you, I don't really know what happened.”
RCMP open investigation

In a statement to CBC News, officials with Emergency Health Services Alberta said paramedics responded to the area of 4th Street and 13th Avenue in Nisku at 8:50 p.m. on July 14, where a patient was found in serious, potentially life-threatening condition.
In response to questions about Dworkowski’s case, RCMP said a formal police investigation did not begin until Sept. 5.
RCMP said officers did not initially attend the scene when Dworkowski was found and the incident was not formally reported to them until last week.
Police said the investigation remains in its early stages but they have received no report of a collision or a hit and run at the time and location where Dworkowski was found.

Dworkowski said he met with RCMP after a missing person’s file, created when his family reported him missing that night, was closed. He said he felt his injuries were traumatic enough to warrant further investigation.

He said he called the detachment more than a dozen times to ask for an investigation before the file was formally opened last week. He hopes his own research will help speed along the police investigation.
Long recovery ahead

Dworkowski said doctors have told him it could be months or longer before his memory might improve. He's decided to shut down both his truck-polishing operation and the Hot Wheels collectibles shop he owns, to focus on the long recovery ahead.
He said the ordeal has been most traumatic for his wife and four children, who wrote about his experience on a community fundraising campaign page.
But Dworkowski admitted he has been struggling with the lasting effects of his traumatic brain injury as well as anxiety about the memories he’s missing.
“I need to know what happened so I can heal.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Wallis Snowdon is a journalist with CBC Edmonton focused on bringing stories to the website and the airwaves. Originally from New Brunswick, Wallis has reported in communities across Canada, from Halifax to Fort McMurray. She previously worked as a digital and current affairs producer with CBC Radio in Edmonton. Share your stories with Wallis at wallis.snowdon@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Over 1,800 docs for marking for VP Duterte’s wealth scrutiny
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — More than 1,800 documents, including bank and insurance records produced under court-issued subpoenas, are set for marking as prosecutors prepare to present the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — More than 1,800 documents, including bank and insurance records produced under court-issued subpoenas, are set for marking as prosecutors prepare to present the unexplained-wealth article in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Rep. Chel Diokno, lead prosecutor for the second impeachment article, told the court on Tuesday.

The marking of the documents has been set by the Senate impeachment court for Wednesday and Thursday, Sept. 9 and 10, during which the trial proceedings will be suspended so that both the prosecution and the defense can be there.
The proceedings will resume on Monday, Sept. 14.
Diokno asked the court for time to mark the documents and identified the financial records involved in the preparations for the next article against Duterte.
“I am referring, Your Honor, to the bank records and other insurance records,” he said.
Defense seeks more time to study documents

Because of the volume of documents, the prosecution asked for more than a single marking session. At first, Diokno initially sought the whole of Wednesday and raised the possibility of extending the activity to Thursday and Friday.

Presiding Officer Francis Escudero set aside Wednesday and Thursday for marking, with both sessions beginning at 10 a.m. Friday, he noted, could be used for budget proceedings as the Senate manages its legislative work alongside the impeachment trial.
The defense agreed to the arrangement. Defense counsel Michael Poa raised a concern, however, about whether there would be enough time to study the large volume of material before Monday.

Though acknowledging the prosecution’s prerogative to determine the sequence of its presentation, Poa requested at least two weeks to prepare and offered to give up the equivalent days from the defense’s own presentation to offset the requested period.

Escudero kept the Monday hearing date, explaining that the court would have limited time available because of budget deliberations. He proposed allowing the defense the flexibility to choose when it would cross-examine prosecution witnesses, potentially permitting the next witness’s direct testimony to proceed first.
The records preparation also coincided with the prosecution’s filing of a 104-item request for admission as evidence.
Escudero confirmed the number of items with Diokno, while Poa said the defense had received the document that morning and had only briefly reviewed it.
“We will have to study it, Your Honor, because we really did not have time to really peruse through the document,” Poa said.
The defense’s comment concerned the length of the response period rather than the substance of the requests.
Poa asked the court to allow at least 15 days, citing Rule 26, Section 2 of the Rules of Court — not the prosecution’s proposed seven days.

Escudero said the court would rule on that period at the appropriate time. No substantive defense response to the 104 items was given in the exchange, and the court proceeded to arrange the next witnesses without waiting for those requested admissions.
Diokno said the prosecution would submit its subpoena requests and notices identifying the witnesses for the following week within the day or by the next morning.
Escudero directed him to provide the witness information by the following day, together with any proposed stipulations.

The court reiterated the five-day witness-notice agreement reached during the pretrial. That instruction set the timetable for the parties to prepare for the second impeachment article presentation while the records were being organized for marking.
“That would be fine for the prosecution for the marking, Your Honor,” Diokno said when the court proposed the 10 a.m. sessions. /atm

articles.title: Philippines’ reading, math, science scores improve in 2025 PISA
articles.summary: The Department of Education says the Philippines’ ‘strongest PISA performance’ to date ‘should be seen as a starting point,’ with much more to be done

blocks.text: BACK TO SCHOOL. Students of Carmona National High School in Carmona City, Cavite, attend the opening of academic year 2024-2025 on July 29, 2024.
Bonz Magsambol/Rappler
The Department of Education says the Philippines’ ‘strongest PISA performance’ to date ‘should be seen as a starting point,’ with much more to be done

items: The Philippines improved its reading, mathematics, and science rankings in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment.
Education officials emphasize the need to sustain this momentum and continue reforms.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ performance in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) improved in 2025, with the country climbing out of the bottom 10 in the subjects covered.

The Philippines ranked 72nd out of 90 countries in reading, 74th out of 90 countries in mathematics, and 77th out of 91 countries in science, according to the 2025 PISA results released on Tuesday, September 8.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which conducts the test, found that Filipino students had average scores of 373 in science (up by 17 points from the previous PISA edition), 371 in mathematics (up by 16 points), and 367 in reading (up by 20 points).

The Department of Education (DepEd) noted that this is the Philippines’ “strongest PISA performance” to date since the country first joined the global assessment in 2018 and again in 2022, where it saw dismal results both times.
Although an improvement, it “should be seen as a starting point” and “highlights the work that remains,” added the DepEd.

“This is a significant achievement for our learners and for the entire Philippine education system. But more than the numbers, we are seeing evidence that our learners are capable of making real and meaningful progress,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a press release.
“We should be proud of how far our learners and teachers have come, but we should be even more determined about how much farther we can go.”

The Second Congressional Commission on Education said the task now is to sustain the momentum, stressing that education reforms require “consistency of purpose, continuity in implementation, and the commitment of the entire country.”
In 2018, the Philippines was ranked lowest in reading, and second to the last in science and mathematics. Four years after that, the Philippines was still among the bottom 10.

blocks.caption: Philippines’ reading, math, science scores improve in 2025 PISA

blocks.text: The average scores among OECD countries for 2025 were 482 in science, 463 in mathematics, and 461 in reading.

“PISA 2025 recorded the lowest OECD-average performance observed so far in science, reading, and mathematics,” the international group said. “Reading has declined after peaking around 2012, while science has declined more gradually over the past decade, and mathematics has fallen especially sharply after 2018.”
Globally, the Chinese jurisdictions of Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, along with Singapore, were the highest performers across science, mathematics, and reading in 2025.
Also among the top 10 performing education systems in all three subjects were Estonia, Japan, Korea, Macau (China), Chinese Taipei, and the United Kingdom.

According to the DepEd, around 8,000 15-year-old students from 208 schools in the Philippines took part in PISA 2025 through a computer-based assessment. Most of the participating schools were regular public schools, but there were also public science-oriented schools and private schools. – Rappler.com

USWAG Ilonggo Party List Representative James "Jojo" Ang, Jr. on Tuesday entered a plea of not guilty to two charges of graft in cases allegedly involving multi-million contracts with the Department of Public Works and Highways.
The Sandiganbayan ordered Ang’s arrest in July in connection to 14 graft cases filed by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The lawmaker is accused of holding a stake in a company that won P214 million worth of contracts from the Department of Public Works and Highways while he was in office. The firm was awarded P199 million of the total amount.

articles.title: As peso lingers at record-low P62, what does it mean for Filipinos?
articles.summary: The Philippine peso has never been this weak. Here's how that could affect everything from fuel prices to remittances.

blocks.text: The Philippine peso has never been this weak. Here's how that could affect everything from fuel prices to remittances.

items: The Philippine peso has reached record lows against the US dollar, sinking past P62 for the first time, which raises concerns about inflation and economic growth.

Despite the peso's weakness benefiting overseas Filipino workers by increasing their remittances in pesos, the overall economic impact is negative due to rising costs of living and potential higher interest rates.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The Philippine peso has pushed deeper into territory it had never entered before.

For the first time in history, the currency sank past P62 to the US dollar on August 28, closing at a then-record low of P62.265. The peso then touched an unprecedented P62.775 intraday on Monday, September 7, before closing slightly stronger at P62.586.
On Tuesday, September 8, it weakened again to a fresh record-low closing rate of P62.625 to $1.

The peso’s slide began in March 2026, when it sank to an all-time low of P60 to the dollar. A month later, it sank to an all-time low again, breaking past P61. Now, it has sunk to an all-time low yet again, this time beyond P62.
So what does a peso sinking deeper into record-low territory actually mean for the economy?

A weaker peso can make its way to fuel pump prices and grocery checkouts, raise costs for businesses, complicate the central bank’s fight against inflation, and weigh on the Philippines’ economic growth.

For OFW families, a weaker peso might provide some relief since they get more pesos for every dollar sent home. But that gain is partly eroded if the same currency weakness pushes up the cost of fuel, food, transport, and other everyday expenses anyway.

Currency depreciation hits the Philippines particularly hard because it is a country of imports – bringing in large amounts of fuel, food, machinery, raw materials, and other goods all priced and paid for in dollars.

As the peso weakens, Philippine importers have to spend more pesos to pay for exactly the same dollar-priced shipment. Companies can absorb some of that increase through lower profit margins, but they’re more likely to pass the cost on to consumers.

blocks.caption: MAP: Where Filipino families earn the most and least

blocks.text: Fuel is one of the clearest examples of how quickly the exchange rate can ripple through the economy.

At the Department of Energy’s September 7 briefing, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the peso’s depreciation was adding pressure to domestic pump prices because petroleum products are bought in dollars.

DOE officials said the peso weakened by around 68 centavos during the latest pricing period, compounding an increase of roughly $9 to $10 per barrel in petroleum import costs caused by renewed Middle East tensions.

In other words, Filipinos are being hit twice because global oil prices are rising at the same time as the peso is falling. The fuel itself becomes more expensive in dollars, while each dollar needed to buy it also costs more pesos.

The impact goes beyond just motorists having to pay more for their trips. Diesel powers trucks moving food and merchandise around the country too, while businesses depend on imported machinery, fertilizers, ingredients, and other inputs. As those costs rise, companies may eventually pass on at least some of them through higher prices.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] The Philippine economy is stuck in a rut

blocks.text: BPI lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. warned that the recent peso depreciation could fuel further inflation through higher import costs, with headline inflation in August already at a worrying 6.1%. That’s why peso weakness is also becoming a headache for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) as it tries to bring inflation back within its 2% to 4% target range.

The BSP will not, however, defend the currency at a particular level. At an August 27 Senate budget hearing, BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said the central bank can smooth out sharp movements in, but trying to fix the peso at a particular rate would burn through the country’s dollar reserves.
Nevertheless, BSP data show that ammunition remains substantial.

blocks.caption: Photo from the BSP.

blocks.text: The country’s gross international reserves rose to $104.8 billion at end-August, from $103.3 billion in July, largely because higher gold prices boosted the value of the BSP’s holdings and because of income from its overseas investments. The increase was partly offset by government withdrawals of foreign currency to service external debt.

Still, the buffer has thinned from $110.8 billion at the end of 2025. At its August level, reserves could cover about 6.8 months of imports and around 3.7 times the country’s short-term external debt.

“These provide sufficient foreign currency to meet the country’s import needs, service its external debt obligations, and serve as a buffer against external economic shocks,” the BSP said in a statement on Monday.

If depreciation keeps inflation elevated, the BSP may instead have to keep interest rates high for longer or tighten further. Higher borrowing costs can then weigh on household spending, business expansion, housing, and investment, creating another drag on an economy already struggling with slower growth. – Rappler.com

articles.title: House approves bill extending barangay, SK officials' terms
articles.summary: The House of Representatives on Tuesday approved a bill extending the terms of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials.

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 7:19pm
The House of Representatives on Tuesday approved a bill extending the terms of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials.

Lawmakers approved House Bill 10971, which seeks to grant barangay officials a five-year term instead of the existing four-year term, with 211 lawmakers voting in favor, 13 against and one abstaining.
The measure would postpone the next barangay and SK elections to 2028, instead of holding them this year.
House Assistant Minority Leader Renee Co of Kabataan party-list, who voted against the measure, said it was a clear example of perpetuating political patronage.

“The Supreme Court had said that postponement of elections needs a compelling governmental interest, like protecting the right to suffrage, and a real emergency. The law giving them a four-year term is not even a year old, and yet here we are extending it again,” Co, a lawyer, said, referring to the existing law that extended the terms of barangay and SK officials from three to four years.
“This makes this bill, for me, without basis and unconstitutional,” she added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Argentina targets oil company operating in Falklands
articles.summary: The move comes days after President Javier Milei stepped up Argentina's claims of sovereignty over the Falklands.

blocks.text: The Argentine government has said that it would file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands.
The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean.
Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.
The simmering dispute heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the Falklands.
Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.
In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that."
The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty.
He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory.
Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination".
The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering".

Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives.
Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities.
"The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted.

Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development".
Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement.
Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands.
