articles.title: Gen Z uprising reshaped Nepal’s politics. A year on, questions linger
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Rakesh Mahato lies in a hospital bed in Kathmandu with a simple wish—to get up, take a few steps and make it home. The 25-year-old from Sarlahi district has spent the entirety of…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Rakesh Mahato lies in a hospital bed in Kathmandu with a simple wish—to get up, take a few steps and make it home.
The 25-year-old from Sarlahi district has spent the entirety of the past year in hospital after being shot by police while protesting against corruption on September 8, 2025.

Mahato is among the thousands injured during the youth-led uprising, which has come to be known as the Gen Z protests. Although the immediate trigger was the KP Sharma Oli government’s ban on social media, the youth were protesting systemic corruption and decades of power-sharing among a small group of ageing politicians.

The protests began as a peaceful demonstration but soon spiralled out of control, leading to massive casualties and the loss of private and public property. As many as 76 people were killed and 2,638 were injured during the demonstrations on September 8 and the violence that followed the next day. The spontaneous protests became a historic political event—triggering a major upheaval in the young democracy and turning the lives of thousands, including Mahato’s, upside down.
People, however, have yet to see the promises of the monumental movement translate into their daily lives, activists who took part in the protests say.

The faces in Singha Durbar, the country’s administrative centre, have changed. For the injured and families of those killed, however, life remains frozen on the two days of the uprising. Kantipur spoke to nearly a dozen people affected by the protests. Their demands were strikingly consistent—an end to corruption, better governance and a state that answers to its citizens. The movement transformed Nepal’s political leadership. Shah, once mayor of Kathmandu, became prime minister after the election. The party secured a near two-thirds majority. But for those who bled on the streets, little has changed, Mahato says.

blocks.caption: Prakash Bohora, 29, from Dailekh, became a symbol of the Gen Z uprising after an image of his blood-stained white shoes went viral. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Mahato was one of thousands of ambitious young men who travel to Kathmandu every year from across Nepal, seeking opportunities beyond their rural villages and small towns. He was studying for a bachelor’s degree at a commerce college and preparing for Loksewa, Nepal’s civil service examinations. He hoped to support his struggling family, get his younger brother a good education and make it big himself. Even in the capital city, jobs were scarce and the economy was in freefall. Like thousands of others, the Mahato brothers grew disillusioned by what they saw. Attributing these systemic issues to entrenched corruption, nepotism, and favouritism, they joined the protests together.

The demonstration was peaceful until shortly after noon, when gunfire suddenly erupted. One protester, Dipendra Basnet, was shot in the head in front of Parliament. Mahato and others rushed to help him. “That’s when police opened fire from behind,” Mahato recalled to Kantipur from his hospital bed. “I was shot in the belly and then I collapsed on the spot.”

The bullet entered through the right side of his abdomen and lodged on the left. Mahato regained consciousness three days later. By then, the protests had already set in motion a dramatic political transition. Gen Z representatives had proposed former chief justice Sushila Karki as interim prime minister during talks with army chief Ashok Raj Sigdel, while discussions were under way at the president’s office over forming a new government.

Mahato, meanwhile, was struggling to move his legs in the intensive care unit at the National Trauma Centre. He could not. A doctor eventually told him that he would never walk again and would probably depend on a wheelchair for the rest of his life. The nerves below his waist had been severed.
Mahato was devastated.

On September 12, four days after Oli resigned, an interim government was formed under Karki, following the violent uprising. Six months later, parliamentary elections brought the Rastriya Swatantra Party to a near two-thirds majority, and Balendra Shah, the rapper, structural engineer and former mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, became the prime minister. That a 35-year-old political novice had become the prime minister was a tectonic shift for the country’s politics dominated by a handful of geriatric men.
Mahato watched from his hospital bed as Shah took office. He was hopeful.

A year later, that hope has receded. “They haven’t even investigated who shot us and why,” Mahato said. “No one has been punished. Sometimes it feels like this government is no different from the previous ones.”

An inquiry led by former chief justice Gauri Bahadur Karki concluded that police had used excessive and indiscriminate force during the protests. The panel said security forces fired continuously for about four hours before a curfew was imposed and that the police and the political leadership failed to intervene.

The report prompted police to arrest former prime minister Oli and former home minister Ramesh Lekhak on charges linked to the deaths during the crackdown. Shah’s first Cabinet meeting had decided to implement the inquiry’s recommendations. The two were later released after the Supreme Court considered a habeas corpus petition.
But police have yet to file a case against them. Home Minister Sudan Gurung told Kantipur recently that investigators were gathering enough evidence.

For the injured protesters, however, the legal process offers little comfort. Many say the government has failed to honour earlier commitments to provide full medical treatment, jobs for one family member of the injured and employment suited to injured protesters’ qualifications.
For some, life has become unbearable.

An agreement reached between the Gen Z representatives and Karki’s interim government on December 10 said the state would establish a permanent body to promote integrity and good governance, fight corruption and end impunity. It also promised an emergency task force to address the immediate and long-term needs of families of those killed and injured, including compensation, free medical care and psychological counselling, education, employment, social security and a permanent memorial.
Many now say the government has forgotten those promises.

blocks.caption: Kamal Ghimire was discharged around mid-December last year. He now regrets taking part in the protest. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Kamal Ghimire of Kavre still carries the scars of a gunshot wound to his chest. He has become accustomed to the physical pain. But the disappointment is harder to bear, he says. “Doctors had said I might not survive, and that’s perhaps why the wound no longer hurts as much,” he said. “But my heart hurts. I feel that this pain will stay with me for the rest of my life…They call this a Gen Z government. Then why have they forgotten the injured?”

Ghimire was discharged around mid-December last year. He now regrets taking part in the protest. “Those who went into government came out untouched,” he said. “Their lives carried on as normal. We’re the ones left with ruined bodies and no way to rebuild our lives. We can’t go abroad to seek work, and there’s little we can do here. So what do we gain from the movement if the government still can’t give us proper access to education, healthcare or jobs?”

The government had promised to cover Ghimire’s medical expenses. Yet he says he has been paying for follow-up treatment himself and previously had to buy medicines outside the hospital. His family has spent about Rs1.5 million on his treatment, he said.

Shree Krishna Shrestha, an additional secretary at the Ministry of Health, said the government could not reimburse bills for medicines or treatment bought independently outside the designated hospital system. Under government rules, hospitals treating injured protesters must submit claims themselves, he said.

According to Health Ministry figures, one Gen Z protester, Daulat Thapa, is still being treated at the Kathmandu Medical College in Sinamangal. “He is still in a coma and is receiving intensive care, but there has been no improvement,” Shrestha said. Mahato continues to receive regular physiotherapy.
For others, the financial burden is becoming overwhelming.

blocks.caption: Bhandari lives in a rented room in Lokanthali and counts the days until his next hospital visit. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Rabi Bhandari, 29, from Sindhuli, survived a gunshot to the leg. But survival has not felt like a victory. At times, he says, he wonders whether it would have been easier to be among the 76 protesters who were killed.

Bhandari lives in a rented room in Lokanthali and counts the days until his next hospital visit. But every appointment brings the same question: how will he pay the bills? He was treated at B&B Hospital, where staff have told him he will now have to pay for treatment.

Additional Secretary Shrestha said the government prefers public hospitals because private treatment can be prohibitively expensive. But he acknowledged that officials were considering how to address cases involving protesters treated in private facilities.

Karki’s interim government had also introduced a system to classify injured protesters according to the severity of their disabilities. Those classified as very seriously injured receive a monthly allowance of Rs18,000, those in the serious category Rs9,000, and those classified as moderately or mildly injured Rs4,000.

Bhandari says the classification was poorly handled. “Many people were placed in the moderate or mild categories without properly examining their injuries and medical reports,” he said. “I was initially classified as moderate. I kept appealing, and only this year was I moved to the serious category.”

He now receives Rs9,000 a month. “But what can you do with Rs9,000?” he said. He has received only the monthly subsistence allowance and an additional Rs35,000 from the government so far. “The allowance does not even cover my rent,” he said.

Law Minister Sobita Gautam said the government was doing what it could within its authority. She said the government was also helping protesters who had travelled to India for treatment and was committed to providing free treatment within Nepal.
The frustrations extend beyond healthcare.

Ambika BK, from Udayapur, took a contract job in the administration section of the Nepal Electricity Authority’s Ratnapark office two months ago. But with limited pay and few benefits, the job has done little to ease the financial strain. “Most of what I earn, around Rs20,000 to Rs22,000, goes on rent and food,” she said. “There’s hardly anything left for my children’s education and healthcare.”

The job has brought another source of pain. She says people sometimes insult her in front of her colleagues, saying she got the job only because her husband died in the protest. “Sometimes I feel like quitting because of that,” she said.

BK’s husband, Santosh, was 28 and worked in a jewellery factory. On the morning of September 8, he returned home for lunch after work. He told his wife that the Oli government had shut down social media and that a peaceful protest was taking place.
“We have to go,” he told her. He left home at around 11.30am.
He never returned.

BK says the government that came to power on the back of the Gen Z movement has given families like hers little reason for hope. “Most of what was done happened under Sushila Karki’s government,” she said. “The government that followed has barely cared about the families of those killed.” She added she sent 14 or 15 demands through Home Minister Sudan Gurung but received no meaningful response.

She also holds Shah responsible. “Balen did not even visit the injured in hospital or pay tribute to the dead,” she said. “Promises about free education, healthcare and jobs for our children remain unfulfilled.”
Her children were eventually offered free education through grade 12 by Golden Peak Group.
For BK, that has not erased the loss. She often breaks down while looking at her husband’s photograph hanging on the wall.

The organisations representing the injured and bereaved families say the government’s record is equally disappointing. Gen Z leader Sarisma Thapa said several demands, including the creation of a Gen Z council, remain unresolved. “Even getting identity cards issued to injured protesters took sustained pressure,” she said. “Some people have been kept in limbo with token offers of jobs in government offices, on contracts or as administrative assistants.”

Despite the promise of free treatment, she said many injured protesters still have to buy medicines themselves beyond what public hospitals provide. She also said young protesters arrested in connection with the unrest remain in jail even though the government had agreed not to prosecute people simply for participating in the demonstrations.
For the families of those killed and the protesters who survived, September 8 remains an event that continues to shape daily life.

blocks.caption: Ambika BK, from Udayapur, took a contract job in the administration section of the Nepal Electricity Authority’s Ratnapark office two months ago. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Roshan Gautam, secretary of the Gen Z Martyrs’ Families Welfare Society, said the government had effectively abandoned them. “The prime minister has not even met the families of the dead and injured once,” he said. “Compensation is still a distant prospect.”

Some injured protesters also tried to turn their place in the movement into a role in Parliament, government or the ruling party. Prakash Bohora, 29, from Dailekh, was one of them. He became a symbol of the Gen Z uprising after an image of his blood-stained white shoes went viral. But he never secured a political role.

Bohora now relies on crutches to walk, and even passing through New Baneshwar can bring back painful memories. “Sometimes, when I pass the parliament building, it still hurts,” he said. “I find myself wishing I never had to go there.”

He is now staying at a hostel in Kathmandu while making regular follow-up visits to Bir Hospital. He still needs four more operations on his left leg, which was shot during the protests on September 8. He was discharged only five months later, on February 3.

Bohora contested the parliamentary election on a proportional-representation ticket for the Rastriya Swatantra Party but was not elected. He later ran for the party’s central committee at its general convention in Chitwan, but lost.

He is now frustrated by the absence of Gen Z victims in both government and Parliament. Their lack of representation, he says, has left their grievances easier to ignore. “But we will not stop asking questions until the demands and issues we raised are addressed,” he said. “And if the government forgets what citizens expected from this movement, we will continue to hold it to account.”
Even those who joined the protests and survived are wondering whether the movement will actually change their future.

Dhiraj Joshi, a Gen Z protester who took part in talks at the Nepali Army headquarters in the early hours of September 9, said protesters never took to the streets expecting to be injured, killed or rewarded. “No one joins a protest thinking they will be injured, killed or honoured,” he said. “But once people have been killed and injured, the government has a responsibility to honour the commitments it made.”

The movement was ultimately driven by demands for accountability, transparency and an end to corruption, Joshi said. Those in power must also recognise the sacrifices made by the injured and the families of those killed, he added. “A year on, it does not feel like the government is moving towards greater accountability,” Joshi told Kantipur. “The government appears to be falling short on accountability, responsibility and democratic values.”

Law Minister Sobita Gautam said the government was in regular contact with injured protesters and families of those killed and that the Gen Z Council would provide a more formal channel for that engagement.

“It’s not that we have stopped talking to them,” she said. “But it can sometimes be difficult to speak to everyone individually. That is why we want the Gen Z Council to serve as a channel through which their concerns can reach the government.”

She said the government was already in direct talks with the affected families and protesters and acknowledged their frustration over the delays. “Understandably, they feel things are taking too long,” she said. “But we needed time to work out how to implement the agreements and set up the necessary mechanisms. That work is under way, and it should not take much longer.”
Meanwhile, a year after rallying in Kathmandu for a corruption-free Nepal, injured protesters say they are left with little more than frustration and regret.

Mahato, who was shot in the belly and collapsed on the spot, says he is disappointed that the current government hasn’t investigated who shot them and why. He adds he keeps repeating the same question to himself: “When will I be able to stand and walk again?”
Bhandari, who sustained a gunshot in his leg, says he regrets his decision to join the protests. “Sometimes I ask myself why the bullet hit my leg,” he says. “Why didn’t it hit my chest?” /dl

articles.title: Russia, North Korea open first road bridge across border
articles.summary: SEOUL — North Korea called the first road bridge across its narrow border with Russia a concrete sign of tightening bonds, state media reported Tuesday, as the Ukraine war draws the…

blocks.text: SEOUL — North Korea called the first road bridge across its narrow border with Russia a concrete sign of tightening bonds, state media reported Tuesday, as the Ukraine war draws the Western-sanctioned nations closer.
The bridge over the Tumen river, which Russia said is designed to accommodate a projected growth in freight and passenger traffic, adds to the rail and air links between the neighbours.
The ceremony on Monday marking its opening came as Russia and North Korea have heavily boosted military and economic ties since Moscow launched its Ukraine offensive in 2022.

“The completion of the bridge is a significant event adding a new dynamic movement to the overall bilateral cooperation,” North Korean official Pak Thae Song said, according the official KCNA news agency.
Video published by the Russian government showed trucks from both sides crossing the bridge, as crowds lining the road applauded.
“The launch of the first automobile route will further strengthen the connection between our friendly countries,” Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in a video link at the ceremony.

KCNA added that the new bridge ensures “safe passage of various forms of transport and the movement of people,” and has “strengthened a key infrastructure component for economic cooperation between North Korea and Russia.”

North Korea dispatched thousands of troops to Russia in 2024 to help ward off a Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region, while Kyiv has accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles in its nightly barrages.
The two countries signed a defence treaty in 2024 that provides for mutual support if either country is attacked.
One of the world’s most isolated and repressive countries, North Korea bars most its citizens from leaving and heavily monitors incoming travellers.
Russian tourism to North Korea has increased in recent years, although Pyongyang sometimes closes its border at short notice.

South Korea’s central bank estimated in July that North Korea’s economy grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, citing it’s expansion of economic cooperation with Russia as a “major drive.”
The bank’s official said North Korea’s gross national income also “received a boost from a sharp rise in foreign currency earnings” linked to the deployment of its troops to Russia.

Ukrainian rights group Truth Hounds, meanwhile, previously warned that the new bridge could become “a direct artery for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, with Russian technology and resources flowing in the opposite direction”. /dl

articles.title: Nepal flood death toll rises to 1,355, nearly 5,000 unaccounted for
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The confirmed death toll from catastrophic flash floods in northern Nepal has risen to 1,355, with 4,996 people still unaccounted for, according to government data released on…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The confirmed death toll from catastrophic flash floods in northern Nepal has risen to 1,355, with 4,996 people still unaccounted for, according to government data released on Monday.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said search and rescue teams had recovered 1,355 bodies from eight districts following the late-August floods. Chitwan recorded the highest number of fatalities with 363, followed by Nawalparasi East with 222 and Nawalparasi West with 221.
Of those still unaccounted for, 2,340 are from Nuwakot and 1,967 from Rasuwa. The figure also includes 589 foreign nationals and around 100 security and government personnel.

Emergency teams have rescued 13,396 people so far. More than 21,000 security personnel remain deployed in the worst-hit mountain areas, including 9,287 soldiers from the Nepali Army, 7,912 personnel from the Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force. Preliminary estimates put losses to property, housing and infrastructure at Rs387.5 billion ($2.56 billion).

Helicopters have been crucial in reaching isolated areas of the Himalayas. Military, paramilitary and private operators based in Kathmandu have carried out nearly 1,500 flights to deliver supplies and evacuate survivors.

The government has allocated Rs160 million ($1.06 million) in emergency funds to affected district offices and municipal councils. More than 3,500 displaced people are being housed in 39 holding centers, while medical teams have treated 6,672 injured people.

Restoration of essential infrastructure is under way. Electricity has been restored to more than 78 percent of households in Rasuwa, over 96 percent in Nuwakot and more than 99 percent in Dhading. Telecommunications operators have also restored nearly 98 percent of damaged mobile towers.
Humanitarian agencies say difficult access and damaged roads remain the main obstacles to delivering heavy equipment and sustaining relief operations in remote parts of the affected districts. /dl

articles.title: A flood of bad news leaves Nepal’s tourist hubs eerily quiet
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The impact of the floods in the Bhotekoshi River is beginning to ripple through Nepal’s tourist industry, with hotels reporting a wave of cancellations just as the peak autumn…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The impact of the floods in the Bhotekoshi River is beginning to ripple through Nepal’s tourist industry, with hotels reporting a wave of cancellations just as the peak autumn tourist season gets underway.

Hotels in Pokhara, Chitwan and Lumbini say domestic and foreign tourists have cancelled their bookings following reports that have portrayed Nepal as unsafe in the wake of the August 26 disaster. Domestic travellers have also called off their plans because of difficult road conditions.
As a result, hotels in some of the country’s major tourist destinations are largely deserted during what is normally one of the busiest times of the year.

Sauraha in Chitwan, for instance, would be bustling with tourists at this time of year. This year, however, only a handful of tourists can be seen in the popular jungle destination. The Regional Hotel Association said hotel occupancy has fallen below 5 percent.
“There are hardly any tourists at the moment,” said Suman Ghimire, former president of the Regional Hotel Association Sauraha. “Hotel occupancy is below 5 percent.”

Ghimire’s Jungle Safari Lodge has 34 rooms. But after bookings were cancelled, most of the rooms are now empty, he said. Tourists have stopped travelling to Chitwan by road after the Krishnabhir section of the highway was washed away by floods.
Although the Bhotekoshi flood did not cause any damage in Chitwan, Ghimire said the destination was suffering because negative reports about Nepal had spread through travel advisories.
“There is no problem on the East-West Highway,” he said. “But tourism has been hit because reports have spread internationally portraying the situation in Nepal as disastrous.”

As alternatives to the damaged Mugling-Kathmandu section of the Prithvi Highway, the Hetauda-Kathmandu road, also known as the Kanti Lokpath, the Tribhuvan Highway and the Hetauda-Kulekhani road are operational. Tourists can use these routes to reach Chitwan. There is also no difficulty in reaching Chitwan by air from Kathmandu to Bharatpur.
Royal Tulip Chitwan Hotel, operated by KTM Hospitality, has 65 rooms. Rameshwar Sah, chairman of Royal Tulip, said 80 percent of bookings have been cancelled so far.

“The tourism sector has been severely hit by the floods,” Sah said. “Although the destinations themselves have not been affected by the floods, rumors and misleading reports about the situation have had a significant impact.”
Sauraha has 125 small and large hotels with a combined capacity to accommodate 8,000 tourists a day.
Gunaraj Thapaliya, vice-president of the Regional Hotel Association, said the impact was particularly visible in Sauraha.
“Except for a handful of Chinese tourists, there are no visitors in Sauraha at the moment,” he said.

Large hotels in Patihani and Meghauli are also waiting for tourists to return. At the Soaltee Westend Chitwan Resort in Patihani, Bharatpur, the number of guests has dropped sharply since the floods, said Choplal Pandey, general manager of the hotel.

“We are receiving messages from foreign tourists cancelling their bookings one after another,” he said. “Forty percent of bookings have already been cancelled. We became more concerned when guests also began cancelling bookings made through November.”
Pokhara, the tourist city in Kaski district, has also not escaped the impact.
Hari Bhujel, chairman of the Tourism Council, said the Bhotekoshi floods and damage to the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir have added to the challenges facing tourism in Pokhara.
“The tourist season for foreign visitors has begun,” he said. “But up to 30 percent of hotel bookings have been cancelled at present.”

He said the closure of the Prithvi Highway, increased airfares, inadequate flights between Pokhara and Kathmandu and the continued charging of dollar-denominated fares to foreign tourists have directly affected tourism in Pokhara.
The damage at Krishnabhir has also affected the arrival of Indian tourists travelling from Sunauli to Pokhara, then to Muktinath and on to Pashupatinath, he said.

“With the recent increase in fuel prices making airfares more expensive, the arrival of domestic tourists is also expected to decline,” he said. “However, it is necessary to convey the message to foreign tourists that destinations other than the areas affected by the floods are safe.”
Lumbini, the birthplace of Buddha, has also begun to see fewer tourists.

Lilamani Sharma, president of the Lumbini Hotel Association, said foreign tourists travelling to Lumbini via Kathmandu have been cancelling their hotel bookings. Bookings made for the main October-November season are also being cancelled, he said.
He said bookings were being cancelled because information was being circulated abroad in a way that made it appear that Nepal as a whole had been affected by the floods.
“The problem travelling to and from Kathmandu is because one or two sections of the Mugling-Kathmandu road have been damaged,” he said. “Even that situation is gradually improving.”

Khim Shrestha, operator of Hotel Suramma in Lumbini, said the government should take the initiative to communicate through foreign diplomatic missions in Nepal and international media that the situation in the country is improving and that Nepal is eager to welcome foreign visitors.

Bhavishwar Adhikari, operational manager of Hotel Hokke, a four-star boutique hotel in Lumbini, said 100 room-nights booked on various dates over a two-month period have been cancelled. He said the tourism sector would be badly affected if the government failed to immediately communicate internationally that the situation in the country was normal.
Prakash Bhattarai, operator of Shakya Guest House, said the problem was being compounded by the failure to communicate accurate information.

“One or two problems seen on the roads should not be exaggerated,” he said. “The local and federal governments should prioritise both information dissemination and repair and maintenance work to revive the tourism sector.”

Chandra Prakash Shrestha, president of Hotel Association Nepal’s Lumbini Province chapter, said Indian tourists arriving on package tours through border points such as Belahiya to visit various destinations have also been affected.

Indian tourists come to visit religious sites in the high Himalayan region. Following reports that the Himalayan region had been devastated by floods, they are understood to have cancelled their bookings.
Although tourists continue to visit border towns and nearby destinations for short stays, Shrestha said there had been a sharp decline in tourists travelling on package tours.
The tourist bus park at Mustang Chowk in Pokhara, which normally sees a steady flow of passengers from morning until night, is now deserted.
Twenty-four buses used to leave the bus park for Kathmandu in the morning and eight at night.

According to Buddhi Sagar Paudel, an employee at the Mustang Chowk branch of Prithvi Highway Bus Operators Company, 14 tourist buses used to leave from Prithvi Chowk, eight from Lamachaur, two from Hemja and two from Zero Kilometre.
At present, only tourist buses travelling to Chitwan and Lumbini are operating.
The Nepal Association of Tour and Travel Agents (NATTA) Gandaki also inspected an alternative route to bypass Krishnabhir on Saturday.

Sangita Paudel, president of NATTA Gandaki, said the association studied a route that involves crossing a suspension bridge from Krishnabhir to reach Jyāmire on the opposite side and then travelling 11 kilometres to reach Benighat.

“A diversion is currently being constructed at Krishnabhir and it is expected to come into operation within a week,” Paudel said. “But it is uncertain how long it will remain operational. If it cannot operate for a long period, the Jyamire-Benighat route could serve as an alternative.”

She said an alternative was being sought because large vehicles cannot travel along the Tribhuvan Highway from Hetauda to Naubise. The disruption to tourist vehicles has directly affected nearly 1,000 business operators and workers, Paudel said.
Meanwhile, the Lumbini Development Trust has said Lumbini, the birthplace of peace, remains completely safe and open despite the difficult situation in the country caused by the Bhotekoshi floods.

In a statement issued on Sunday, the trust said Lumbini had not been affected by the floods or the disaster and that, at a time when people were engaged in relief, rescue and assistance efforts, the Buddhist values of compassion, loving-kindness and harmony remained equally relevant. Visiting Lumbini, it said, could be meaningful for those seeking a sense of peace and spiritual energy.

“The recent floods have not affected the greater Lumbini area,” said Himal Upreti, acting member-secretary of the Lumbini Development Trust. “Lumbini, Kapilvastu, Devdaha, Ramgram and other major tourist destinations remain open to visitors.”

“The Bhotekoshi flood has created a negative message that the entire country is experiencing fear and hardship,” he said. “That is why we have to reassure the international community that Lumbini is safe and accessible.” /dl

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 10:59am
This photo take on July 3, 2026 shows media workers in Senate preparing their equipment ahead of the start of impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — A proposed measure in the Senate seeks to grant hazard pay and additional benefits to media workers who face occupational hazards while performing their duties.

Senate Bill No. 2440, or the proposed Media Workers Hazard Pay Act, seeks to require employers of public and private media entities to provide a minimum P650 daily hazard pay for media workers assigned to dangerous, embattled, or disease-infested areas.

“Media workers working for government or private entities who are already enjoying similar benefits equal or superior to the above amount shall no longer be entitled to such hazard pay,” the bill read.
It also proposed to provide mandatory additional insurance to media personnel in the event of death or injury in the course of their duties.

Among the proposed additional insurance benefits are a death benefit worth up to P200,000 for each media worker, a disability benefit also worth up to P200,000, and medical insurance worth up to P100,000.

The proposed bill also included a clause for overtime work and night shift differential pay for media personnel who are required to work beyond the normal eight-hour duty and for those who work between 10:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. the next day.

The bill said the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) will coordinate with the Civil Service Commission and other relevant agencies to establish the guidelines to accredit media workers for such benefits.
The bill was filed by Sen. Mark Villar, who cited the role of the media in providing information to the public during challenging conditions, such as in the middle of conflicts and rough weather.

“Media workers serve as the eyes and ears of the public during the most difficult and dangerous situations. If we expect them to face danger to keep our fellow citizens safe and well-informed, it is also our duty to ensure that they are protected, insured, and fairly compensated,” Villar said in a statement.

articles.title: Praying for rain as fires, haze plague Indonesian Borneo
articles.summary: PONTIANAK, Indonesia — Wildfires ravaging the Indonesian part of Borneo island are choking communities as far away as Malaysia with putrid haze, testing the resources and resolve of those…

blocks.text: PONTIANAK, Indonesia — Wildfires ravaging the Indonesian part of Borneo island are choking communities as far away as Malaysia with putrid haze, testing the resources and resolve of those having to endure them.

Blamed partly on one of the worst episodes of the drought-inducing El Nino weather phenomenon in decades, the disaster threatens millions of people’s access to necessities such as clean water and air — even education.
Here is the situation as seen from the perspective of three community leaders in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province, one of the worst-affected regions:
The teacher
Syarifah Hatifah, the 57-year-old vice principal of a junior high school in provincial capital Pontianak, fears some of her nearly 600 pupils may be falling behind.
They are in the third week of the second school closure this fire season. It’s the longest closure Syarifah can remember in her 30-year career.
Hundreds of schools have been closed indefinitely in West Kalimantan due to air pollution, with about 200,000 pupils learning from home, according to the provincial education ministry.
The kids are being kept home for their health, Syarifah told AFP in a classroom empty but for two teachers presenting classes online, both with dozens of pupils scattered across their screens.
“The hope is that at home, in terms of health, they can be protected… because they are inside the house. They don’t have to go through roads full of dust and smoke,” she said.
But Syarifah said not every child has stable internet or access to a computer, making live sessions difficult for some.
“Sometimes… there is a power outage at their home, or they forget to charge their phones”, and some students live in faraway areas with patchy connectivity, she said.
The school’s teachers have been showing up every day as usual, giving lessons online in classrooms with no air purifiers. They work maskless so students can understand them clearly.
Syarifah said the school would offer extra lessons for free once in-person learning resumes.
“We hope that this haze will pass quickly. Usually after the rain falls, the haze will disappear,” she said.
West Kalimantan’s wetter season usually starts around October or November.
The health official
Iwansyah, head of the Kubu Raya regency’s health agency, is responsible for the welfare of some 700,000 people spread over 123 villages, served by one general hospital and 21 clinics.
His staff focus on efforts to prevent illness caused by “the unhealthy air people inhale every day”.
So far in September, more than 1,400 people in the regency have been treated or hospitalised for acute respiratory infections, said Iwansyah, who like many Indonesians has one name.

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows the Ampera Bridge over the Musi river shrouded in haze caused by forest fires in Palembang, South Sumatra on September 3, 2026. Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: In August, the number was 6,396.
“We distribute masks to the public every day, about one thousand masks per day. Of course our stock is starting to run low,” the official told AFP.
Iwansyah said the agency had requested additional masks from the provincial government, and was encouraging people to buy their own.
The agency also monitors cases of diarrhoea brought on by reduced access to clean water due to the drought, with 225 cases so far this month.

With Indonesia’s BMKG weather agency warning of little respite in the weeks ahead, “we will have to work even harder on mitigation and preparing for a potentially very severe situation”, said Iwansyah.
This includes stocking up on medicines and equipment at clinics and intensifying surveys of water and air quality.
“Hopefully there will be rain between now and November,” Iwansyah said.
The hamlet head
For Yonas, deputy head of the Lintang Batang hamlet outside Pontianak, the priority is firefighting equipment.

“The residents here even pooled money to buy a (water pump) machine and hoses, and other equipment,” he told AFP on Sunday night while battling a peatland fire that had been raging for four days, emitting acrid smoke.
“We’re still short of hoses, which makes it hard for us to extinguish this fire.”

Volunteer firefighters were using “whatever we have. Sometimes we use buckets, and even those aren’t enough”, said Yonas, adding that the teams were also in need of food and protective gear, including masks.
He said the smoke posed a danger especially for children, pregnant women, the elderly and people with asthma.
Scientific observations show the haze contains levels of toxic small particle pollution far exceeding the World Health Organization’s recommended safe limit.
“It’s very hazardous to the health of us who live in this village,” said Yonas. /dl

articles.title: Prosecutors ask ICC to examine documents linking ex-Pres Duterte to DDS
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors have asked Trial Chamber III to examine documents submitted by a witness that may link former President Rodrigo Duterte to the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors have asked Trial Chamber III to examine documents submitted by a witness that may link former President Rodrigo Duterte to the Davao Death Squad or DDS.

According to the document made public Monday, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang filed a request on August 31 seeking permission for the witness, identified as “P-1100,” to submit a statement instead of testifying in person.

The prosecution cited Rule 68 of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which allows parties to invoke prior recorded testimony before a witness’s scheduled testimony. However, such submissions remain subject to cross-examination and questioning by the Trial Chamber.
“The Prior Recorded Testimony of P-1100… is particularly relevant to the policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines,” Niang wrote.
He continued: “It also provides evidence of the Davao Death Squad’s modus operandi as well as [Duterte’s] criminal responsibility, including in relation to his knowledge and intent.”
Primarily, the prosecution reasoned that the request is to expedite Duterte’s proceedings, “having the health of [Duterte] in mind.”
Niang also wrote that, should the request be granted, the length of the witness’ direct examination would be reduced from seven hours to two hours.

Duterte is facing two counts of murder as crimes against humanity, and one count of attempted murder and murder as a crime against humanity for his supposed role in the drug war as president of the Philippines and as Davao City mayor.
His trial is scheduled to commence on November 30, 2026. /jpv

articles.title: Romualdez seeks hospital custody until medically cleared
articles.summary: The former speaker cited Manuel Bonoan who was allowed to remain hospitalized while in custody.

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 9:54am

Rep. Martin Romualdez (Leyte) lies in a hospital bed at Cardinal Santos Medical Center as police place him under custody on Sept. 7, 2026, following the Sandiganbayan's issuance of a warrant in a P7.44-billion plunder case.
Philstar.com / Contributed photo

MANILA, Philippines — Rep. Martin Romualdez (Leyte) asked the Sandiganbayan to allow him to remain under custody at Cardinal Santos Medical Center until doctors clear him for transfer to a detention facility.

In a manifestation and urgent motion late Monday, September 7, Romualdez's lawyers said his request was not an attempt to avoid arrest or custody, but an accommodation for what they described as documented medical needs requiring continued inpatient care.
"Accused Romualdez has a documented cardiac history and has remained under continuing care for that condition," the manifestation read.

Romualdez proposed a court-supervised arrangement that would include round-the-clock guards, visitor restrictions and a visitor log, periodic medical certificates, independent verification of his condition and a prohibition on leaving or transferring from the hospital without court approval except for medical emergencies.

"Accused seeks no exemption from arrest, custody, booking, security restrictions, court appearances, or eventual transfer to the detention facility designated by the Honorable Court," the motion said.
His lawyers asked that he remain at Cardinal Santos "for so long as inpatient confinement remains medically necessary" and until he is medically cleared for transfer.

The filing cited Romualdez's history of cardiovascular disease and several other conditions, as well as an angioplasty he underwent in October 2024. It also lists other conditions including hypertension, coronaru artery disease, Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and hypothyroidism.

It also cited a June Sandiganbayan ruling that allowed former Public Works secretary Manuel Bonoan to remain under hospital arrest despite a no-bail recommendation, subject to government medical evaluation, security and regular reports to the court. Bonoan has since been released from detention on the promise of his testimony as state witness to how public flood-control funds have been siphoned through private contractors and substandard or nonexistent projects.
Romualdez was arrested Monday night at Cardinal Santos after the Sandiganbayan issued a warrant over a P7.44-billion plunder case filed by the Ombudsman.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said police would check Romualdez's condition daily until he was well enough to be presented to court. Armed police were stationed outside his room while he remained under custody.
The Sandiganbayan has said it would make its own assessment of whether Romualdez's medical condition affects his transfer to a regular detention facility. — with reports from Ian Laqui

articles.title: Quebec moves to protect supply chains, expand relief to more businesses as trade war intensifies
articles.summary: With Canada's new counter-tariffs against the United States set to take effect Tuesday, Quebec's government has announced measures it says will diversify the economy while protecting local businesses…

image.caption: Premier Christine Fréchette, seen at an event in Gatineau, Que., last week, took a break from the election campaign to plan a response to the trade tensions between Canada and the United States. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal

With Canada's new counter-tariffs against the United States set to take effect Tuesday, Quebec's government has announced measures it says will diversify the economy while protecting local businesses and jobs.
15% local content requirements on public construction, broader access to trade relief funds

"The government aims to be prepared should the situation escalate further," reads a news release issued late Monday evening by the Treasury Board Secretariat and the Ministry of Economy, Innovation and Energy.
Premier Christine Fréchette stepped back from the provincial election campaign Monday to call a special cabinet meeting on the intensifying trade war with the United States.

The move comes as Canada plans to retaliate against the latest U.S. tariffs, slapping new duties ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on hundreds of American products. Those Canadian counter-tariffs are set to take effect Tuesday.

The new Canadian duties are part of the dollar-for-dollar response promised by Prime Minister Mark Carney last August, following the breakdown of negotiations with the U.S. — and the implementation of 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian products.
Under the procurement changes outlined in the release, the Centre d'acquisitions gouvernementales can now reserve public contracts for companies with an establishment in Quebec or Canada.

items: No talks scheduled as Canada's counter-tariffs against U.S. set to take effect at 12:01 a.m.

blocks.text: Public tenders can also require goods to be manufactured or processed locally, and bidders can receive a 15 per cent preference margin based on Quebec or Canadian value-added content.
"The government is using its purchasing power to support the local economy — creating more opportunities for businesses, sustaining jobs and reducing reliance on the U.S. market," the release says.
Contracts need Quebec, Canadian sourcing

Additionally, for construction contracts valued under $9.2 million, the Transport Ministry, Santé Québec and the Société québécoise des infrastructures will have to require that at least 15 per cent of the value of materials and equipment be Quebec- or Canadian-sourced.

The release notes that the $9.2-million threshold on construction rules aligns with flexibility allowed under international trade agreements. The 15 per cent local content rule was chosen to boost regional suppliers without causing material shortages or supply-chain overheating.
For projects exceeding $9.2 million, more ambitious requirements could be imposed on a case-by-case basis by decree, the news release says.

items: Trump to Canadian plane maker Bombardier: You can't sell in U.S. unless you build in U.S.

blocks.text: The province is also expanding direct financial support. The Fonds offensif pour le renforcement des capacités économiques will be made more flexible to help businesses access needed liquidity, including by allowing available funding to be disbursed more quickly and allowing a company to repay an existing loan.
Emergency assistance for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) is also being expanded, with businesses reporting annual revenue between $200,000 and $2 million now eligible.

To reduce reliance on the U.S. market, the province is deploying a dedicated interprovincial task force led by Investissement Québec International, the release says. The team will help SMEs expand into other provinces by finding buyers, securing contracts and replacing American supplies with Quebec products.

items: Retaliatory tariffs could raise costs for Canadian businesses already weathering the trade war

blocks.text: The government is also asking Crown corporations to adopt a Quebec-focused purchasing strategy amid the tariff war. It says they will be allowed to depart from the province's public-contracting law to do so, with administrative discussions already underway.
The news release says the government is not ruling out additional measures.
Party leaders weigh in
The premier held a meeting with party leaders after discussing the matter with her cabinet.

In a news conference following that meeting, Québec Solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal said Fréchette couldn't specify how severely the counter-tariffs would impact Quebec compared to the rest of Canada.
"Everyone knew very clearly that Quebec is the province most impacted by Trump's tariffs. How come we don't know regarding Carney?"
On X, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon dismissed the briefing as little more than a "lecture" of decrees and measures already slated for public release.
St-Pierre Plamondon said opposition leaders still have not received the detailed breakdown of Canada's retaliatory tariff list or recent updates.

In reply to St-Pierre Plamondon's post, Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime said he felt validated in his decision to not attend Fréchette's meeting, which he called a "great theatrical piece."
Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard questioned the premier's readiness.
"I came out of there not at all reassured," he told journalists after the meeting with Fréchette.

He said Fréchette told him she had not yet spoken with other provincial premiers about the tariff crisis. On X, he had accused the Coalition Avenir Québec government of "inaction and improvisation" and waiting until its back was against the wall before acting.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Isaac Olson is a journalist with CBC Montreal. He worked largely as a newspaper reporter and photographer for 15 years before joining CBC in the spring of 2018.
With files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: Trial over alleged murders of Australian surfer brothers starts in Mexico
articles.summary: The bodies of Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend were found with gunshot wounds to their heads.

blocks.text: Three men have gone on trial in Mexico for the alleged murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in 2024.

The bodies of Callum Robinson, his younger brother Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad from California - all in their early 30s - were found at the bottom of a well with gunshot wounds to their heads, days after they went missing during a surf trip in Baja California.
Prosecutors are seeking jail sentences of more than 200 years for the defendants, who also face charges of violent robbery and auto theft.
The parents of the brothers were in court on Tuesday in the coastal town of Ensenada, telling the media that it was "incredibly important and overwhelmingly difficult".

"We want the men accused of murdering our sons to see, in person, the human consequences of what happened," Martin and Debra Robinson said in a statement, according to Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC.
"Callum and Jake were not simply victims in a case file - they were our sons, deeply loved by their family and friends, with lives, dreams and futures that were brutally taken away."

On the opening day, the accused - Jesús "El Kekas" Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús - were moved to a smaller courtroom amid accusations that some witnesses had been intimidated by people associated with the defendants.
Dozens of witnesses are expected to give evidence during the four-week, judge-only trial.
The 2024 alleged killings of the Robinson brothers and their US friend shocked Australians as well as many residents of the normally peaceful town of Ensenada.
Despite high levels of cartel violence in the northern Mexican border states, tourists are rarely targeted for such violent attacks in Baja California's surf towns.

The ex-girlfriend of one of the accused, Ari Gisell, became the first person to be convicted over the tourists' killings last year and was sentenced to 20 years in prison for her role in their murders.
Mexican prosecutors are pursuing jail sentences of more than 200 years for each of the defendants, as well as an additional 168-year sentence for the alleged ringleader.
Prosecutors say the victims were killed due to a bungled robbery, while the defence argued there was not enough evidence to prove that theory.
Callum Robinson was a member of Australia's national lacrosse team and lived in San Diego where he was a professional lacrosse player.
His younger brother Jake had travelled from Australia for the surf trip and was due to start a job as a doctor when he returned while their friend Rhoad was killed a few months before his wedding.

articles.title: New prize named for late author Andrew Pyper will recognize horror and thriller writers
articles.summary: Heidi Pyper says she's frustrated that horror and thriller writers like her late husband, Andrew Pyper, don't get the recognition they deserve, noting that he wasn't considered for Canada's top…

image.caption: Heidi Pyper, left, is shown with her late husband, author Andrew Pyper. She says the Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction honours his legacy and will encourage other horror and thriller authors. (Submitted by Heidi Pyper)

blocks.text: The Current·New

Heidi Pyper says she's frustrated that horror and thriller writers like her late husband, Andrew Pyper, don't get the recognition they deserve, noting that he wasn't considered for Canada's top literary prizes because of the genre of his books. She hopes a new prize will help honour his legacy and encourage other writers.
Announcement of $20,000 award coincides with release of Pyper's final novel
LISTEN | New $20,000 literary prize created to honour Andrew Pyper's legacy:
The Current8:12A new writing prize honouring Andrew Pyper
Heidi Pyper says her late husband, Andrew, wasn't just a bestselling author. He was also generous, curious and truly cared about people.
Affectionately known as "Canada's Stephen King," Andrew died in January 2025 of complications from cancer at the age of 56.

He was a prolific and acclaimed writer of horror, thrillers and other types of speculative fiction, including The Killing Circle and The Demonologist, and Pyper said her husband wrote characters who had great depth.
But she said she's frustrated that writers like Andrew don't get the recognition they deserve, noting there aren't many genre-specific awards available for horror or thriller writing.
That's why Andrew's friend and fellow author, Craig Davidson, helped create the Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction.

items: Acclaimed thriller writer Andrew Pyper dead at age 56

blocks.text: The $20,000 prize will be administered through the Writers’ Trust of Canada. To be eligible to win, writers must have published at least three books in the horror, thriller or speculative fiction genre. Thanks to a massive campaign, enough money has been raised to support the prize for seven years.
The announcement for the award coincides with the release of Andrew's final novel, Driven.
As a reader and writer of horror, he believed that the genre could expand people’s understanding of the human condition.
Pyper said she hopes the prize will help support and encourage authors like Andrew. She spoke to Matt Galloway, host of The Current, about the prize and legacy she wants it to leave.
When you listen to Andrew talk about horror and the human condition, what's going through your mind?

It brings such a smile to my face hearing Andrew talk about horror, thriller and genre writing in a way that's deep and meaningful because he brought a lot of depth to his writing. Particularly with the characters that he put under great duress. I remember my dad reading The Wildfire Season and saying, "Why does he keep putting these people I care about in such jeopardy?" And I was like, "That's the trick."
When he died, there was this huge outpouring of sadness from this country and beyond. There are people who perhaps only know him from his books. Tell us a little bit more about Andrew.

It's hard to talk about Andrew without sounding hyperbolic, but he really was a lovely man. He was smart, funny and talented. I would be remiss if I didn't mention how good-looking he was. People really loved him.

items: Remembering celebrated Canadian thriller author Andrew Pyper

blocks.text: Many writers told stories of him and his generosity towards them, encouraging them to write, agreeing to come into classrooms to talk to students. The other thing that people kept saying was how he made them feel, he made them feel important. I think that stems from his curiosity. So when you were talking to Andrew, he didn't want to talk about himself, he wanted to hear about you and what was going on in your life.
This idea for this writing prize, in many ways, speaks to the generosity that he had. I'm sure he’d love this idea.
I think he'd be quite chuffed.
Tell me more about this prize and how the idea for this sparked.

Andrew played poker with a group of guys – writers, bookish-professor types – and he was no gambler, but he was dedicated to this group. About six months after Andrew died, Craig Davidson came to me and floated the idea, asked me what I thought and if it was OK if they tried to pursue this. Of course, I thought it was a wonderful idea.

Then he made the mistake of asking if I wanted to help. I'm sure he regretted that because I'd show up with my to-do list and a work-back schedule. But it came out of love and friendship amongst these men who played cards together.
But also from the fact that Andrew, despite the fact that he was a bestseller and wrote great books, didn't get the nod from some of those "literary prizes in Canada."
Yes, I think that was a frustration for him that he was disqualified before even being considered.

It wasn't like he was nominated and didn't win. It feels like there's a gap. Genre props up the publishing industry, people gobble it up. Movies and television are made from our writing, and it feels like a missing piece in the awards landscape. They recognized that, and the Pyper Prize began in that spirit.
It'll be $20,000.
It's a good chunk of change.

I think that's the distinction. There are awards for thriller writers and horror writers that exist. There's the [Bram Stoker Award], the Shirley Jackson [Award], I think there's the International Thriller Writers Awards but none of them come with a prize purse. So this really is a one-of-a-kind prize, not just in Canada, but we have yet to find one that is the equivalent.
The prize arrives at the same time as his new book comes out.

Yes. So Andrew left us with a few final words. Driven is the third and final book under his pseudonym Mason Coile. So the confluence of these two things happening at the same time is really meaningful.
How are you doing in all of this?

It's a lot, I'm not going to lie. I say it's very weird to have someone who has left us be so top of mind and such an ongoing concern, I kind of live with him in my head. I've elected to keep his social media active. His publisher offered to do it, but I just felt like I wanted to keep control of that.
In some ways, the book and the prize mean that the legacy lives on, there's a voice that’s still there.

I just reread Driven a couple of weeks ago. I read it when he finished it, but he was so sick when he was writing, it was right at the end of his life. He had said to me, "Should I write another book?" And I said, "Yeah, what else are you going to do? It's the thing that's going to get you up in the morning.” I started to read it then, but it was too dark. I said, “Our life is too scary for me to read this.” So I just read it again and you can really hear his voice. The sound of it is very clear in my mind.
Interview produced by Enza Uda

articles.title: Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster
articles.summary:
Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions

Nepal is demanding…

blocks.text: Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.

Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.

Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.
In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.

Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.

blocks.caption: An excavator repairs a damaged road in Nepal near the Trishuli River on Monday. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

blocks.text: “This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”

Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.

“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”
For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.

“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”

Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.

Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.

While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”

blocks.caption: Damaged buildings on the banks of the Trishuli River. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

blocks.text: He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.

The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.
Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.
“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.
He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.

Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.
“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.

“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

articles.title: Habagat rains to persist over Luzon, Visayas
articles.summary: Several areas in Luzon and Visayas may experience rains on Tuesday, September 8, as the southwest monsoon or habagat continues to affect the country, PAGASA said.

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 8:32am
Pedestrians struggle with their umbrellas against strong winds during a sudden heavy downpour in Quezon City on Aug. 28, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Several areas in Luzon and Visayas may experience rains on Tuesday, September 8, as the southwest monsoon or habagat continues to affect the country, PAGASA said.
In its 5 a.m. weather forcecast, the state weather bureau said that no tropical cyclone is being monitored inside or near the Philippine area of responsibility.
Weather specialist Veronica Torres, however, said the possibility of a low-pressure area forming remains.
Zambales and Bataan will bear the brunt of the habagat, with 100 to 200 millimeters of rainfall expected in the next 24 hours.
“Asahan natin 'yung monsoon rains sa Zambales at Bataan. Kapag monsoon rains, ito 'yung halos tuloy-tuloy na moderate to heavy rains,” Torres said.
(We can expect monsoon rains over Zambales and Bataan. These monsoon rains are almost continuous, ranging from moderate to heavy.)
The rainfall forecast may trigger flooding, particularly in urbanized, low-lying and riverside areas, while landslides may occur in areas highly susceptible to the hazard.
Meanwhile, Pangasinan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro may experience occasional rains, with rainfall amounts reaching 50 to 100 mm.
Flash floods and landslides are also possible in these areas due to moderate to heavy rains.
Metro Manila and the rest of Luzon will have cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms. PAGASA said flash floods and landslides may occur due to moderate to at times heavy rains.
Torres said the habagat may affect a wider portion of Luzon in the coming days before its influence gradually weakens.

Western Visayas will have cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the habagat. The rest of the region will experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms.
Mindanao, meanwhile, will have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.
PAGASA warned of possible flash floods and landslides in areas affected by severe thunderstorms.
Winds over Luzon and Visayas will be light to moderate and generally move from the southwest to west, while coastal waters will remain light to moderate.
Mindanao will have light to moderate winds moving from the south to southwest, with slight to moderate coastal waters.
No gale warning is currently in effect over any seaboard in the country, PAGASA said.

articles.title: Second-hand smoke causes to nearly 1.7M deaths globally – study
articles.summary: PARIS — More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday…

blocks.text: PARIS — More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday in The Lancet.

Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many “non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke” were among the estimate total of 8 million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
“Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognized health risk, with no safe level of inhalation,” it said.

By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, Tuesday’s study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.

This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the “sidestream smoke” from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.

“The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered… carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds” than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.

Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable due to population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
“Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health,” it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke. /dl

articles.title: Eiffel Tower shut by staff protest after women moved for religious visit
articles.summary: The mayor of Paris said an investigation would be launched into the incident, which left female employees "humiliated", according to a union representative.

blocks.text: The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers and management said.
A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the landmark in the French capital on Saturday.
Staff union representative Diane Davoine says as they arrived at the monument, women were told to move.

"During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," she told Reuters. Davoine also said management had since apologised to workers over the incident.
"So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," Davoine said.

She added: "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again."

Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), the company that operates the monument in Paris, confirmed the delegation had asked the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women", according to the AFP news agency.
The firm told AFP that "these conditions should not have been accepted".
They added they "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women".
SETE president Ariel Weil said: "It is clearly not an acceptable practice.
"I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women."
The BBC has contacted the Union Confédération générale du travail (CGT) for a response.
BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in the suburbs of Paris.

In a statement on X, the BAPS temple in Paris said their trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".
It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".
On its website, BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.
It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said there would be an investigation into the circumstances of the visit.
"I am taking note of the anger expressed by the employees of the Eiffel Tower, and I want to tell them that their discontent is legitimate," he wrote on X.
"Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city. It must be applied everywhere, for everyone."
French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."

Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."

articles.title: A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
articles.summary: Tukaram Mundhe has gone viral after a series of aggressive inspections of restaurants to detect hygiene lapses.

blocks.text: The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.

They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.

His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.

An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.

In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.

"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".
