Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".

Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.

"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.

Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.

In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.

"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.

Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.

Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

articles.title: Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US
articles.summary: The threat against one of Canada's largest companies comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours.

blocks.text: President Donald Trump has warned Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it can no longer sell in the US unless it moves its manufacturing there.
"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank.'"
The move comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours, and hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs are set to be imposed on $20bn (£14.7) worth of US goods.
The BBC has contacted Prime Minister Mark Carney's office and Bombardier for comment.
It is unclear how Trump intends to block Bombardier from doing business in the US.
The Montreal-based company already operates a factory in the US state of Kansas that builds special mission military planes, and employs 3,500 American workers.
About half of its fleet – 5,100 aircraft – is operated by Bombardier customers based in the US.

Bombardier's jets are built at facilities in Canada, the US and Mexico, according to the company's website. They also comply with the North American free trade agreement signed by Trump during his first term, known as CUSMA in Canada and the USMCA in the US.
The company is one of Canada's largest, having contributed C$7.4bn ($5.4bn; £4bn) to the country's GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombardier.
It is also one of the largest employers in Quebec's manufacturing sector.
In a post on X on Monday, Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a source of pride" for her province and "a flagship of our economy".
She added that she has reached out to Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and offered her government's full support.
On Trump's threat, Fréchette wrote: "I will not respond to provocation with provocation."
"Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market."
Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed late last month after Canada walked away from the negotiating table, after which the US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of presenting last-minute terms that were "unfair" and "uneconomic", while US officials accused him of refusing to sign a deal for political reasons because of Trump's unpopularity in Canada - an accusation he denied.

articles.title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs set to take effect as trade dispute grows
articles.summary:
Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods

Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American…

blocks.text: Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports early on Tuesday, escalating a trade fight with its largest trading partner as tensions between US president Donald Trump and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney intensify.

The tariffs, which take effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, will range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering C$27.6bn in imports from the US. The measures will target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.
The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $27.6bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian government said.
“Canada’s counter-measures do not apply to US goods that are in transit to Canada on the day on which they come into force,” it added.

Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.

Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” – which Canadians have rejected.
US vice-president JD Vance has also reportedly mocked Carney, apparently saying the Canadian prime minister “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”
Last month, Trump announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”, adding: “We don’t need Canada, they need us!”

Carney said last month Canada would not accept a US trade deal that weakened French-language protections, saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.

Quebec has long maintained laws aimed at protecting French and preserving its distinct cultural identity. Those measures have become a sticking point in the trade talks between the two countries, with American negotiators raising concerns about rules they say can disadvantage US businesses.

articles.title: AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
articles.summary: The head of chip designer Arm says modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer cannot be done now, but computers are "going to solve it".

blocks.text: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.

Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.

Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.
However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.
Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe.
Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.

Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.
"Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.

"However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.
Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.
He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples.

"It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements.
"That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."

In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade.

"With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."

Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities.
He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.
Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.

This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.
There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres.
He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space.
"We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."

But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here.

"I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."
As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.
But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

articles.title: Flight recorders recovered from 'devastating' Amazon cargo plane crash
articles.summary: Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300 overshot the runway at Miami International Airport.

blocks.text: Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from the Amazon cargo plane that crashed at Miami International Airport, but the priority remains the recovery of victims, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has said.
Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway shortly before 14:00 local time (19:00 BST) on Sunday.
The plane hit two vehicles, including a white van carrying seven people within the airport perimeter, and a Toyota with three passengers.
NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it was too early to draw conclusions about what caused the crash, with investigators still in the "fact finding stage".

Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.
The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.
It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla, coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.
Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating", with debris from the aircraft, vehicles and airport fencing scattered across the area.
"It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well," she said.
She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait."
The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation.
Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene.

Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing.

The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation.
Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots.
The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation.
Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said.
"Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again."

Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash. Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews.
The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US.
Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities.
21 Air, the company operating the aircraft, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation.

articles.title: Illinois mother charged with killing toddler 'invested' in Lindsay Clancy case: prosecutors
articles.summary: An Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been closely following the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy and was texting friends about the case just hours before…

image.caption: Police in Illinois have charged a woman with first-degree murder after her two-year-old son was found dead in the basement of the family's suburban Chicago home on Sept. 1. (Matt Rourke/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

An Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been closely following the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy and was texting friends about the case just hours before her son was found dead, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors allege Corie Walsh texted friends about trial hours before son found dead

Corie Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after her son, Barrett, was found dead in the basement of the family's suburban Chicago home on Sept. 1, according to court records obtained by NBC Chicago.

Prosecutors said Walsh had become "very invested" in Clancy's nationally watched trial and was discussing it with friends until about 12:30 p.m. that day. A neighbour found Barrett less than four hours later.

Walsh was found elsewhere in the home with injuries that authorities said were self-inflicted. Prosecutors said she later told investigators that she killed her son because she believed he was the "devil" and the "anti-Christ." Her lawyer, Andrea Lyon, told reporters Walsh was experiencing a psychotic episode and called the boy's death a tragedy for the entire family.

Police were called to Walsh's home in Frankfort, about 56 kilometres southwest of Chicago, shortly before 4 p.m. after a neighbour discovered Barrett in the basement, according to prosecutors' petition seeking to keep Walsh jailed before trial.
Mistrial declared over deadlocked jury in Lindsay Clancy case

The neighbour found the boy and began CPR while calling 911, prosecutors said. He was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. An autopsy determined that he died from asphyxia caused by ligature compression of the neck.

Police searching the house found Walsh fully dressed in a bathtub containing bloody water, prosecutors said. She had cuts to her wrists and thighs and was taken to a hospital with injuries authorities described as not life-threatening.

The disclosure that Walsh had been following Clancy's trial came days after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in that case on Friday, when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.

items: Will Lindsay Clancy face a new trial? What's next after mistrial declared

blocks.text: Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, was accused of killing her three young children in 2023. Her lawyers argued that she was legally insane and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors maintained that Clancy understood what she was doing and knew it was wrong.

Authorities in Illinois have not alleged that Clancy's trial played a role in the killing of Walsh's son, and no evidence made public so far establishes a connection beyond her discussion of the case.
Frankfort police and prosecutors in Will County did not respond to calls for comment on Monday.

articles.title: Social media posts reveal wider habitat of Philippine tarsiers
articles.summary: With their huge eyes and bodies small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, Philippine tarsiers are among the best-known inhabitants of the country’s tropical forests. The tiny nocturnal primates are…

blocks.text: With their huge eyes and bodies small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, Philippine tarsiers are among the best-known inhabitants of the country’s tropical forests.

The tiny nocturnal primates are closely associated with the central island of Bohol, a popular tourist destination, but researchers have found evidence that their range is far more extensive than previously documented.

A study by researchers at the University of the Philippines Diliman found reports of Philippine tarsiers in 29 provinces, more than double the 14 provinces previously identified as habitats by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
The findings were based largely on an unlikely source: Facebook.

Graduate student Simeon Bejar, 30, and fellow researcher Maria Tabeta, 25, examined more than 1,000 Facebook posts dating back to 2006, gathering information on tarsier sightings and analyzing where photographs of the animals had been posted.
More habitats
The IUCN had previously identified tarsier habitats in just 14 of the Philippines’ 82 provinces.
They also found numerous sightings in northern Leyte and indications that forests there may have tarsier population densities comparable to those in protected areas in Bohol.
“I think it’s really appropriate to do it here because a lot of Filipinos use Facebook,” Bejar said.
More than 80 percent of the Philippine population is estimated to use Facebook, giving the researchers a vast pool of information posted by people across the archipelago of more than 7,000 islands.

The Philippine tarsier, an endemic species measuring little more than 10 centimeters in body length, is difficult to find because of its small size and nocturnal habits. Much about its ecology remains unknown.
It is classified as “Near Threatened” on the IUCN Red List.
The study also highlighted shortcomings in efforts to protect the animals.
On Bohol, where ecotourism is a major attraction, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and local authorities have stepped up management of forests inhabited by tarsiers.
Protected areas open to tourists have also introduced rules aimed at minimizing stress on the animals, including asking visitors to keep their voices down.
But the researchers found signs of problems elsewhere.
“Some of the Facebook posts featured photographs of tarsiers being inside cages, which is illegal. Some are leashed … some were dead,” Bejar said.
Illegal trafficking
Illegal trafficking for the pet trade is one of the main threats facing Philippine tarsiers, and poaching appears to be taking place in areas beyond the reach of authorities.
Bejar and Tabeta have set up a dedicated Facebook page for their research and hope to expand the scale of the study.
“If maybe we get another student who can work with us or a project where we can use funds to focus on this, then we’ll try to scale up what we are doing right now,” Bejar said.—KYODO NEWS

articles.title: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward to ban vacation rentals
articles.summary: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward plans to ban, as a general rule, vacation rentals such as Airbnbs in residential areas and areas near schools, local officials said on Monday. The ward in central Tokyo hosts…

blocks.text: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward plans to ban, as a general rule, vacation rentals such as Airbnbs in residential areas and areas near schools, local officials said on Monday.
The ward in central Tokyo hosts the largest concentration of vacation rentals in the country. The policy will also apply to existing properties, the officials said.

There were 3,775 registered short-term rental properties in the ward as of July 15, according to the Japan Tourism Agency. The ward estimates that approximately 2,000 of them may have to cease operations under the plan.

The agency and other relevant bodies notified local governments in July that they could effectively ban short-term rentals in specific areas through local ordinances if the properties were found to be harming the residential environment, citing a series of incidents.
The ward plans to solicit public comments in October and submit an amendment to its short-term rental ordinance at the first regular session of the ward assembly in February next year.
According to the officials, the ban will apply to areas zoned for residential use only or designated as cultural and educational districts.
Exceptions will be made for vacation rentals that meet certain requirements, such as those whose owners live on-site and manage the properties appropriately. —KYODO NEWS

articles.title: Australia politics live: John Howard warns about limiting immigration; Barnaby Joyce says super plan to have ‘minute’ inflationary effect
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

Former prime minister, John Howard, has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the

blocks.text: John Howard says blocking immigration from certain countries won't stop terrorism
The former prime minister John Howard has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the debate over Australia’s immigration settings continues.

The 87-year-old was in Canberra last night for an hour-long chat with Australian National University national security professor Rory Medcalf before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks in the US.
The discussion began with last year’s alleged terrorist attack in Bondi, before turning to whether immigration settings can prevent potential terrorists from entering the country.
Howard said the “law of averages” meant some people with nefarious intentions could enter the country but he did not believe the “evidence is overwhelming”.
He continued:

double quotation markBut I think the mood is overwhelming that we have to try very hard to stop terrorism creeping in under the cover of immigration, and you can’t do it by just stopping immigration, and it’s very hard to do it by stopping categories of immigration. When some people say you stop it by saying ‘we won’t take migrants from any country that has got a reputation for terrorism’, well, it might be a lot more limiting than those people imagine.

Neither major political party has proposed a country-wide ban on specific countries for permanent migration. One Nation has said it would like to see country-wide migration bans on people coming from countries the foreign affairs department has listed as “do not travel”.
Key events

items: 17m agoGood morning
17m agoJoyce says super plan has 'minute' inflationary effect
17m agoJohn Howard says blocking immigration from certain countries won't stop terrorism

blocks.text: Joyce says super plan has 'minute' inflationary effect

One Nation’s deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, has defended his party’s new policy allowing renters and mortgage holders to dip into their superannuation to boost their pay, saying it will have a “minute” impact on inflation.

The superannuation industry has warned the policy – which Labor and the Coalition have said they do not support – would stoke inflation. The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive, Mary Delahunty, said the proposal would be “economically disastrous” and make people poorer in retirement.

Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30 on Monday night, Joyce – the party’s Treasury spokesperson – said withdrawing your superannuation from your fund due to financial hardship was currently a “protracted” system.
Asked if the party had modelled the inflationary impact of the policy, Joyce said it would have a minimal impact but did not point to any modelling:
double quotation markNow are you saying that it has no effect whatsoever? No, I wouldn’t say that but I’d say it is almost minute.
Joyce says allegations against Victorian One Nation leader are ‘contested’
Barnaby Joyce was also asked about One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, who continues to attract scrutiny over allegations made against him by an ex-partner about alleged drug use.
Pickering said his ex-partner’s claims were false. “They are extremely hurtful and I just hope the public can see through them,” he said in a statement, according to The Australian.
Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30, Joyce said the historical allegations were “contested”.
He said he did not hear about the allegations before story was published in The Australian on Monday:

double quotation markIf he’s good enough to serve our nation in the defence force, as determined by our nation, then I presume he’s good enough to serve the people of Victoria. If we’re saying that any person will be held to account for any action they ever did, no matter how far in the past it was, I would suggest there are lot of people in this parliament who will no longer have a job Monday morning.
Good morning
Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live news coverage for Tuesday.
Krishani Dhanji will be with you shortly.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Charles confirms Harry and Meghan to remain non-working royals after their return to U.K.
articles.summary: King Charles authorized a letter to senior British officials on Monday confirming that his youngest son, Prince Harry, and Harry's ‌wife, Meghan, remain non-working royals following their return to…

image.caption: Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, are shown after sailing on Sydney Harbour with veterans from the Invictus Australia community, in Sydney, Australia, on April 17. (Hollie Adams/Reuters)

blocks.text: World

King Charles authorized a letter to senior British officials on Monday confirming that his youngest son, Prince Harry, and Harry's ‌wife, Meghan, remain non-working royals following their return to the U.K.
Couple stepped down from duties and moved to the U.S. in 2020

The letter, which was shared with Harry's team and sent as guidance to senior officials ​in the government and military, said that after ​Harry and Meghan stepped down from official royal duties in 2020, they "are no longer working Members ​of The Royal Family."

"This position, distinct from the State ⁠and Royal duties undertaken ⁠by the working Royal ‌Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be ⁠fully respected," the letter said.

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of ‌Sussex.... The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.
"In short, their position is akin to ​private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."

items: The 'shockwaves' of Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K.

blocks.text: Prince Harry and his family arrived ⁠back in Britain late last month, six years after quitting royal ⁠duties and moving to the United States.

The couple had left ⁠for ⁠the U.S. in 2020, ​stepping down from official royal duties to chart independent careers, but ​they never left the ⁠headlines as Harry accused the royals of neglect, the tabloid press of ruining his life and the government of failing to provide enough security for him to ever return home.

articles.title: Senate OKs five international resolutions on third reading
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved, on its third and final reading, five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved, on its third and final reading, five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher education, and taxation.
In a roll call vote, 19 senators, with no abstentions or objections, approved the following resolutions aimed at strengthening the Philippines’ participation in international agreements:

items: Senate Resolution No. 622, which seeks concurrence in the accession to the Protocol to Amend the Convention on Offenses and Certain Other Acts Committed on Board Aircraft, strengthening the legal framework for offenses committed aboard aircraft.

Senate Resolution No. 624, providing concurrence in the ratification of the Philippine-India Treaty on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters, which establishes mechanisms for cooperation in investigating, prosecuting, and preventing crimes between India and the Philippines.

Senate Resolution No. 625, concurring in the ratification of the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, providing a framework for liability and compensation for damage caused by space objects.

Senate Resolution No. 626, which seeks concurrence in the Philippines’ accession to the Asia-Pacific Regional Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications in Higher Education, facilitating the recognition of Filipino academic qualifications abroad.

Senate Resolution No. 628, concurring in the ratification of the Philippines–Cambodia Agreement on the Elimination of Double Taxation and the Prevention of Fiscal Evasion with respect to Taxes on Income, which seeks to prevent double taxation and strengthen bilateral economic ties.

blocks.text: The approval of these measures is expected to improve the country’s cross-border cooperation while also supporting the country’s economic, educational, and security interests. /cb

articles.title: UK set to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban
articles.summary:
Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and Israel

Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.

In an intervention that is expected to draw fierce criticism from the US and Israel, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements. He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert the call for a two-state solution to the conflict with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.
In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices facing Palestinians in Gaza.

The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank – widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian woman waits at a bus stop decked out with Israeli flags raised by settlers between Nablus and Ramallah in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Israel has already threatened reprisals over Miliband’s previous claim that the Israeli military has held back aid into Gaza, and the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has claimed the Labour government is gripped by Jew hatred. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies such as Qatar on Monday to brief them on his plans in the region.

Miliband’s intervention comes as polling released to the Guardian shows Britons across the political divide strongly favour banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements by a margin of more than two to one.

The polling, conducted by Opinium and published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, shows that only 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements, compared with 46% in favour. Support rises to nearly three-quarters when those who did not express an opinion are excluded.

Miliband’s statement will stand by his claim that the Israel Defense Forces, in the name of security, are placing unnecessary controls on aid entering Gaza, creating a horrific situation. It is understood, however, that he is sceptical of the UK’s leverage to resolve the situation apart from calling for the restrictions are lifted.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian woman and her children make their way through a destroyed neighbourhood of Gaza City.  Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: His claim that aid had been held back was hotly denied by the Israeli foreign ministry at the weekend.

Miliband is also likely to go further than his predecessors in placing the settlement measures firmly in the context of upholding international law, including the findings of its key institutions, the international criminal court and the international court of justice (ICJ), two bodies under attack by the US.

The package is not likely to include sanctions over aid restrictions into Gaza, or to describe what has happened in the territory as a genocide. The UK has kept open the option of joining countries such as South Africa at the ICJ to claim Israel is in breach of the court’s previous rulings.

But by acting decisively on trade, Miliband has set aside warnings that a polarising UK intervention might help Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances in Israel’s 27 October election. British sources pointed out that even Israeli military officials have warned their prime minister that the IDF will struggle to defend new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, because they lack basic security infrastructure and were established for political rather than security reasons.

Despite US criticism of the UK stance, Washington has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu on the settlements issue to the point that he has called for some to be dismantled saying they were not established with the necessary permits. Israel has previously demolished some outposts, but they are often rebuilt soon after.

The UK ban on trade in settlement goods, long parried by the Foreign Office as impossible to implement, is in line with the ICJ advisory opinion in 2024 requiring governments not to aid or assist an Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, not just illegal settlements. The UK government has never formally replied to the opinion, but ministers in Sir Keir Starmer’s administration said it was broadly compliant.

The measures on settlements may require primary legislation to ban the trade in goods rather than an easier statutory instrument, while the trade ban will extend to some services including financing and and advertising illegal settlements.
after newsletter promotion

The Foreign Office has previously argued that it was impossible to distinguish between products emanating from illegal settlements and those from Israel. The UK officially regards all Israeli civilian settlements built on territories captured by during the 1967 six-day war as illegal under international law.
Total trade in goods and services between the UK and Israel in 2025 was £6bn, and the scale of the disruption may depend on Israeli reprisals.

Products produced in Israeli settlements located within the territories occupied by Israel since 1967 have not been entitled to preferential tariff treatment upon entry into the UK since 2005. The country has also issued guidance on misleading labelling and urged businesses not to trade with or be engaged in economic and financial activities in Israeli settlements. The new measures make such investments unlawful.

The UK reset was made more urgent by Israel’s E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem that is poised to effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two from November. But the Burnham government also feels compelled to act because of the increase in settler violence in the West Bank and the failure of Trump’s Board of Peace after six months to secure the twin objectives of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.

blocks.caption: Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, holds up a map showing the E1 settlement project. Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP

blocks.text: Labour is also under domestic pressure from the Greens on Palestine. The party leader, Zack Polanski, is expected to stand in the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection triggered by Starmer’s resignation as an MP. The new Labour policy may give the party’s candidate some political cover against Polanski.
In a sign of the potential ramifications for Miliband, Netanyahu’s older son, Yair, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina and not to Britain.
He is not a minister, but after his comments Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.

Trump said last Thursday that he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade islands, telling GB News: “Your country was not there to help me” when the US and Israel began their war on Iran in February.

articles.title: Alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in Mexico
articles.summary:
Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024

The alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing…

blocks.text: The alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot in 2024 have gone on trial in the border resort where the three were murdered.

The Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were shot dead after being robbed in Mexico’s violence-hit Baja California.
They were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found hidden on a cliff.
The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the trial.
“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” Martin Robinson told reporters as he entered the court with his wife, Debra.
“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said.

blocks.caption: Jake (left) and Callum (right) with their parents, Debra and Martin Robinson. Photograph: Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation

blocks.text: Three men are on trial for homicide.
The girlfriend of one of the accused was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery.
The crime sparked outrage and sadness in Australia and the United States.
Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was due to marry.
Other foreign tourists have previously been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa.
Their bodies were later burned.

articles.title: Quebec overhauled its bottle deposit-refund system. Is it working?
articles.summary: Since the rollout of its first phase in 2023, Consignaction’s bottle deposit-refund system has received mixed reviews from users. Here’s a breakdown of what’s working and what needs improvement.

image.caption: Consignaction has centralized Quebec’s bottle deposit-refund system. (Djeneba Dosso/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
Since the rollout of its first phase in 2023, Consignaction’s bottle deposit-refund system has received mixed reviews from users. Here’s a breakdown of what’s working and what needs improvement.
Thousands of machines were removed from retailers to standardize Consignaction sorting centres
In less than three years, Consignaction changed how Quebecers return empty beverage containers and get paid for it.
With the help of the province, the company has centralized Quebec’s bottle deposit-refund system by removing thousands of return points from retailers.

Instead of using the bottle deposit machines usually found in grocery and convenience stores across the province, people can now go to two types of sorting centres: Consignaction, for single-unit returns, and Consignaction+ for bulk deposits.
Since the rollout of its first phase in 2023, Consignaction’s new system has received mixed reviews; some users love it, others, not so much.
CBC spoke with some users, waste management experts and the company behind the new system. Here’s a breakdown of what’s working and what needs improvements.
Quebec tried to modernize its bottle recycling system. Did it work?
Long lines, limited access
Before Consignaction took over the network, empty containers could be returned to thousands of businesses participating in Quebec’s deposit-refund system.
Many of these return points, often located within walking distance to users, are now gone, and only 172 Consignaction sorting centres have opened in their place.
Karel Ménard, executive director of the Quebec Common Front for Ecological Waste Management, says that’s not nearly enough to meet the needs of Quebecers.

“We used to have around seven to eight thousand depot centres: confectionery, retail stores and so on. It wasn’t perfect, but we had a lot,” he said. “We have billions more containers but thousands less deposit centres.”

items: Bottle deposit machines are being removed from some Quebec grocery stores. Here's why

blocks.text: Ménard says this creates two outcomes: long lineups at centrally located return points or “access deserts” for people living in areas where a Consignaction isn’t easily accessible.
The waste management expert believes Quebec needs at least 2,000 deposit-refund centres for the system to run smoothly.
Some users like Marie Claude agree. She frequents the Consignaction location on Beaubien Street in Montreal’s Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie borough.
“The wait times are very long, some days it can take two to three hours. Only having two machines to collect containers for the entire neighbourhood is not nearly enough,” she said.

Long lines are usually caused by one of the two machines being out of service or not handing out cash. Users say both occurrences are common.Some also say it can take days or weeks to receive electronic refunds for a return.
Hiccups to be expected, Consignaction says
Consignaction says it’s listening to feedback from retailers and users, attributing most issues to hiccups with any new launch.
“This network did not exist just a bit over two years ago,” argues Jean-François Lefort, the company’s vice-president of strategy.
“Whatever happens, we address it quickly, but we just have to be aware this is a transition phase.”
Lefort points out that employees work at Consignaction + locations to facilitate the deposit process or help with broken machines.
He adds opening more locations will reduce long lines.
'It's out of money'
It might not be that simple for "binners" — people who collect cans and bottles from waste bins to earn money.
Les Valoristes Co-op, an organization supporting unhoused people who rely on the system for extra income, have noticed the new model creates barriers.

“The biggest one that always comes about is that the machine that gives money is not working, it’s out of money,” explains co-founder Marica Vazquez Tagliero, who argues supermarkets were more efficient.
“Yes, there were machines that would break here and there but they always had money. This is very important for those who collect every day and need that cash every day.”
When asked about this, Consignaction said users can either be reimbursed through their app or by receiving a redeemable coupon.
If the machine is down at one location, that coupon is still valid at other points to ensure users get their money, even if they don’t have a bank account or phone.

items: As Canada's income gap widens, some of those who are struggling sort trash to survive

blocks.text: But Tagliero argues this extra step can be discouraging for binners who spent their night collecting cans and bottles.
“We need more machines and we need a diversity of collection systems,” she said.
Her organization created their own bottle depot made for and by binners. They’ve noticed more turnout since some return points were removed from retailers.
Out with the old, in with the new
Meanwhile, others don’t just like the new system — they prefer it.
Joseph Gonzalez and his partner made the move from returning cans at their local grocer to making deposits at the nearest Consignaction + location.
So far, the transition has been smooth.

“It’s great, it’s a lot easier than it is at the stores,” he said. “Usually at the shops, the machines would break down and there would be no staff, so it’s much nicer to have dedicated service versus rolling your luck.”
Gonzalez’s Consignaction + centre in Saint-Laurent is the latest to open, joining 171 other sites across the province.
Quebec has given Consignaction until March 2027 to open at least 400 dedicated bottle deposit facilities and 800 modernized return points inside retailers.

March 2027 is also the deadline for the final phase of the system. Consignaction will extend bottle deposits to all glass containers, including wine and spirit bottles, as well as milk and juice cartons.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Djeneba Dosso is a journalist based in Montreal. She previously worked as an associate producer for CBC Manitoba and did a brief internship with CBC Ottawa. You can reach her at djeneba.dosso@cbc.ca

articles.title: Werner Herzog: Germany's wild man of cinema is back
articles.summary: As his latest movie, "Bucking Fastard," premiered at the Venice Film Festival, DW talked to the boundary-breaking director.

image.caption: Werner Herzog and his latest film's stars, Rooney Mara and Kate Mara, at the Venice Film FestivalImage: Yara Nardi/REUTERS

blocks.text: When Werner Herzog needed a title for his memoirs, he reached back to one of his own films: "Every Man for Himself and God Against All," the original German title of his 1974 feature known in English as "The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser." For Herzog, the last wild man of European cinema, it's less a title than a worldview.

Over more than 60 years as a provocative, boundary-breaking filmmaker, Herzog has made films on the slopes of active volcanoes, and in the middle of the Sahara. He's filmed in the jungle and north of the Arctic Circle, telling stories of characters who live at the edges of human achievement. Often, in making these films, Herzog has pushed himself, and his collaborators, to the edge as well.
Now 84, Werner Herzog shows no signs of slowing down. He's back with a new feature film, "Bucking Fastard," his first drama in seven years, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival.
The film is the story of Jean and Joan Holbrooke, two sisters who speak, think and move in unison. They even share the same dreams and love the same undeserving man.
Hollywood stars and real-life siblings Kate and Rooney Mara play the sisters, their performances synced up to an uncanny degree.

blocks.caption: Kate and Rooney Mara portray twin sisters in 'Bucking Fastard'Image: Gateway to Orkney LLC

blocks.text: The film is loosely inspired by real-life twin sisters Freda and Greta Chaplin, who became a tabloid sensation in England in the 1980s. The film's title is a reference to an inadvertent simultaneous spoonerism the sisters made in court, when describing their former lover.

In Herzog's version, the Holbrooke sisters, after being rejected by their true love (played by Orlando Bloom), decamp to the wilds of Ireland and begin digging a tunnel in a cave, convinced they can dig their way to the Orkney Islands — a mythical place where true love is possible.
Reaching out for the extraordinary
The Holbrooke sisters are two ecstatic dreamers striving to do the impossible. Typical Herzog protagonists.

Herzog himself sees the through-line: "With 'Fitzcarraldo,' there is a great dream about opera in the jungle, and for that the protagonist moves a big ship over a mountain," he told DW in Venice, referring to his 1982 epic adventure drama in which he had his crew actually haul a 320-ton steamship over a hill in the Peruvian jungle to tell the story of a man who dreams of building an opera house in the middle of the rainforest.
Similarly, added Herzog, "Bucking Fastard" is "the dream of an ideal country, which doesn't really exist."
In the world of Werner Herzog, art imitates life, and vice versa.
While filming "Aguirre, the Wrath of God" (1972), the story of a mad conquistador in search of El Dorado, Herzog and his crew, including star Klaus Kinski, nearly went mad themselves.
In his 1999 documentary on Kinski, "My Best Fiend," Herzog recounts how the actor threatened to leave the film. If he did, the director told him, he would follow him and shoot him dead.

blocks.caption: His 'best fiend': The late Klaus Kinski in 'Fitzcarraldo' (1982)Image: New World Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Real people, real extremes
Herzog is, if anything, even better known as a documentarian and his real-life protagonists are as extreme as his fictional characters.
In "Grizzly Man" (2005), he ponders the life of Timothy Treadwell, an animal rights activist who spent years getting up close and personal with bears in the wild, until one of them ate him.
"Little Dieter Needs to Fly" (1997) follows the German-born American Vietnam War pilot Dieter Dengler, who survived a harrowing escape from a Laotian prison camp.
For "La Soufriere" (1977), Herzog filmed in an abandoned town in Guadeloupe, next to a volcano on the brink of eruption, to talk to the one man who refuses to evacuate.

blocks.caption: One of Herzog's most popular documentaries: 'Grizzly Man,' from 2005Image: LionsxGate/Everett Collection/IMAGO

blocks.text: In search of 'ecstatic truth'
Herzog sees little difference between his fiction and non-fiction films. He admits to inventing scenes for his documentaries, and to filming real events for his features.

For "Rescue Dawn" (2006), a feature adaptation of the Dieter Dengler story, Herzog got star Christian Bale to devour live maggots on camera (the director showed him how, gobbling up some himself) and wrestle with a real live snake for a scene.
"Film does not have so much to do with reality as it does with our collective dreams," Herzog said. He thinks of himself less as a director than "as a poet."
'Just go out and do it'

In his often haunting tales of man's struggle with nature, Herzog aims to achieve an "ecstatic truth" beyond mere reality. His goal, he said, is not to depict the extreme as bizarre or extraordinary. It is to inspire everyone to be extraordinary.
"Every grown-up man should move a ship over a mountain. Every grown-up woman should dig a tunnel through a mountain range," he told DW. "[The message] is very simple: Just go out and do it."
Rooney Mara agreed: "Being willing to show up every day and dig a tunnel through a mountain for love — that's not crazy. Everyone else is crazy for not wanting to do that."

blocks.caption: 'Dig a tunnel through a mountain': Herzog hopes to inspire everyone to be extraordinaryImage: Gateway to Orkney LLC

blocks.text: A divided response in Venice
"Bucking Fastard" is an odd, and oddly funny film, especially for a Herzog movie.

"Thank you for seeing that," said Herzog, who argued there is humor in all his films, if you look for it. "Sometimes it's a dark humor. Sometimes it's a very Bavarian humor that even Germans wouldn't understand. For Americans, it's easier. Mexicans, yes, they immediately get it."

The Venice audience gave "Bucking Fastard" a warm welcome, but critics were more divided. A few embraced Herzog's new piece of ecstatic weirdness. Most dismissed it as confusing, clunky and utterly nonsensical. An "uddled-mup fairytale," wrote one, playing on the film's mixed up title.
Why Herzog still matters

Herzog critics are legion, but his fans probably don't care. The 84-year-old director is as popular as he's ever been. He launched an Instagram account last year, even though he still doesn't own a smartphone, and it has become a huge hit with Gen Z.

"My younger son does it, he knows how, and he tells me 85% of those who read it and love it are between 15 and 20 years old," Herzog said. "And because my films are now available on the internet, on streaming platforms, all of a sudden [young people] are discovering it."

Mara said Herzog remains an inspiration, as "a singular human being [who] really doesn't give a sh**." Speaking to the German director, she noted: "You march to the beat of your own drum so thoroughly, and people love that because that's what we all want to do."
Next stop: outer space?
For his part, Herzog is not slowing down. He's already put "Bucking Fastard" behind him and is deep in post-production on his new film and has a Taschen photo book in progress.
And he still hasn't given up on his impossible dream: making a film in space.

"I spoke to NASA, but they didn't take me. And then there is a Japanese billionaire who is planning a spaceship around the moon [but] he refused to take me on board," he said. "[But] Elon Musk promised me that if he goes on a mission to Mars, I would be on board."

articles.title: Syrian reactor could have been used for nuclear weapons if completed, UN says
articles.summary:
Chief of nuclear watchdog says secret Assad-era facility would have been able to produce fissile material

A nearly complete nuclear reactor built secretly during the rule of the toppled…
articles.byline: Guardian staff and agencies in Vienna

blocks.text: A nearly complete nuclear reactor built secretly during the rule of the toppled Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad would have been able to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the chief of the UN nuclear watchdog has revealed.
Inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir ez-Zor and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities.
The IAEA head, Rafael Grossi, said on Monday it was “obvious that the previous government was pursuing a number of clandestine” activities.
“They didn’t want the world to know what they were doing,” he told reporters after opening the Vienna-based agency’s quarterly board of governors meeting.

“Given the configuration, the technical features of that type of reactor, this is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” he said, adding that building the reactor was a “very important step”.
Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear programme under Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in the eastern Deir ez-Zor province.
After Assad was ousted in December 2024, the new government agreed to give IAEA inspectors access to suspected former nuclear sites.

During a visit to Syria in August, IAEA inspectors confirmed that “the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor”. Grossi and a team of senior inspectors also visited a previously undeclared site in the country.
In 2018, Israel admitted carrying out a top-secret air raid on the site 11 years earlier.
In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.

blocks.caption: An image from a video released in April 2008 by the CIA showing a photo of a covert nuclear reactor being built in Syria’s eastern desert, according to the narrated video.  Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Syria notified the agency of the site’s existence in a 17 July letter and invited the IAEA “to cooperate with the Syrian authorities in the inspection and verification of the site and of any nuclear material to be potentially found”.

The IAEA said in its confidential report circulated to member states last Tuesday and seen by the Associated Press that this new site contained “natural uranium metal in the form of fuel rods with cladding”. The agency verified the material and confirmed “the presence of around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal”.

Grossi said that when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had boxes scattered all over the place, he said.
Grossi said “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras at the location.

Asked if the nuclear material would remain in Syria or be removed, Grossi said this was “a matter that the Syrian government will have to decide”. He added: “We are not requesting them to do this or to do that. For us what’s important is that we know all the time where this [material] is until the last gram.”

Logan Mintz, a director for nuclear materials security at the Washington-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said natural uranium metal was not directly usable for a nuclear weapon but could be “diverted to a covert weapons programme that further processes it into plutonium for a nuclear weapon”.

She said that once deemed safe to move, the material could be “transported in certified containers” to a third country that could “safely and securely disposition it into a more chemically stable and more widely used form” for possible use in nuclear power plants.
“As with any transport of nuclear material, this movement would require robust security from theft or sabotage,” she said.
Associated Press and Agence France-Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Nicaragua challenges German arms exports to Israel at ICJ
articles.summary: Germany has asked the International Court of Justice to dismiss the case on jurisdiction grounds. It also said its arms exports to Israel were documented, published, and subject to more stringent…

image.caption: The latest hearing opened on Monday in The Hague, but if the judges deem a full trial necessary, that's likely to take yearsImage: Mouneb Taim/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany on Monday asked the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to dismiss a case brought by Nicaragua, accusing Berlin of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention by supplying arms to Israel amid its war with Hamas in Gaza.
If the ICJ, otherwise known as the World Court, decided to hear the case, the process would likely take years and be contingent on the findings from separate Gaza-related cases in The Hague.
But Germany is arguing it shouldn't even go that far, saying that Nicaragua did not follow proper processes and that the dispute does not fall in the international court's jurisdiction.

Nicaragua, on the other hand, argues that the case should be heard because it and Germany are both signatories to the Genocide Convention — despite neither side being directly involved in Israel and Hamas' war in Gaza and although the ICJ hearing on whether Israel committed genocidal acts in Gaza could take years.

blocks.caption: Nicaragua's legal team tried and failed to secure an emergency court order to halt weapons exports in 2024 at the height of the conflict in Gaza after Hamas's October 7, 2023 terrorist attack on IsraelImage: Mouneb Taim/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the case about?
Nicaragua accuses Germany of aiding and abetting genocide in Gaza by selling weapons to Israel, some of which it says have been used in Gaza.

An initial bid for an emergency injunction ordering a halt to exports failed in 2024 at the height of the war in Gaza, but Germany also failed in its bid to have the case summarily and permanently dismissed at the earliest opportunity.

The German government suspended weapons exports to Israel for around three months in 2025 as the conflict continued and casualty figures rose. But it has since restarted them amid the truce struck late last year that largely stopped the fighting, without ending Israeli strikes entirely.
Germany walks a fine historical and political line in the case.

On the one hand, the 1948 Genocide Convention was born in very large part from the lessons of the Holocaust and the spirit of "never again" after World War II. But to the same token, Germany has always sought to maintain close and cooperative ties with Israel, a state formed in very large part as a consequence of its mass extermination of Jews in Europe. It considers Israeli security part of its own raison d'etre as a modern democratic state.

blocks.caption: Germany's advocate Julia Monar said the case should be dismissed on procedural grounds, but also said Germany's arms exports transparency standards exceeded international requirementsImage: Mouneb Taim/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israel's war in Gaza was launched against Hamas after Hamas carried out the October 7, 2023 terror attacks on Israel. October 7 was the single deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Hamas is a Palestinian Islamist group based in the Gaza Strip.
What is Germany arguing?
Germany is arguing both that the case should be dismissed on procedural grounds, and that Nicaragua's allegation of aiding and abetting genocide is unsubstantiated.

Although Germany, Nicaragua and Israel are all signatories to the Genocide Convention, a case like this where neither side is a direct party to a conflict is unusual. Its represenatives told the court that Nicaragua had not taken the proper steps before filing the legal challenge and arguing much of the case falls out of the ICJ's jurisdiction.
"Germany respectfully requests the court ot reject Nicaragua's claims," Julia Monar, legal adviser to the German Foreign Ministry, told the judges.

"All German weapons exports to Israel and other countries are subject to strict review procedures that are more stringent than international regulations," Monar also told the court, a reference to Germany's intentionally restrictive weapons export policies adopted after World War II.

In mid-May this year, the Bundestag, or Germany's parliament, published information saying that between November 2025 — shortly after the truce was brokered — and March this year, exports worth around €167 million (roughly $194 million) were approved.
Could Trump's Gaza plan cost Palestinians their property?
What's likely to happen next?
Nicaragua's case is based on the South African lawsuit at the ICJ accusing Israel of genocidal acts in Gaza.

In a preliminary hearing — the findings of which Israel rejected — the court found it plausible that Israel could have committed genocidal acts in Gaza and called for a full hearing. That process will take years, with court sessions not expected until 2029.
A full hearing in Nicaragua's case against Germany, should the ICJ adopt to pursue one, could well rely on a resolution in the broader genocide allegations against Israel.
More immediately, Nicaragua is expected to lay out its arguments in The Hague on Tuesday.
A decision on Germany's bid to shelve the case entirely is tentatively expected some time this year.
The ICJ is the top UN court dealing with disputes between states and alleged violations of various international treaties. Its rulings are final and cannot be appealed.

articles.title: AfD wants to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt — but how?
articles.summary: Following its record election success, the far-right Alternative for Germany aims to form a government. What options does it have without the absolute majority?

image.caption: The AfD leaders were very upbeat as they addressed the press in Berlin on MondayImage: Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved its best-ever election result in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, winning well over 40% of the vote and leaving all other parties far behind.

However, the party lacks the majority of seats in parliament needed to govern on its own. Because the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as "confirmed far-right extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency, other parties announced that cooperation with the AfD was out of the question. This will make forming a government in the eastern German state quite difficult.

The day after the election, party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla held a press conference in Berlin. They were joined by the winner of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund.

Even though the AfD narrowly missed its main election goal of being able to govern alone with an absolute majority, it is now more confident than ever before. The party leaders made clear that they are thinking not just about Saxony-Anhalt, but about all of Germany, and are convinced they will govern the whole country in the not-so-distant future.

"The CDU/CSU will never again be able to win a federal election. That is a fact," party co-chair Weidel announced in reference to the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union, which leads the national government.
"My stated goal is to widen the gap as quickly as possible and reach at least 40% in the next federal election," said Weidel, who wants to become Germany's next chancellor.
Cooperation: Yes — but with whom?
But how exactly to proceed in Saxony-Anhalt? Who does the AfD want to bring on board to form an AfD state government?

Much remains unclear even the day after the election. AfD lead candidate Siegmund repeatedly emphasized on Monday: "We extend a hand to every political actor in Saxony-Anhalt." However, he always adds that his willingness to compromise is very limited.
"We will remain true to ourselves. We will not compromise our principles," Siegmund said.
The AfD leaders say they want to form a stable government. This would rule out a minority government that would have to seek majorities in the state parliament on a vote-by-vote basis.
On election night, Siegmund emphasized that implementing the AfD's platform was more important to him than the prospect of power: "There will be no compromise with me."
Leading up to the vote, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate repeatedly stated that he was only interested in governing alone in order to usher in a fundamental political change in Germany.
The AfD's radical governing platform

For months, the AfD's political program has sparked heated debates across Germany. That's because the party wants to drastically tighten asylum and immigration policies. It wants to speed up the deportation of illegal asylum seekers and introduce a general work requirement for all other asylum seekers.

Above all, however, it wants to make Saxony-Anhalt and Germany less attractive to immigrants and is calling for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy." During its election campaign, the party repeatedly blamed migrants for crime in German cities and for the housing shortage.

What's more, the AfD is planning a radical restructuring of society: It has declared war on public broadcasting, wants to cut funding for democracy projects, intends to establish a kind of vigilante group against migrants and aims to combat social diversity — all of which is laid out in its platform. And Ulrich Siegmund emphasized in an interview with public broadcaster ARD that these issues are non-negotiable.
Now, one option involves a minority government led by the AfD, in which it would need to secure support from other parties to advance its policies.
On behalf of the CDU, the party's secretary-general, Franziska Hoppermann, categorically ruled out a coalition: "There will be no cooperation with the far left or the far right."
Could the BSW help the AfD form a government?
The biggest unknown in this power struggle is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which cleared the 5% threshold for representation in parliament.

The small party campaigns primarily on a left-wing economic platform and — similar to the AfD — calls for a foreign policy that is more friendly toward Russia. In the past, party founder and former member of the socialist Left Party, Sahra Wagenknecht, has repeatedly expressed openness to substantive cooperation with the AfD. However, for ideological reasons, the party is not considered a particularly attractive partner within AfD circles.

As the AfD celebrated its victory into the night and even before the vote count was complete, some AfD state politicians announced that, if necessary, they intended to remain in the opposition and keep the other parties on the defensive until they could secure a majority of their own.
This article has been translated from German. It was published on September 6 and updated the following day to reflect news developments.

articles.title: Legarda, Leviste eyed as next big fish
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla vowed to go after “big fish” Sen. Loren Legarda and her son Batangas 1st district Rep. Leandro Leviste, whom he accused of “running to hide” in…

blocks.text: Headlines
September 8, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla vowed to go after “big fish” Sen. Loren Legarda and her son Batangas 1st district Rep. Leandro Leviste, whom he accused of “running to hide” in France.

“Loren Legarda hasn’t returned yet. Maybe she doesn’t want to come home. She and her son Leandro Leviste, mother and son legislators, are now rushing to hide in another place,” he said at a media briefing yesterday.
Remulla said he would fly to France in the coming days “to talk to French authorities,” particularly its justice ministry.

“We’ll tell them it’s not good to have a reputation of being the hiding place of ill-gotten wealth, the wealth stolen from the people who could have used the money to improve the lives of those in need,” he said.
Remulla believes Legarda, who has extended her medical leave to Sept. 16, and Leviste might consider not returning to the country to evade liability.

Previously, the ombudsman launched preliminary investigation into plunder and graft complaints against Legarda, Leviste and former energy secretary Alfonso Cusi over the failure to provide solar power despite more than P10 billion worth of contracts being awarded to Leviste’s solar power company. It accused Legarda of using her position to secure the congressional franchise for her son’s company.

In addition, the National Bureau of Investigation said it may file qualified human trafficking charges against Leviste and others for his alleged involvement in the honeytrap plot directed at Executive Secretary Ralph Recto.
The NBI earlier divulged both Legarda and Leviste left the country through separate flights to Hong Kong and were both bound for France.
Fugitive former congressman Zaldy Co, who was previously spotted in the Czech Republic, could have also been staying in France, the ombudsman said.
Extended leave
Legarda has extended her medical leave until next week, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. said.
Bantug said Legarda has filed for medical leave for Sept. 7-9 and Sept. 14-16.
Legarda’s Senate colleagues have commiserated with her on her medical condition, supposedly a serious lung condition.
The senator has denied all allegations against her and defended her right to seek treatment abroad after Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano found her extended medical leaves “suspicious.”
Money trail
Meanwhile, the NBI is tracing a possible money trail in the alleged honeytrap operation involving Leviste, including a reported request for P5 million, Matibag said yesterday.
“We have already written to the AMLC (Anti- Money Laundering Council) to find out whether there were transfers of that kind of money. We are tracing them,” Matibag said over True FM.
The NBI director said investigators already have accounts from people involved in the alleged operation indicating that money changed hands. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab
