articles.title: AUDIOJUNKIE: The Ella Langley effect
articles.summary: By now you’ve probably heard the song “Choosin’ Texas” by Ella Langley on the radio. I don’t know about FM radio in Manila, but in the US, Langley is ridin’ high. I mean, I always hear “Choosin’…

blocks.text: By now you’ve probably heard the song “Choosin’ Texas” by Ella Langley on the radio. I don’t know about FM radio in Manila, but in the US, Langley is ridin’ high. I mean, I always hear “Choosin’ Texas” every time I open my radio. More often while driving, in the morning, which I never miss, and once more in the evening on my way home. There’s something to be said about that. For one to play on radio so dominantly (even in this day and age) you’ve got to be a big time artist. And these days, no one is as big as Langley. By now, “Choosin’ Texas” has already spent 45 weeks in the Hot 100 Billboard Charts. I don’t know how long it stayed on number one, but as I’m writing this, it’s still enjoying the top spot as we speak. Now that’s something! Ok, I researched it: “Choosin’ Texas” has spent 20 weeks (!) on the singles charts. Not only that, in its course, it has broken and made several records among which, it is the longest female song on the chart, beating out Mariah Carey and BoyZ II Men’s “One Sweet Day.” It is also the longest leading non-holiday song in the charts’ history. And it is the longest running No. 1 country song by a female artist in the 68-year history of the singles charts. Not bad. But who is Langley, really? Well, she was born May 3, 1999 and she is from Hope Hull, Alabama. This home grown country girl stands about 5’6”. She made her debut as a country artist back in 2024 with a duet (with Riley Green) titled “You Look Like You Love Me.” This song is a ditty, simplistic enough to listen to and sing, and the melody is not that hard to retain, but far from being a hit. But that’s the great thing about artists, you don’t know which of their songs can be a hit. “Choosin’ Texas” is different. After a four-bar intro that can be likened to any classic 80’s country song, the song comes in easy: “Just when I thought I got him to fall in love with Tennessee / I shoulda known better than to take him back to Abilene / I put him right back into her arms / I wasn’t a match for that kinda spark.” I mean, what’s in Abilene? And who is that other woman? From there, you just gotta see where it takes you. You don’t need to be a country music fan (I mean look at me) to be reeled into the mystery. And it’s even plain speak: “She’s from Texas, I can tell by the way / He’s two steppin’ ‘round the room.” Why the hell is he doin’ that? “And judgin’ by the smile that’s written on his face / there’s nothin’ I can do...” Just about seems to seal this sorry girl’s fate! Even the song references are on point! “Smoky Mountain Rain” is a Ronnie Milsap tune, and “them old Hank tunes, the Memphis blues we used to sing” refer to Hank Williams! And “he always loved ‘Amarillo By Morning’” is a George Strait song. That’s an old country gangster roll call right there. But other than that, this brown-haired girl really sings a pretty tune. She’s this season’s Shania Twain; this summer’s Linda Ronstadt; and she’s just about to enter the Dolly Parton era of her career. That’s the Ella-Langley-effect there!

articles.title: Tropical Storm Krovahn may not re-enter PAR but continues to enhance ‘habagat’
articles.summary: The tropical storm with the international name “Krovahn” now has only a slim chance of re-entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), but it will continue to enhance the southwest monsoon…

blocks.text: The tropical storm with the international name “Krovahn” now has only a slim chance of re-entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), but it will continue to enhance the southwest monsoon or “habagat” and bring more rain over parts of Luzon, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said on Monday, Sept. 7. PAGASA weather specialist Aldczar Aurelio said Krovahn, formerly called “Pilandok,” was located 1,155 kilometers east-northeast of extreme Northern Luzon as of 3 a.m. Monday, moving eastward at 10 kilometers per hour. Krovahn exited the PAR on Sept. 3. Over the next 24 hours, occasional heavy rains may persist over Zambales, Bataan, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro due to the enhanced habagat. Metro Manila, Ilocos Region, Abra, Benguet, Antique, and the rest of Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and Mimaropa may experience cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms. The rest of the country may have partly cloudy skies with chances of isolated rain showers or thunderstorms. Meanwhile, Ambuklao and Binga dams in Benguet and San Roque Dam in Pangasinan continued to spill excess water, based on PAGASA’s monitoring. As of 8 a.m. Monday, two gates of Ambuklao Dam were open. Its water level was at 751.41 meters, just 0.59 meter below its 752-meter normal high water level. Binga Dam’s water level was at 573.9 meters, or 1.1 meters below its 575-meter normal high water level. Two of its gates remained open. San Roque Dam was at 279.46 meters, just 0.54 meter below its normal high water level, although this was lower than the 282.08 meters recorded the previous day. Two of its gates also remained open. The three dams form part of a cascading system, with water released from Ambuklao mostly flowing into Binga Dam before Binga’s releases move downstream to San Roque Dam.

articles.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ makes it 6 weeks in a row at No. 1 as Hollywood wraps a banner summer
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” remained the No. 1 movie in theaters over the weekend, becoming just the second film this decade to top the box office for six straight weeks. Since the…

blocks.text: NEW YORK (AP) — “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” remained the No. 1 movie in theaters over the weekend, becoming just the second film this decade to top the box office for six straight weeks. Since the end of July, the Sony superhero movie has ruled over cinemas with rare dominance. The last release to enjoy such a long stretch leading the box office was 2022’s “Avatar: The Way of Water.” “Brand New Day,” the fourth standalone Spider-Man film starring Tom Holland, collected $18 million over the weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday. Sony is forecasting $23.3 million for the four-day holiday weekend. “Brand New Day” has grossed $2.4 billion worldwide. Universal Pictures’ “The Odyssey,” as it has for much of the “Spider-Man” run, remained in second place. Christopher Nolan’s epic added $13 million domestically over the weekend, bringing its global haul to $1.63 billion. More than $1 billion of that has come from overseas sales, making “The Odyssey” the first to achieve that international milestone since 2009’s “Avatar.” Both blockbusters — “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” — helped lead Hollywood to its best summer since before the pandemic. Through Aug. 31, the domestic box office totaled $4.6 billion for the season, according to Rentrak, an increase of 26.1% from 2025 and just shy of 2013’s record summer. On Sunday, Rentrak forecast that, including the Labor Day weekend, the summer will end up with $4.759 billion, a whisker above the $4.758 billion of summer 2013. That time frame, though, spans 130 days this year, compared with 123 days in 2013. Accounting for inflation and higher ticket prices, Hollywood’s summer wasn’t quite so historically sensational. Admissions are still well below pre-pandemic marks. But it’s nevertheless a remarkable rebound for a film industry that has struggled to string together such a hit-filled summer through the pandemic, labor strife and the expansion of streaming. Labor Day weekend is typically a sleepy time in theaters. And neither new release — Paramount’s “By Any Means” and A24’s “Onslaught” — made much of a mark. One of the weekend’s best performers was “Coyote vs. Acme,” the hybrid live-action-animated Looney Tunes movie. It dipped a modest 29% to gross $11.3 million in its second weekend. “Coyote vs. Acme” is turning out to be a good investment for Ketchup Entertainment. The indie distributor acquired the film for approximately $50 million after Warner Bros., which produced the $70 million film, opted to can it. In two weeks, “Coyote vs. Acme” has ridden strong reviews and good word-of-mouth to $33.8 million domestically. “By Any Means,” a 1960s-set civil rights action thriller starring Mark Wahlberg and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, opened with $7.4 million. Paramount is projecting $9.2 million for the four-day holiday weekend. Audiences gave it a “B+” CinemaScore. “Onslaught,” however, flopped with $1.9 million on 1,918 screens for the three-day weekend and a projection of $2.3 million for the four-day weekend. The A24 release, directed by Adam Wingard, stars Adria Arjona as a former Army sniper who defends her trailer park home from three escaped, experimental super soldiers. “Onslaught” cost a modest $15 million to make. But reviews (57% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes) and audience scores (a “C” CinemaScore) weren’t good. Meanwhile, “Buddy,” a low-budget dark comedy, has turned into a surprise success. Made for just $3 million, the film, directed by Casper Kelly and from the producers of “Weapons,” is about a group of children trapped inside a surreal 1990s children’s television series. After overperforming in its opening weekend, “Buddy” actually increased its ticket sales over its second weekend. The film grossed $5.7 million, up 5%, to bring its two-week total to $14.3 million. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” $18 million. 2. “The Odyssey,” $13 million. 3. “Coyote vs. Acme,” $11.3 million. 4. “By Any Means,” $7.4 million. 5. “Insidious: Out of the Further,” $6.5 million. 6. “Cars” (20th anniversary): $6.1 million. 7. “Buddy,” $5.7 million. 8. “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie,” $3.3 million. 9. “The End of Oak Street,” $2.9 million. 10. “The Dog Stars,” $2.7 million.

articles.title: 'Lego Mandalorian': Cute, silly, fun
articles.summary: Announced earlier at D23, Mano and Grogu get the Lego treatment in a new one shot special on Disney Plus. Star Wars and Lego are old friends having collaborated on some of the best (and most…

blocks.text: Announced earlier at D23, Mano and Grogu get the Lego treatment in a new one shot special on Disney Plus. Star Wars and Lego are old friends having collaborated on some of the best (and most expensive!) Lego sets in recent years. If you’re a fan of the Lego film, then you’ll sink into this one pretty easily. The premise is that Manodo and Grogu get suckered into a surprise birthday party for Mando under the pretense of a new and dangerous bounty. Once there they get the best kind of ambush, one with friends, party hats and lots of blue milk. The short is a summary of sorts, a retelling of the three seasons of the acclaimed Mandalorian show, told in the unique Lego style. Being a recap, I’d have thought that this would be released before the Mandalorian and Grogu movie to catch people up on the story thus far but unfortunately it did not. Still, it is a blast seeing the story of Mando and Grogu retold in the off-beat, self aware style that the Lego movies are known for. It is jam-packed with visual gags that make full use of the fact that the characters and sets are lego building blocks. And the wit is there as well, as the characters take turns exaggerating events from the past, lampooning what happened or spinning tall tales, hilariously embellishing what actually took place. If anything the short suffers from being too short. There is so much material to draw from and make fun of over the three seasons of the Mandalorian that often the show seemed overly-stuffed. Taking the extra fifteen minutes to make it a full hour could have spaced the jokes out a bit more, but that’s a small little nitpick. ''Lego Mandalorian'' is a cute, silly way to look back on what was definitely a highlight of the Disney Plus Star Wars crop of shows. It does feel a bit like a farewell, especially knowing that a new season is nowhere on the horizon. It its good to know in whatever form, Mando and Grogu are fixtures now in Star Wars lore, and one way or another, they’ll keep coming back.

articles.title: Amazon cargo plane overshoots Miami runway: 5 dead, 5 injured
articles.summary: MIAMI, United States — At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught…

blocks.text: MIAMI, United States — At least five people were killed when an Amazon cargo plane overshot a runway after it landed Sunday at Miami International Airport, crashed into vehicles and caught fire, officials said.

Miami-Dade County fire chief Ray Jadallah told reporters that in addition to five fatalities, three people were transported to trauma centers “in critical condition” and two more were treated at a local hospital.
“The airplane did strike a couple of vehicles,” which left “a couple of victims that were actually trapped in the vehicles,” Jadallah said.
“A complex extrication with our technical rescue team” was needed, “including a search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot that were trapped in this aircraft.”
Jadallah did not clarify whether the pilot or co-pilot survived, and officials declined to answer questions after brief statements were made.
Video showed thick smoke billowing from the blue and white Boeing 767 that had arrived around 2 pm (1800 GMT) from Puerto Rico, as fire trucks raced to the scene.
The plane operating as Prime Air Flight 7598 caught fire as a result of the “crash,” fire officials said.
“A total of 60 fire apparatuses arrived, just short, just shy of 200 men and women from Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, to begin the actual search and rescue and firefighting,” Jadallah said.
“The actual cause of the incident will be determined by the FAA and the NTSB,” he added, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board.

The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have “launched a go team to investigate Sunday’s runway excursion accident.”

The airport closed all runways and taxiways because of the incident and posted an update to its website Sunday evening that travelers should check directly with their airline before heading to the airport.
Amazon put out a statement saying the aircraft “experienced an incident while attempting to land.” It did not say if anyone was hurt or killed.

“This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in the statement.
Miami Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz told reporters Sunday that her officers encountered a “really tragic scene,” but there was “no apparent threat to public safety.” /dl

articles.title: ICC chief Akane vows to continue job no matter what amid US sanctions
articles.summary: Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court, vowed on Sunday that she will continue to do her job, despite the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump imposing sanctions on her…

blocks.text: Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court, vowed on Sunday that she will continue to do her job, despite the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump imposing sanctions on her and other officials of the Hague-based judicial body.

“No matter what happens, my convictions will not waver. I will continue to conduct investigations, prosecutions and judicial proceedings as I have until now,” she said, appearing online at an event in Tokyo.
She is among the ICC judges targeted by U.S. sanctions that freeze assets in the United States, with Washington accusing the ICC of encroaching on state sovereignty.
Akane, the first Japanese national to head the ICC, described the punitive measures as a threat to judges and to the principle of neutrality.
Speaking about the threat to the rule of law from the sanctions, Akane said, “Silence is tantamount to accepting rule by overwhelming pressure or force,” adding, “I will not give up.”
The Trump administration has strongly objected to ICC probes into alleged war crimes committed by U.S. military personnel.
Akane also urged Japan to take a proactive role in efforts to cooperate with many countries and prosecute serious crimes, calling on it to “actively join the global effort now.”

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has said the sanctions were “incompatible” with her country’s commitment to the rule of law, after initially coming under scrutiny over her initial remarks that the measures were “very unfortunate,” in language seen as stopping short of criticizing Japan’s sole treaty ally.
On Friday, Gen Nakatani, a former defense minister who leads a nonpartisan parliamentary group advocating human rights diplomacy, called on Takaichi to urge Washington to retract the sanctions.
“Upholding the Japan-U.S. alliance and defending the rule of law is not a choice between two options,” he said.
A former prosecutor, Akane became president of the ICC in March 2024. Japan is the largest financial contributor to the court. /dl

articles.title: 1 dead, 6 hurt as SUV rams 6 vehicles
articles.summary: A sport utility vehicle (SUV) driver was arrested after his vehicle rammed into three cars and four motorcycles, killing one person and injuring at least six others as it traveled from Tomas Morato…

blocks.text: A sport utility vehicle (SUV) driver was arrested after his vehicle rammed into three cars and four motorcycles, killing one person and injuring at least six others as it traveled from Tomas Morato Avenue toward Elliptical Road in Quezon City around 3 a.m. Sunday, Sept. 6. The Quezon City Police District (QCPD) Traffic Sector 4 identified the SUV driver as alias “Carl.” The SUV was first involved in a collision along Tomas Morato Avenue before heading toward Quezon Avenue, where it crashed again, and later toward Elliptical Road, where it figured in further accidents. Responding personnel from Traffic Sector 4 immediately took the driver into custody. The motorcycle rider was declared dead, while the injured victims were rushed to East Avenue Medical Center and Quezon City General Hospital for treatment. The QCPD is conducting a follow-up investigation to determine the exact circumstances surrounding the successive collisions and the liability of the driver.

articles.title: U.S. investigators to focus on crucial moment of touchdown in Amazon cargo plane crash

image.caption: An Amazon cargo plane sits at the Miami International Airport on Monday, after it overshot the runway on Sunday, killing five people. (Lynne Sladky/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. federal investigators examining why an Amazon cargo jet barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport and into vehicles, killing at least five people, are likely to focus on a crucial moment in the landing: whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.
It wasn't clear if the pilots were among the 5 people killed in Sunday's incident

Video of Sunday's landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Aviation experts said investigators will seek to determine exactly where the plane landed and, if it was beyond the normal touchdown zone, why the pilots did not abandon the landing and circle back for another attempt.

Investigators will also examine the plane's speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft's mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has sent a team led by chair Jennifer Homendy to Miami, where she is expected to give the agency's first briefing on the investigation Monday.

The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. ET on Sunday after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people died, three were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.
Pilots, people in cars trapped

The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and co-pilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle. It wasn't immediately clear if the pilots were among those killed.

The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 914 metres of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.

It wasn't raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
"A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you've already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away," Schiavo said.
5 dead after Amazon cargo plane leaves runway, smashes into cars
No safety system on Miami runways

The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports countrywide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.

Miami's airport appears to be in compliance and wasn't required to have an arresting system because it has a 1,000-foot (304-metre) safety buffer at the end of its runways, said Mike O'Donnell, the FAA's former director of airport safety and accident investigations.
The requirement was prompted by American Airlines Flight 1420 overrunning a runway at Little Rock National Airport in Arkansas in 1999, killing nine.
The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
History of aircraft

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.
The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon.

items: At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barrels off Miami runway and smashes into cars: police

blocks.text: More than 160 flights were cancelled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320 kilometres north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there.
Amazon said in a statement that it would co-operate with any investigation.

"We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss."

Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville's Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.

articles.title: The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?
articles.summary: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’…
articles.byline: Ben Doherty, Andy Ball and Nick Evershed

blocks.text: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.

New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.
In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.

“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …

“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”
The US military-industrial complex in Australia
Each square represents one facility
United States-controlled facilities with Australian access (17)
Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access (24)
Australian facilities with US military access (51)
Australian facilities with US corporate access (18)
Australian facilities with no significant US access (41)
Australian facilities with US access unresolved (17)
Guardian graphic
‘Aligning ourselves completely’
The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:

items: Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.
Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.
Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.
Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.

blocks.text: Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.
Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.

Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.

Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.

Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.
Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.

Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.

blocks.caption: Workers with a missile at the Port Wakefield facility. Photograph: Lockheed Martin

blocks.text: The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.
Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.

The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.

The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.

Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.

“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.
“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”

Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.

“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”

There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.

Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.
“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”
‘Waltzing its way into a war’
At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.
Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.
“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.

blocks.caption: US defense secretary Pete Hegseth meets Australia’s defence minister Richard Marles at the Pentagon. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA

blocks.text: Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.
Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.
“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”

Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.

The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.

But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.
The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.
Australians’ fragile faith
Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.
But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.
A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.
Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.
Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).
Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.

Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).

More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.

This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.
“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”

Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.

“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.
“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”
Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.
“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”

She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.
“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”

Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.

“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.
Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.
“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.
“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”

Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”

articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD celebrate projected win in state election
articles.summary: AfD leaders celebrated tonight as exit polls projected a big lead in the Saxony-Anhalt vote.

blocks.text: Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is celebrating as exit polls show they are set to win more than 44% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD's projected result is higher than earlier opinion polls suggested and the party has hailed the news as a "historic outcome".
However, party leaders will not know if they have enough seats to govern until they see which of the smaller parties get into the state parliament.
That may hinge on whether one of the smaller parties gets over the required threshold of 5%.
Berlin correspondent Jess Parker reports from the AfD party HQ as supporters celebrated the projected results.

articles.title: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth
articles.summary:
Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to…

blocks.text: China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.

A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.

The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.
The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.

The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry ​of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital.

The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.

The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.

“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.
Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.
after newsletter promotion
The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.

The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share ​placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco ​Corp and its subsidiaries.

The two lenders said the ​proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them ​sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks ​to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

articles.title: Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports
articles.summary:
Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities

Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international…

blocks.text: Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano.
Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing.
Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday.

Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday.

The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, the airport operator, Angkasa Pura, announced. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday.
The Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”.
“Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement.
“Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.”
Volcanic ash can damage jet engines – baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens.

blocks.caption: Passengers wait in the check-in lounge at Soekarno-Hatta international airport.  Photograph: Faisal Ramadhan/EPA

blocks.text: Ash ‌reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000 feet) ‌on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said.
Several ​schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents ​suffered eye irritationand fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported.
The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could ​include cloud-seeding to promote rain.

“If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference.
More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore.
Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said.

Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed.
Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited to go within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Jamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles
articles.summary:
Slavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of state

A landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles…

blocks.text: A landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles by Jamaican over slavery reparations, aiming to confront historical crimes that still disadvantage former British colonies, the Caribbean nation’s culture minister has said.
The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.

“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.
“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so.”

First announced in June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.

It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.
Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.
Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to the Americas and sold into slavery.

Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery, that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.

“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.

“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.

“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.

He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.
after newsletter promotion

There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.

In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbean launched a manifesto outlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmer resisted pressure from member states to include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.
Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.

On Sunday, the delegation will host a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum, to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.

She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.

“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”

articles.title: Why a famous Montreal sandwich shop has been forced to swap its soda
articles.summary: Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has changed suppliers for its black cherry soda.

blocks.text: Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has stopped serving the iconic US-made black cherry soda that has been a fixture at the restaurant for decades.
The sandwich shop had struggled to maintain supply of the cola for the last eight years as the distributor cut back production due to the rising cost of aluminium.
But it didn't expect the cans to vanish permanently. Now it has switched to a locally-made version, which the venue's customers have largely embraced.
Video by Eloise Alanna

articles.title: Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that…

blocks.text: Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.

Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.

“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”

Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.
During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.

He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.
The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.

blocks.caption: Tan Dhesi asked Andy Burnham whether he backed the 2030 commitment to defence spending at Wednesday’s PMQs. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: “There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”

Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”

blocks.caption: Javier Milei threatened oil sanctions against firms planning to exploit oil close to the islands.  Photograph: Mariana Nedelcu/Reuters

blocks.text: His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.

He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.

articles.title: Watch: Moment 64-year-old Nepali woman is found alive in mud-buried home
articles.summary: Chandika Shrestha was airlifted to hospital after spending more than 10 days in her partially buried house.

blocks.text: More than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud tore through a Himalayan valley in Nepal, rescuers continue to find survivors.

Chandika Shrestha, a 64-year-old woman, was discovered alive on the fourth floor of her partially buried house in the Nuwakot district by Nepal's Armed Police Force on 5 September, according to Reuters.
She was airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment, Reuters reported.

articles.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
articles.summary:
Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffick drugs

An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for…

blocks.text: An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.
The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.
Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.
The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.
Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.
According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK
articles.summary:
US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands

Donald Trump…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.
It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.
But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.

Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.

The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.

Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.

An uneasy peace has reined in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their less than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.

This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?
Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.

Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past.

The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.
And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.
In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.

“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”

Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.

It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.
Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.

Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.

He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.

The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.
Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.
Turbulence under Trump

But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.

Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.

This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.

But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.
“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”

In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.

He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.

Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.

But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

articles.title: PVL: PLDT stays focused amid noise as title defense hits rough patch
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines— Defending champion PLDT got the brunt of criticism on social media after absorbing back-to-back losses in the PVL Invitational Conference. After sweeping 13 games en route to…

blocks.text: Savi Davison and the PLDT High Speed Hitters during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference. –MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net
MANILA, Philippines— Defending champion PLDT got the brunt of criticism on social media after absorbing back-to-back losses in the PVL Invitational Conference.
After sweeping 13 games en route to back-to-back titles in the PVL on Tour and Invitational last year, PLDT lost two of its first three games in its title defense.

Savi Davison, however, came to the rescue, dropping 32 points as the High Speed Hitters revived their title hopes with a 25-16, 25-22, 23-25, 25-20 win over Farm Fresh on Friday at Smart Araneta Coliseum.
Aware of the outside noise, coach Rald Ricafort is trying to ease the pressure by focusing on one game at a time rather than defending their title.

“The defending champion tag isn’t really relevant to us this conference because it just adds hype and becomes a distraction,” said PLDT coach Rald Ricafort in Filipino. “What’s more important for us is how we responded after the losses to Nxled and Vietnam, which were really tough for us, especially because we didn’t have much time to recover mentally.”

“I told them before the game that if that’s the lesson we’re going to get from this conference, then we have to maximize it. There are so many distractions outside of the game, but this is our job, so we really have to stay focused,” he added.

blocks.caption: PLDT High Speed Hitters' Savi Davison during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference.

blocks.text: PLDT High Speed Hitters’ Savi Davison during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference. –MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net
Team captain Kath Arado, who had 24 digs, said the High Speed Hitters have also learned to lean on one another amid the criticism.

“Honestly, you can’t really avoid it because social media is huge now and fans are really invested in volleyball. Personally, I’m not really active on social media, so that helps me avoid the noise,” said Arado in Filipino.
“It also helps that we have our coaches handling the technical side. We check on each other whenever we see each other and ask, ‘How are you?’ From there, we can tell if everyone is doing okay.”

“But what we really want to build is our relationship as a team. Whatever we hear outside or whatever happens within the team, we need to stay together. We’ll just listen to what the coaches tell us because that’s what will help us grow as a team,” she added.
Ricafort also credited the squad’s growth after three seasons together, particularly in handling adversity.
Kath Arado and Savi Davison on PLDT’s final elimination game against Creamline. #PVL2026 @inquirersports pic.twitter.com/H4bdXo4WT8 — Lance Agcaoili (@LanceAgcaoilINQ) September 4, 2026

“The team is definitely growing, and credit to all the teams because the games have been really tough. I think the biggest growth I’ve seen from us is that we’re now able to pinpoint the technical things we need to fix. Before, there were still a lot of differences among the players, but now we’re more solid even when we lose,” the PLDT coach said.

“We’re already at the point where we need to focus on growing as volleyball players. We really want this conference, but because of what happened, we weren’t able to get the games and results we wanted. It’s not over yet, though. We still have to fight until Tuesday,” he added.
PLDT hopes to stay in finals contention against Creamline on Sunday.

“They’re champions, they’ve been together for a long time, and they know each other really well. They’re a tough team to play against, but that’s our job. If we want to win, we have to work harder and stay focused,” Arado said.

“Creamline won’t give us an easy win. It’s not going to be like previous conferences where we could just expect to win. We have to think that we’re back to zero. We won today, but now we’re back to zero. We have to keep working and study them.”

articles.title: VP Sara's 2 ex-security officers, alleged bagman dropped as witnesses
articles.summary: MANILA- The House prosecution has dropped plans to present two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s former security officers and alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga as witnesses in her impeachment…

blocks.text: MANILA- The House prosecution has dropped plans to present two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s former security officers and alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga as witnesses in her impeachment trial, saying evidence already presented is sufficient to support allegations of misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds.

House impeachment team adviser and spokesperson Ace Barbers identified the two former security officers as Col. Raymund Dante Lachica and Col. Dennis Nolasco, who have both figured in testimonies on the handling of Duterte’s confidential funds at the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).

“The three allegations in this article have already been substantiated by the previous witnesses na iniharap, ‘yun nga ’yung sinasabi natin sa misuse, misappropriation, at saka irregular liquidation (presented on the misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds),” Barbers said during an online press briefing Friday.

“Sa prosecution panel, with the witnesses na iniharap, napatunayan na po natin ’yan (The prosecution panel had already proven that with the witnesses already presented) … So there is no need for additional witnesses like Col. Lachica, Col. Nolasco, and Madriaga,” he added.
Acosta testified as a hostile prosecution witness that Duterte instructed her to turn over four PHP125-million tranches, or a total of PHP500 million in OVP confidential funds, to Lachica.
She also disclaimed personal knowledge of how the money was ultimately distributed after turning it over to him.
Nolasco, meanwhile, was linked to DepEd’s confidential funds through the earlier House testimony of former DepEd SDO Edward Fajarda.

Fajarda testified during House proceedings that he turned over three PHP37.5-million confidential fund releases, totaling PHP112.5 million, to Nolasco upon Duterte’s instruction when she was education secretary.
Madriaga had been considered a potentially significant prosecution witness after identifying himself during House impeachment proceedings as Duterte’s former aide and alleged bagman.

In a sworn testimony before the House Committee on Justice in April, Madriaga claimed that he personally handled and distributed the first PHP125 million in OVP confidential funds released in December 2022 and disposed of the entire amount in less than 24 hours.

He alleged that he delivered bags containing millions of pesos to several locations upon Duterte’s instruction and implicated Lachica and Nolasco in the alleged movement of the money. Duterte has denied Madriaga’s allegations.

Despite Madriaga’s earlier inclusion among prospective witnesses, Barbers said the prosecution now believes his testimony, along with those of Lachica and Nolasco, would no longer be necessary given the evidence already on record.
The prosecution will instead proceed with its remaining witnesses as it seeks to complete its presentation of evidence on the confidential fund charge.

The witnesses are Fajarda and his wife, DepEd Assistant Secretary Sunshine Charry Fajarda; Philippine Statistics Authority Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande; Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay; and Commission on Audit official Bresilio Sabaldan.
The Senate impeachment court has issued subpoenas for the five to appear as prosecution witnesses in the Sept. 7 to 9 trial proceedings.

Edward Fajarda’s personal appearance, however, could still be dispensed with because of his medical condition if the prosecution and defense agree to stipulate on the matters his testimony is intended to establish.

The prosecution is targeting Sept. 9 to finish presenting evidence on Article I, which covers the alleged misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of PHP612.5 million in confidential funds. (PNA)

articles.title: Nick Kyrgios gets month ban for cocaine, enters treatment program
articles.summary: SYDNEY–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios was cleared Friday to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for using cocaine and entering a treatment program. The 31-year-old, who reached the final…

blocks.text: FILE–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios reacts during the Australian Open first-round (AO1) singles match at Rod Laver Arena in Melbourne on January 14, 2026. (Photo by DAVID GRAY / AFP)
SYDNEY–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios was cleared Friday to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for using cocaine and entering a treatment program.
The 31-year-old, who reached the final at Wimbledon in 2022, failed a doping test during an ATP event in Mallorca on June 22.
He was provisionally suspended on August 4 by the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA), admitting he made “a huge mistake”.
In a statement Friday, the doping agency said Kyrgios had explained his use of the drug occurred socially during a night out before he was due to play in Mallorca.
The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory, who found his explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.
“As a result, the ITIA accepted that Kyrgios’ use of cocaine was outside of competition,” the ITIA said.
Under WADA rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be reduced to one month if an individual commits to a treatment program.
“Kyrgios has entered into a treatment programme,” the ITIA added.
“As such, the player’s suspension will end on September 3, 2026, subject to completion of the program. Prize-money and ranking points from the Mallorca event will be forfeited.”
Boasting a big serve and booming ground strokes, Kyrgios has won seven singles titles on the ATP Tour and rose to a high of 13 in the world in 2016. He is now ranked 918.
His finest performance was on the grass at Wimbledon in 2022, when he reached the championship match, losing in four sets to Novak Djokovic.
Despite his natural talents that is as good as it got, with a series of injuries taking their toll.
He has had numerous surgeries, the most serious a complete reconstruction of his right wrist in 2024.
The Australian last played as a wildcard entry in the men’s doubles at Wimbledon in July this year, when he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.
Kyrgios was contrite when the news of his cocaine use emerged last month.
“I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” he posted on Instagram at the time. “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.
“I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me.
“I know the example this sets and I’m deeply disappointed in myself.”
